<!-- https://it-rat.com/two-sites.html -->

# Two sites, one control plane, no VPN

> Sites reach one hub over outbound HTTPS through one narrow door: every site by name, one policy everywhere, and a quiet site never mistaken for a dead one.

A team with agents in more than one place wants one view of what they spend and one place to set what they may do, and it does not want to install and run a VPN to get it. **Here the sites reach the hub over ordinary outbound HTTPS, through one narrow door, each with a key that names it.** One script on the hub, one command per site, four variables at each site's gateway, and every site shows up by name, obeys the same policy within seconds and stays visible while it is quiet.

## One hub, a gateway at every site.

**The hub** is the cluster that runs the control plane, the policy plane and its store. **A site** is wherever agents run: another cluster, a single box, a machine in an office. Each site keeps its own gateway, so every model call is still priced, budgeted and policy-checked next to the agent that makes it, and nothing about a call waits on a round trip to the hub.

What travels to the hub is what a gateway already produces: its telemetry, and its questions to the policy plane. It travels out of the site, over HTTPS, to one public entry on the hub. Nothing at the site accepts a connection from outside, and nothing at the hub is reachable except that entry.

**The entry is deliberately narrow.** It is a small proxy with a free certificate in front of the hub's planes, and it routes exactly the eight paths a remote gateway calls. Everything else answers 404 at the edge, the console included, so the entry cannot become a second way into the parts an operator uses.

One of the eight lets a site's gateway read back what its own runs have spent, so a restart or a move to another hub does not start every run at zero. It reads only that site's runs, and after a move the site's new key must carry the same site name the old hub recorded. It was measured on release binaries behind a stand-in for the entry, not yet behind the real one on a live hub.

## Three steps.

### Open the entry on the hub

One script applies the entry, waits for the cloud to hand it an address, derives a name for that address, waits until both certificates are issued, and prints the two addresses a site needs. It is not part of the default install: a cluster that never runs it publishes nothing new.

```
# on the hub, from the cluster launcher
./hub/up.sh
```

### Give each site its own keys

One command per site mints two keys: one the control plane accepts only for pushing and reading, bound to that site's name, and one the policy plane accepts for reading decisions. It writes them to a file only the operator can read and prints no secret. Asked again for a site that already has keys, it refuses rather than minting a second pair.

```
# on the hub, once per site
./hub/add-site.sh warehouse-east
```

### Point the site's gateway at the hub

At the site, four variables on the gateway: where the control plane is and its key, where the policy plane is and its key. That is the whole change. Calls keep flowing through the same gateway, and from then on its spend appears at the hub under the site's name and its calls are decided by the hub's policy.

```
# on the site's gateway
TOKENFUSE_CLOUD_URL, TOKENFUSE_CLOUD_KEY
TOKENFUSE_WARDRYX_URL, TOKENFUSE_WARDRYX_KEY
```

## One view, one policy, and a quiet site that is not mistaken for a dead one.

**Every site by name.** The control plane lists each site with its spend, its calls and when it last reported, and labels every run with the site it came from.

**One policy, everywhere.** A rule written once at the hub applies at every site's gateway within seconds, and lifting it lifts it everywhere.

**A quiet site stays visible.** A gateway with nothing to report still sends a heartbeat every 30 seconds, so a site with no traffic and a site that has gone down no longer look the same.

**A cut link fails the way you chose.** A site that loses the hub keeps its telemetry queued and replays it when the link returns, and a kill issued at the hub stops a site's run within seconds.

## What the runs showed.

On 2026-09-26 and 2026-09-27, a hub of three virtual machines on a public cloud and a second site on a small box at home, the site reaching the hub only by outbound HTTPS:

- **From the public internet, the entry answered exactly as designed in 16 cases out of 16:** the site's calls with its key succeeded, a call with no key was refused, and the console and every other path answered 404 at the edge.

- **The hub script, certificates included, finished in 66 seconds.**

- **One policy written once at the hub** refused calls at both sites' gateways, and both answered again within 5 seconds of its removal.

- **With the home site cut off from the hub,** its gateway refused in 255 ms, the hub was untouched, and the site's telemetry was queued and replayed with nothing lost when the link came back.

- **A run killed through the hub** was refused at the site within 4 seconds.

- **With the site idle,** its last report at the hub aged from 34 to 286 seconds in four minutes without the heartbeat; with it, the hub kept hearing from the site, so the gap between reports stayed short.

## Where this sits.

[From zero to your first alert](https://it-rat.com/first-alert.html) is the single-machine start, [what runs where and what it costs](https://it-rat.com/what-runs-where.html) covers the cluster shapes a hub runs on, and [what is proven here](https://it-rat.com/what-is-proven.html) is where each of these runs is recorded. Everything named here is Apache-2.0 and runs on infrastructure you own.

## What people ask before connecting a second site

**Q: Does a site need a VPN or an open inbound port?**
No. A site only makes outbound HTTPS calls to one public entry on the hub, the same kind of connection an agent already makes to its model provider. Nothing at the site accepts a connection from outside, so there is no tunnel to run, no firewall hole to open and no client to install on anyone's machine.

**Q: Does every model call now travel through the hub?**
No. Each site keeps its own gateway, and the call goes from that gateway straight to the provider, priced and budgeted next to the agent that made it. What reaches the hub is the gateway's telemetry and its questions to the policy plane, not the prompts and not the provider traffic.

**Q: How does the hub know which site it is talking to?**
From the key the site pushed with. Each site gets its own pair of keys, bound to its name, and the hub never takes a site's word about who it is. That also means a copied key is that site, so the key file belongs wherever the site's other secrets live.

**Q: What happens at a site when the link to the hub drops?**
What you configured. With the policy plane set to fail closed, the site's gateway refuses calls until the hub is back, which is what a governed fleet should do. Its telemetry is kept in a queue meanwhile and sent when the link returns; in our run nothing was lost.

**Q: How do I tell a quiet site from a dead one?**
By its heartbeat. A gateway with nothing to report still checks in every 30 seconds by default, so the hub shows when each site last reported whether or not it had traffic. Without the heartbeat, an idle site in our run looked nearly five minutes stale; with it, the hub kept hearing from the idle site.

**Q: What does the public entry cost?**
The software costs nothing. The entry is a load balancer, and your cloud bills it by the hour for as long as it exists, at that cloud's published rate. It is not part of the default install, so a cluster that never opens it pays nothing extra, and taking it down with the launcher's own script removes the billed part first.


---

<!-- https://it-rat.com/what-is-proven.html -->

# What is proven and what is not

> How to read a validation claim: what was measured on this stack, what the measurement does not cover, and the conclusions we published and had to withdraw.

Governance software is in the awkward position of asking to be trusted about trust. So this page is not a scoreboard. It is the method: what a measurement on this stack actually established, what it deliberately does not cover, and the conclusions we published and then had to take back. **The withdrawn ones are the useful part**, because a project that only records its successes is a project whose claims cannot be checked.

## A number that cannot fail is not evidence.

The single most useful habit in this project came out of a boring observation: a check that cannot produce a red result will report green forever, and nobody will notice, because green is what everyone expected.

So the rule is that a passing measurement is only worth reading next to a run where the same measurement fails. The record plane's durability sweep is the cleanest example. Eight hundred million shard ticks across four hundred thousand seeded runs, roughly twelve million injected crashes, zero durability violations. On its own that number is worth very little. The same sweep is then run again with the simulated disk allowed to lie about flushing, and **17,869 of 20,000 seeds fail**. The first number is only evidence because the second one exists.

The rule stopped being about measurements and became about the checks themselves on 2026-08-09, when a harness was put into twenty of the twenty-six repositories that plants each gate's own fault and requires the failure. **Eight gates could not produce one.** Every one had the same silhouette: a counter or a scan reading an empty subject as a clean one, so renaming a directory turned a check on eleven things into a check on nothing while the wording stayed confident. One of them held the only promise its repository makes to a stranger, that a local demo does not publish a money plane onto whatever network the laptop is on, and it was judging zero addresses.

It keeps earning its place. On 2026-08-20 the same harness was pointed at a dependency check written that morning, and reported it toothless: the check read as "every crate has its own justification" and could not hold that, because a comment covering a pair of crates is one decision and deleting a comment in the middle merely merges two groups. The claim was narrowed to what it actually holds, in the script, in the invariant and in the case. Narrowing the claim is the cheaper half of that; the expensive half is that nothing else would have said so.

The same shape applies to everything below. Where a claim has no companion failure, it says so.

## Seven claims and what each one stops short of.

Every figure here was produced by a run with a command and a date behind it, recorded in that repository's own validation file. The line under each is not a disclaimer, it is part of the claim.

### 120 processes killed mid-write, not one acknowledged record lost

Forty each on apfs, ext4 and xfs, killed with SIGKILL while writing, and every sequence number that had been reported as acknowledged survived. That is the sentence the whole design rests on, and it was tested by something other than the simulator that was written to believe it.

### About 2,450 decisions per second per pod, at a p50 of 3.2 ms

Measured on live five-node clusters on three clouds between 25 and 27 July 2026, with no throughput cliff out to 256 concurrent callers on dedicated cores, and a freeze reaching live traffic in one round trip. Every decision is audited rather than sampled, at about 426 bytes each.

### All 500 questions of a public benchmark, not a fixture we wrote

Recall was measured on LongMemEval-S in full on 2026-07-30, with every turn of every question's history ingested as its own episode, 246,738 in total, and no LLM anywhere in the loop. The per-question records are published alongside the numbers so the table can be recomputed rather than believed.

### 25,586 real Linux binaries scanned, plus a live TLS endpoint

Not a fixture directory: an actual filesystem's worth of ELF binaries, a real container image, and a live handshake against a public endpoint whose certificate was correctly flagged as quantum-vulnerable under the NCSC migration timeline.

### Proven on a five-node cluster, then attacked the same night

Every plane answered, the shared event log bound across nodes, and an agent frozen from the browser stayed frozen after the policy plane's pod was restarted. Then the same cluster was attacked, and four real holes came out: a pod that labelled itself as the console deleted a freeze using a literal development bearer while the console still displayed the agent as frozen, secrets were readable in plaintext straight out of the datastore, the kubelet API was open to the internet on every node, and the gateway never asked the policy plane anything.

### A box behind a home router governed two clouds at once, then took sixteen failures

On 2026-09-17 the single-machine installer went onto a small Debian 13 box behind carrier-grade NAT, its gateway published only on a tunnel address. Two clusters standing in for a customer's, one in AWS and one in GCP, joined the tunnel and ran their agents through the box to the real Anthropic API: seventeen calls each, then a 402 on the eighteenth, interleaved on one event log. The box told the clouds apart by key and by identity, froze one of them with a single policy while the other kept running, and ran the FinOps crew through a second door of its own until a monthly cap stopped it. Both cloud accounts were empty afterwards, by direct query, and the day cost USD 0.18.

### One cluster on three kinds of processor, then a second site with no VPN

On 2026-09-26 the cluster launcher built one cluster from AMD, Intel and Ampere machines across three zones, in 13 minutes 46 seconds from bare VMs. Every plane moved onto the two Arm nodes in 49 seconds and back onto x86 in 111, the policy database's volume following it. A rolling upgrade under a probe asking every quarter second lost 1 gateway probe of 1,152 logged, and three later rolling restarts lost none of 825. That night and the next morning, a hub of three cloud VMs took a second site at home that reached it only over outbound HTTPS: one policy written at the hub refused calls at both sites, a run killed at the hub was refused at the site within 4 seconds, and a cut link failed closed at the site in 255 ms, its telemetry replayed afterwards with nothing lost. On 2026-09-27, on a three-node cluster at home, a delegated agent revoked mid-run was refused 2.2 seconds later, the OpenAI-compatible door priced and budgeted real calls, the console's own copilot ran through the stack's gateway under a budget, and the network sensor on an x86 kernel caught an agent reaching PyPI directly.

## Sixteen ways to break it, and what each one did.

Each tile is one injected failure on the box above, with the customer's agents still calling. The colour is the outcome, not the severity: green held as designed, red found something, amber found something that was fixed on main within a day and has shipped in the single-machine release since stack-single v1.1.6.

The run froze at step seven and no plane said anything, at five seconds or at sixty. Absence was undetected; a stalled-run detector now exists.

The agent timed out, resumed afterwards under the same run, and the box saw nothing at all. Same gap, same fix.

Every call refused 403 in 0.3 s, fail-closed, one dependency event per call; the first call after the restart allowed.

Decisions continued from memory, which is right. The health check stayed 200 and a policy write hung instead of refusing; a readiness route and a 3 s deadline followed.

Egress blocked: 502 in 53 ms with an event. A retired model id: 404 with an event. A revoked key: 401 passed through and no event, by design.

Three identical tool calls among the last ten: 402 loop_detected before the provider was asked, at zero spend.

Not a loop by that definition, so the budget caught it instead. Written down so nobody files it as a bug.

The gateway kept enforcing; three calls' telemetry were dropped rather than queued and the fleet view kept the hole. A bounded replay queue followed.

Eight refusals under distinct runs inside two seconds after the hour's twentieth mail: one notice saying eight, all eight lines on the log.

Twenty-eight minutes of high and critical events with no mail and no second notice. A critical now passes the ceiling and the rest is summarised every ten minutes.

It caught up from its cursor, 52 records verified, no gap; the console's own lines refused as foreign, as designed.

The gateway came back exited and stayed down: Docker bound the port before the tunnel held the address. The installer now orders the two; the second reboot was back in 40 s.

Every volume survived. The gateway's in-memory run and unit ledgers did not (26 runs to zero, the month restarted), so a monthly cap could be spent twice. The month is now re-seeded from the control plane.

One byte flipped in a copy of a sealed pack: NOT VERIFIED. The untouched pack verified. The record does what it is for.

Accepted with no event while delegation verification was off. The record holds 32; both doors now refuse more, before anything is forwarded.

An hour forward, then NTP back: nothing changed on the tunnel or in the calls within three minutes. The clock that would matter is the box's own, not injected.

Two things the tiles do not show. The control plane's own incidents never reached the notifier or the record on the released installer, because the control plane could not create its events file and said nothing about it; the installer now creates the file for it, and the images say so at startup. And the crew's runner reported its own estimate as spent, five times under what the gateway settled. Both are in the repositories' validation files with their dates.

## Three things we published and had to withdraw.

Each of these was wrong in a way that a reader could have acted on, which is the only kind worth listing.

We published that throughput collapses past 64 concurrent callers and that a fleet should be designed against that limit. **It does not.** Neither dedicated-core cloud loses any throughput out to 256 concurrent on either chip generation; only latency grows. The collapse was a property of a shared-vCPU instance, which is to say it was a noisy neighbour rather than the software. The retraction is published next to the claim it replaces rather than quietly replacing it.

Our first comparison put one hyperscaler 62% ahead of the other. That gap was a chip generation wearing a cloud costume: the faster run used a newer instance family because the equivalent part on the other cloud was quota-blocked on a new account. **On matched silicon the two are 1.2% apart** and their p50 latencies differ by a hundredth of a millisecond.

We predicted that shared storage would be expensive on both hyperscalers. It is expensive on one and negligible on the other: the same 5 GiB event log is USD 1.80 a month on one and USD 194.56 on the other, because the second sells the capacity by the terabyte. The prediction was wrong in one direction and right in the other, **by a factor of 108**, and the correction is the more useful number.

There is a fourth worth naming that is not a number at all. Pointed at real object stores, one storage adapter failed three separate ways while its entire test suite was green: it sent two `Host` headers, it could not read a response from a peer that closes TLS abruptly, and it sent one cloud's headers to another cloud that refuses them. All three had the same cause. **The fakes in the tests were written from the same reading of the same documentation as the client**, so they agreed with the client's mistakes. The fix was not three fixes; it was teaching the fake to refuse what a compliant server refuses.

## What nobody has established yet.

This list is deliberately visible rather than tidy, and it is the section worth reading first if you are evaluating rather than browsing.

- **One machine has lost power, once.** Everything else about durability is established against process death. On 2026-09-23 a small box running the single-machine install had its plug pulled with two agents calling: it came back by itself, every container restarted, the record's packs from before and after the cut both verified, and no event line was torn. One cut on one box is a data point, not a claim about hardware in general.

- **No external audit of the cryptographic layer.** The primitives match their published vectors and two independent implementations of the verifier agree, which is a different and weaker claim than somebody outside this project having reviewed it.

- **Not every shipped pre-production drill has been fired at a real gateway.** They were written after the campaigns that produced the published "no gaps" result, and that result covers only the drills that were fired.

- **No years of simulated time, and no second I/O backend** to compare the first against.

- **The detectors have not been driven at production scale.** They fire correctly on seeded fleets and against real event data, which is not the same as an estate's worth of identities.

- **The federation completeness rule is specified and its transport is unbuilt.** The rule exists; the wires do not.

- **The figures on this site go stale, and did again this month.** 116 of them name a source repository, the command that produces them and the date somebody last ran it. A gate refuses a service page that states a number nobody owns, and the root pages are not in its scope. That gate cannot tell you an owned number is still true, and on 2026-08-20, when eleven were owned, five of them were not: two test counts out by six and ten, a detector count out by two, a trap count out by three, and a release a whole version behind. None was wrong when written. Re-measuring now costs one command rather than an afternoon, which is the actual fix; being more careful was never available.

Every figure quoted anywhere on this site or in these repositories is meant to carry three things: what produced it, when, and what it is a claim about. A measurement stays true about its moment and is not automatically true about the present, which is why a date is part of a number rather than decoration on it. If you find one here without those, that is a defect and worth telling us about.

## The same questions work on anybody's claims.

- **Has the check ever produced a red result?** A suite with no demonstrated failure reports the same thing whether or not it is working.

- **What is the limit stated next to the number?** If a claim arrives without one, the limit exists and somebody chose not to write it down.

- **Was the benchmark theirs or the field's?** A benchmark written by the vendor measures agreement with the vendor's assumptions.

- **Which reading of the metric is being quoted?** Most retrieval and accuracy numbers have a generous reading and a strict one, and only one of them gets printed.

- **What did the run not cover?** A cluster run that proves deployment shape is often quoted as though it proved throughput.

- **Has anything been withdrawn?** A project with no retractions has either published nothing checkable or has not checked.

- **Can somebody outside the project verify it?** Evidence you have to be trusted about is a statement, not evidence.

## Where this sits.

The numbers behind every claim here live in each repository's own validation file, next to the command that produced it. [What runs where and what it costs](https://it-rat.com/what-runs-where.html) is where most of the cluster figures come from, [one incident, end to end](https://it-rat.com/one-incident-end-to-end.html) is the behaviour they describe, and [the guides index](https://it-rat.com/guides.html) has the rest. All of it is Apache-2.0, including the write-ups that record what went wrong.

## What people ask about the evidence

**Q: What makes a validation number worth anything?**
A companion run where the same check fails. A check that cannot produce a red result reports green forever and nobody notices, because green is what everyone expected. The durability sweep is the clearest case here: zero violations across four hundred thousand seeded runs means very little on its own, and means a great deal beside the same sweep with a lying disk, where 17,869 of 20,000 seeds fail.

**Q: What has been measured on real infrastructure rather than in a simulator?**
Process-kill durability across three filesystems, policy-plane throughput on live five-node clusters on three clouds, recall on a full public benchmark rather than a fixture, a crypto scan over 25,586 real binaries and a live TLS endpoint, an adversarial pass against a running cluster that found four real holes, and, on 2026-09-17, the whole stack on a small box behind a home router governing agents in AWS and GCP at the same time through sixteen injected failures. Each has a limit published beside it, and the limit is part of the claim rather than a disclaimer under it.

**Q: What has this project got wrong and had to withdraw?**
Three published conclusions. That throughput collapses past 64 concurrent callers, which turned out to be a shared-vCPU instance rather than the software. That one hyperscaler was 62% faster, which was a chip generation rather than a cloud. And a prediction that shared storage would be expensive on both, which was wrong on one by a factor of 108. All three retractions are published next to the claims they replace. A project with no retractions has either published nothing checkable or has not checked.

**Q: What has not been established yet?**
Power has been pulled from a running machine once, on one small box, so durability is still mainly a claim about process death rather than power loss. There has been no external audit of the cryptographic layer. Not every shipped pre-production drill has been fired at a real gateway; the ledger records the ones that have. The detectors have not been driven at production scale, and the federation completeness rule is specified with its transport unbuilt.

**Q: Why publish the things that went wrong?**
Because a repository whose history only records its successes is a repository whose claims cannot be checked. The deployment ledger for the cluster now holds 159 entries and 82 of them are our own mistakes rather than platform behaviour, and that ratio is what makes the other classifications worth believing.


---

<!-- https://it-rat.com/agent-tooling-compared.html -->

# Three shapes of agent tooling

> The controls that answer before a call: what each one does, what it does not do yet, and how to check it.

Watching an agent is useful after the fact. A budget, a policy and an egress check have to answer before the action, because by the time the invoice or the incident review arrives, the money is spent. The stack puts those answers in the path of the call. Each one is a decision that either happened or did not, and the rest of this page says what each one does and how to check it.

## Watch it happen.

The same call, sent twice: once with the control plane in the path and once without it. Pick what the agent is trying to do and see where each one ends up.

**The copy is never the control.** Every event also goes sideways into the dashboard, and it arrives after the thing already happened. What decides the call is whether something stood on the wire itself with the authority to stop it.

## Where the stack answers.

Each place answers a different question, and each one leaves a record you can check.

***A**the budget*

### A ceiling on every run

A gateway sits in front of the model calls. It gives every run a budget, prices each call against it before the call goes out, and answers 402 on the one that would cross the line, without forwarding it. Spend is reserved before the call and settled after it. The rest of the spend story, including the cache, the model router and the FOCUS export, is on the TokenFuse room.

**Answers:** may this call spend more money right now?

**Limit:** a budget governs spend. It does not judge whether an answer was good; that is measured in Verdryx.

***B**the policy point*

### Allow, deny or hold, before the action

Wardryx is the decision an agent asks for before it acts. It answers allow, deny or hold. A hold waits for a person, who grants it with a signed approval token. The token is bound to the agent, the run, the tool set and, where the policy names them, the arguments of the call. Holds nobody has decided are swept and reported, not left parked.

**Answers:** may this action happen, and if not yet, who has to say yes?

**Limit:** it decides the actions that reach it. The gateway and the egress plane are the other places that stand in the path.

***C**identity and the record*

### Whose action it was, and proof nothing is missing

Idryx keeps one identity graph for humans, keys and agents, so a delegation chain ends at a person. Trailryx keeps the record. Every answer it gives comes with a completeness proof, a short receipt that the rows shown are all the rows that match the question, and the verifier that checks it has no dependencies.

**Answers:** whose action was this, and can an auditor check that nothing is missing?

**Limit:** an agent with no attestation on record is flagged as a finding, so a chain is only as strong as what it can prove.

*and the planes around them*

### Planes that stand in the path and answer before the action

A gateway that gives every run a budget and answers 402 the moment it is crossed. A policy plane the agent asks before acting, which can hold the expensive one for a person. An egress plane that decides the destination before anything leaves the machine. An identity graph that knows which human a key ultimately belongs to. A record built so that somebody who does not trust you can still check it is complete. Each one is a decision that either happened or did not.

**Not covered:** why the model wanted to do it. The governance events can export over OTLP into your tracing backend when an endpoint is set.

## Twelve controls, and how to check each one.

Every claim below says what makes it true and where to look, so it can be checked without trusting this page. The first six show up on a single request. The second six are the ones a regulated organisation asks about before it signs anything.

### It answers before the call, not after it

The gateway prices every call against the run's budget and, on the one that would cross it, replies 402 with a stable error and never forwards the request to the provider. The policy plane answers allow, deny or hold before the action, and never performs the action itself. Neither of those is a notification.

### The agent stays where it is, and does not have to be declared at all

Integration is one base URL. Nothing is rewritten, nothing is redeployed, no SDK enters the agent. Underneath, an eBPF sensor finds agents that nobody registered, along with the model providers they reach.

### The record answers to somebody who does not trust you

Every query comes back with a completeness proof: a short receipt, checkable on its own, that the rows shown are all the rows matching the question. The verifier that checks it carries zero dependencies, so an auditor can read the whole of it before believing any of it.

### The guardrails are themselves fired, in CI, before release

Adversarial scenarios run against a real gateway with a fake provider behind it. Burn the budget and require the 402. Ask for a forbidden tool and require the 403. Present a forged delegation chain and require it to be rejected. The exit codes differ on purpose, so the pipeline can tell a genuine hole in the defence from a broken test rig.

### Governance is not behind a licence key

Apache-2.0 throughout, the console included. Nothing in the governance layer sits behind a licence key, a seat count or a tier.

### An alert is a coordinate, and a session is not an authority

The mail that wakes somebody at night carries one link into a view, and never a button that acts. A link that acts is a permission held by everyone who received or forwarded the mail, and security gateways follow links before a human reads the sentence next to them. In the console, ten commands take a fresh passkey assertion bound to that command and its arguments, rather than to whoever is signed in: a kill, a budget change, an approval, issuing or revoking a tunnel peer, revoking a delegation, closing a retained reservation, setting a unit's monthly cap, and stopping an agent or lifting its ban.

### Post-quantum sits inside the agent loop, and it has legal dates attached

The scan grades each key, certificate and algorithm it finds for quantum risk and emits a CBOM in the CycloneDX format. The grades are scored against the published CNSA timeline: new systems by 2027, legacy migration by 2030, everything by 2035.

### A person can be erased without breaking the audit trail

Every payload is encrypted under its own key, so erasing a person means destroying their keys. The content becomes unrecoverable, every earlier proof still verifies, and the record itself carries the fact that an erasure happened. Nothing is re-encrypted afterwards, and records written later are reached by the same erasure.

### A refusal is a pure function, so an auditor can rerun it

No model anywhere in the decision path. Given the same policy set and the same request, the answer is always the same, which means a refusal from six months ago can be reproduced today in front of somebody who wants to see it. The policy primitives are deliberately dull: deny a tool, deny an unattested agent, cap the number of steps, restrict the destinations, require a human above a sum.

### The kill switch does not run through the thing it kills

The out-of-band control is a phone and a watch. The signing key is generated inside the device's secure element and never leaves it, not even to the app. A kill is signed on the device and the control plane verifies that signature before it acts, so the stop still works when the agent's own host is precisely what is misbehaving or compromised.

### Changing a limit goes through code review, like changing a firewall rule

Budgets, agent passports and policies are ordinary Terraform resources: in version control, reviewed in a pull request the way an IAM policy or a security group is, planned before they apply, and diffed when somebody has changed them outside the process.

### The money is counted per resolved case, not per token

Token spend says how much was burned. It does not say whether the burning bought anything. The quality plane joins the cost trace to your own outcome tags and returns the price of a resolved case beside the price of an escalated one and an abandoned one, which is the same arithmetic a finance function already applies to everything else it funds.

### And what it costs, since none of this is free

Standing in the request path buys the refusal and charges latency for it, on every call, including the overwhelming majority that were always going to be fine. It also forces a decision: what happens when the control plane itself is unreachable. Both launchers set the gateway to fail closed when the policy plane is unreachable. In the failure drill of 2026-09-17, with the policy plane down, the gateway refused every governed call in about 0.3 s. **That is the trade, and it is named here on purpose.**

## Where each part of the stack answers.

A budget per run, and a 402 the moment it is crossed. The call is refused before the provider sees it.

Allow, deny, or hold for a human, asked before the action, with a hard ceiling that outranks approvals.

Every destination decided before anything leaves, and every redirect hop decided again.

One identity graph for humans, keys, service accounts and agents, so "who did this" ends at a person.

A record nobody can quietly change or shorten, where every answer carries a proof that it is complete.

Quality as the denominator: cost per correctly resolved case, rather than per token.

Fire drills for the guardrails themselves, asserting the 402 and the 403 in CI.

Decides what is worth waking a human for tonight, and mails it with one link and no button.

All of it is Apache-2.0 and runs on infrastructure you own. The governance planes export over OTLP when an endpoint is set, into whatever tracing backend you already run. **Governance data can sit in your observability stack. The enforcement decision is made on the call.**

## What people ask when they have already bought one

**Q: Do we have to drop our tracing to use this?**
No, and we would advise against it. Tracing answers a question this stack does not: why the model wanted to do the thing. Keep it, put the gateway in front of the model calls in shadow mode for a week, then turn on caps where the outliers are.

**Q: Why describe products by shape instead of naming them?**
Because a named comparison is wrong the week after a vendor ships a feature, and a reader who already runs one of these can map the shape to their tool in a second. The shapes are also more useful: they say what a category of tool can and cannot do architecturally, which is the part that does not change with a release note.


---

<!-- https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html -->

# Security by design

> An agent can be persuaded, so its controls sit where persuasion cannot reach. Eight design decisions in the stack, and what happened when we broke each one.

An AI agent can be talked into anything, so everything that keeps it safe has to sit where persuasion cannot reach. Security in a stack for agents is decided by three things: where each decision sits, what happens when a part of the stack fails, and whether its record can prove itself. **These are the eight decisions we made, why we made them, and what happened when we broke each one on purpose.**

- [At a glance: the eight decisions](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#at-a-glance)

- [A refusal we did not count](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#intro)

- [Why security comes first](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#why-security-first)

- [The shortcuts agents usually run on](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#shortcuts)

- [1. The decision sits in the path](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#in-the-path)

- [2. No model in the decision](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#no-model-in-the-decision)

- [3. Every failure has a stated answer](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#stated-failure-answer)

- [4. An identity, not a key](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#identity-not-key)

- [5. Each part holds only what it needs](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#least-held)

- [6. A record that proves itself](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#self-proving-record)

- [7. It stays in your building](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#stays-in-your-building)

- [8. Every control is proven by breaking it](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#proven-by-breaking)

- [What we built](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#what-we-built)

- [Three things to try on Monday](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#monday)

## Eight decisions, one line each.

- [The decision sits in the path, before the action.](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#in-the-path) Identity, policy and budget are decided before the model provider hears a call, and a tool call the model asks for is judged before the agent can run it.

- [No model in the decision.](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#no-model-in-the-decision) Plain rules give the same answer to the same request every time; a model may add a risk signal that can hold a call, never allow or deny one.

- [Every failure has a stated answer.](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#stated-failure-answer) For every dependency we wrote down what happens next, and the installers ship the policy service's answer set to closed.

- [An identity, not a key.](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#identity-not-key) Each agent has its own identifier, a key speaks only for the identities bound to it, and a revocation wins.

- [Each part holds only what it needs.](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#least-held) The part that decides is not the part that enforces, the part that alerts can act on nothing, and the stop is a person behind a passkey.

- [A record that proves itself.](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#self-proving-record) Hash-chained, sealed, and checkable offline by somebody who has no reason to trust us.

- [It stays in your building.](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#stays-in-your-building) Self-hosted and Apache-2.0, with no account and no telemetry; what leaves through the stack is decided first.

- [Every control is proven by breaking it.](https://it-rat.com/security-by-design.html#proven-by-breaking) A check counts only after it has failed on a planted fault, and then we break the running system.

## A refusal we did not count.

On 14 October we hid an instruction for an AI agent inside a configuration note on a small network router, the kind of text an agent reads while doing an ordinary job. The model read it, said it looked like an injection, and did not follow it.

We were glad, and we did not count it.

A model that refused today can comply tomorrow, after an update, a different phrasing or a longer conversation. An agent is a program that chooses its next step by asking a model, and a model can be persuaded. Everything that keeps an agent safe therefore has to sit where persuasion cannot reach it: in the path of the call, decided by code that gives the same answer every time, and still saying no when part of the system is broken.

That sentence is most of our architecture. Each decision below came from one question, **what could an agent do with its credentials if somebody talked it into it**, and each was tested by breaking it.

## Why security comes first.

An agent holds three things a chatbot never did. A key to a model provider is a budget. Access to tools is the power to write, send and pay. A delegation from a person, which most agents acting for somebody carry, is that person's authority. The services we build sit in front of all three. They see every call an agent makes, which makes them the best place to stop a bad one and the most valuable thing in the building to attack.

Security was never one feature on our list; it was the condition every other feature had to meet. A budget that a retry loop can race past is not a budget, and a policy that switches itself off whenever its server restarts is a suggestion. An audit record that an administrator can quietly edit is a diary.

### What supervisors have started to write down

There is a plainer reason too. The first organisations to run agents at scale are banks, insurers and public bodies, and the people who supervise them have started writing down what they expect.

- The **Financial Stability Board**'s consultation report of 10 June 2026 lists steps financial institutions take to oversee agents: an individual identifier for each agent, actions that are prohibited or need human approval at checkpoints, dual authorisation above a certain value, and audit trails.

- On 3 July the **Monetary Authority of Singapore** and the industry published a white paper on governance checkpoints that verify and record an agent's proposed actions before it executes them.

- In August the UK's **National Cyber Security Centre** asked for every agent to have its own identity, and for technically enforced controls beside human oversight wherever the risk is higher.

- The **OWASP Top 10 for agentic applications** opens with goal hijack, tool misuse, and identity and privilege abuse.

Most of those lines describe a control that sits in the path of the action, the rest describe the evidence it leaves behind, and none of them describes a dashboard. How the decisions below line up with those texts is our reading of them, not a compliance claim.

## The shortcuts agents usually run on.

Most agents today run on a handful of shortcuts, and each one is reasonable on the day somebody takes it: a shared provider key in an environment variable, a dashboard of yesterday's spend, a system prompt that asks the model not to do certain things, a second model that reads the conversations and scores them. Then come the default that lets traffic through when the policy service is down, because an outage looks worse than a risk, the log the platform team can edit, and the stop link in an alert email.

Each of them moves the decision somewhere an agent, or a tired person at three in the morning, can get around it. The eight decisions below move it back.

| shortcut | decision instead | held by |
|---|---|---|
| A shared key | An identity per agent | 403 for a key posing as another |
| Yesterday's dashboard | A decision before the call | 402 before the provider hears it |
| A model scoring a model | Fixed rules, and the kernel | Same request, same answer |
| Open during an outage | Closed, chosen out loud | Refused from 2.5 s |
| An editable log | A hash-chained record | One flipped byte fails |
| A stop link in email | A stop behind a passkey | Journaled with its outcome |

## The decision sits in the path, before the action.

Every call an agent makes to a model passes through a gateway ([TokenFuse](https://it-rat.com/services/tokenfuse.html)), and three questions are answered before the provider hears it. Who is calling? May it do this? Can it afford it? A no arrives at once as an ordinary HTTP status: 401 when the caller has no identity, 403 when the action is refused, 402 when the budget is spent. A call refused there costs nothing. It never left.

The fourth question comes back with the model's answer: when the model asks for a tool call, may that call run? A refused one is withheld from the agent and replaced with a refusal.

In August, on a cluster in AWS with a real provider key behind the gateway, a request against a budget smaller than one call came back 402 with no request id from the provider, because the provider never saw it.

On 14 October, on a test box, the gateway refused the tool calls that untrusted text tried to reach: a command after a web page was read, a message out after a planted instruction, an email built from memory. The same day showed why the path matters more than the model. On the router from the opening, a tool call inside a streamed answer reached the agent unjudged, because only buffered answers were being checked. The release that shipped that night judges both.

A report after the call tells you what an agent already did. **A decision before the call is the one place where no is still cheap.**

## No model in the decision.

The policy point that answers allow, deny or hold ([Wardryx](https://it-rat.com/services/wardryx.html)) runs plain rules. A cost line above which a named person must approve. A hard ceiling no approval can pass. Tools an agent may never use, and domains it may reach. The detectors that look for excess privilege or an agent going around the gateway are fixed rules as well, and the sensor that watches outbound connections works inside the Linux kernel, without touching the application (both in [Idryx](https://it-rat.com/services/idryx.html)).

The same request under the same policy gets the same answer every time, which is what an auditor means by reproducible. It is also fast. On 13 September, thirty-four concurrent requests with different rights were decided correctly, 34 of 34, in 16 milliseconds, and one policy instance reached 27,210 decisions a second in runs of 3,000 decisions.

Putting a second model in charge of the first looks like a control and behaves like a second opinion. The text that persuaded one model can persuade the next, and their mistakes tend to travel together.

In our stack a model may add exactly one thing to a decision: a typed risk signal ([Typryx](https://it-rat.com/services/typryx.html)), the probability that a tool call destroys something, sends data out or moves money. **A signal can only hold a call for a person. It can never allow a call, and it can never deny one.**

## Every failure has a stated answer.

Parts of any system fail. A policy service restarts, a node dies, a site loses its link to the hub. For every dependency we wrote down what happens next, and for the policy service the installers ship that answer set to closed.

On 14 October we cut the policy service off from a running gateway for about a minute. From 2.5 seconds on, every call was refused with a 403 that named the closed failure mode, 126 of 155, and the gateway answered again 0.7 seconds after the link came back. In September a second site was cut from its hub: its gateway refused in 255 milliseconds, queued its telemetry and replayed it with nothing lost.

| failure | answer | measured |
|---|---|---|
| Policy service cut off | Refuses from 2.5 s; back 0.7 s after the link returns | 14 Oct 2026 |
| A site loses its hub | Refuses in 255 ms; telemetry queued and replayed | 26 Sep 2026 |
| Policy database pod deleted | Back in 17 s; pending approvals kept | 14 Oct 2026 |
| Five servers reset at once | Serving in 327 s, with the same state | 14 Oct 2026 |
| An unpriced model | Priced high, not waved through | by design |
| A misspelt security switch | Refuses to start | by design |

The same rule runs through the defaults. A model with no price on file is priced high rather than waved through. A call that does not say which run it belongs to is refused. Secret scanning that nobody configured blocks, and a security switch whose value the gateway cannot read stops it from starting.

Failing closed has a cost. We state it. During an outage some legitimate calls are refused. The alternative is that during an outage nothing is checked while every run still looks clean, and that is the outage an attacker waits for.

### A missing signal is not a clean one

The most useful thing the October tests found belonged to the same family. The risk signal from decision 2 arrives for each tool call. Above about 12 kilobytes of arguments the classifier handed over nothing, and a call with no signal was treated like a call with nothing to worry about. The same tool call was held for a person at 11,264 bytes and answered at 13,312. Twelve kilobytes sounds like a lot for one tool call, until you remember that padding a field costs an attacker nothing.

The fix was a rule about absence. The policy point can now be told what a missing signal means, and the rule our installers document says hold the call for a person. It was released the same afternoon, and on two clouds the same day the padded call was held. **A control that only judges what it can see has to decide, in advance, what it does about what it cannot.**

## An identity, not a key.

Each agent has its own identifier, and a key is bound to the identities it may speak for. On 14 October a key issued to one agent presented another agent's identity. The answer was 403 `identity_mismatch`, a high-severity event on the bus, and zero spend. A missing or unknown key gets 401.

When an agent acts for a person, it carries a short-lived token bound to its own key ([Vouchryx](https://it-rat.com/services/vouchryx.html)), so a stolen token is useless without that key. Delegation can only narrow on the way down a chain, never widen.

A revocation wins over whatever the token says about its own expiry: the gateway refuses the token once its next poll of the revocation list lands, every 12 seconds by default. On Google Cloud on 14 October, with the poll set to one second, a revoked delegation was refused 1.5 seconds later.

Agent tokens are the default now, not an option. In the shipped Docker Compose launcher (from stack-single 1.3.0, released 2026-10-19) the gateway and the MCP broker require an agent's own token, a static key is admitted only when its id is on a named list and is refused with 401 otherwise, and vouchryx, which issues the tokens, starts on every default box. The Kubernetes launcher does the same from 1.5.0. On a stack-single box one agent can be enrolled for a token so far; the others stay on the list until the registry takes more than one.

A key answers one question: does the caller know a secret. **An identity answers who is acting, for whom, with which rights, and how to take them away.**

## Each part holds only what it needs.

The service that decides is not the one that enforces. The one that tells people about incidents ([Heraldyx](https://it-rat.com/services/heraldyx.html)) holds no credential for any other service and can act on nothing, and its only way out is mail.

A mail never carries the stop, because mail security gateways open links before people do. The stop is a button in your own console ([Genaryx](https://it-rat.com/genaryx.html)), behind a fresh passkey, and every attempt that passes the passkey, carried out or refused, is written to the console's own journal with its outcome. Ten console commands that move money or authority work that way, from killing a run to changing a business unit's monthly cap.

Two recent changes follow the same idea. The newest change to the policy service makes every policy change made through its API name, on the event bus, the fingerprint of the key that made it, so "who changed the rules" has an answer that does not depend on anyone's memory. The alert service's new quiet hours and maintenance windows can hold an alert, but never a critical one. Both are in [what changed from 1 to 15 October](https://it-rat.com/changes-2026-10.html).

Separation of duties is the oldest control in banking, and here it means **one compromised part does not hand over the others.**

## A record that proves itself.

Decisions, refusals, stops and approvals go into append-only event logs in which each entry carries the hash of the one before it, and a record service ([Trailryx](https://it-rat.com/services/trailryx.html)) seals finished segments. Change one record and every seal after it stops matching, so an edit cannot hide in the middle: it has to rewrite everything after it. Signing the root is no longer missing: Trailryx signs sealed roots with Keyryx when its signer is set (from its 1.3.0 release), and since 2026-10-19 the stack-up and stack-k8s launchers set it by default, which has not run live yet. Keyryx also runs a witness that reads the event bus read-only and writes its findings to its own volume. The stack-single launcher runs that witness on the same host, as a separate user and volume, so it is not an outside party; it points the witness at no Trailryx record and leaves the root signer off, so a stack-single pack from the default install carries neither a root signature nor a witness yet. A witness off the host is not built.

The check runs offline, by somebody who has no reason to trust us. On Google Cloud in September a sealed record verified, and one flipped byte made it fail.

A chain is only worth something if somebody checks it. A verifier on the box reads every stream, and on 14 October it earned its place. When a policy-service pod was replaced, the old one wrote two lines after its successor had taken over the chain, and the verifier flagged the break that afternoon. The fix, one writer at a time held by a file lock, is merged.

The record keeps metadata only. Prompts and payloads never enter it. It also answers the question an ordinary log cannot: whether a reply to "everything agent X did in March" is complete, or partial, with the reason.

## It stays in your building.

Everything we build is self-hosted and Apache-2.0, with no account, no licence key, no seats and no telemetry. The source is public and the container images pull without a login. Prompts and bills never pass through us. We are not in the path.

What goes out through the stack is decided first. A secret pasted into a prompt is refused before the provider sees it. Card numbers, email addresses, phone numbers and IBANs can be masked, or the call blocked. Where the egress gate ([Scopyx](https://it-rat.com/services/scopyx.html)) is installed, a web fetch is decided before it goes out, and the cloud's own metadata address and private ranges are refused. A typed question to an outside model sends only the fields its template names. Where the kernel sensor from decision 2 runs, it sees what tries to go around the stack.

For a regulated firm, "where does our data go" is the first question in any review. The best answer is "nowhere you did not choose", and it is easiest to prove when the code is yours to read.

## Every control is proven by breaking it.

A control nobody has fired is a guess. In our repositories a check counts only after it has been shown to fail on a planted fault, and every new test must fail on the broken code before it passes on the fixed one.

Releases of the gateway, the policy point, the record and the delegation service are signed and carry a software bill of materials and build provenance. The verifier for the record has no third-party dependencies and forbids unsafe code, and 650,000 fuzzed inputs to the record's parsers produced no crash.

Then we break the running system. On 14 October, on two clouds and on a server at home, we killed every service's process, deleted the policy database's pod, stopped a node, rebooted a server and reset all five machines of a cluster at once.

*327 s*

five servers reset at once, back with the same state

*2.5 s*

policy service cut off, and every call after it refused

*0 lost*

event lines, after 14 processes were killed one by one

*650,000*

fuzzed inputs to the record's parsers, no crash

Four numbers from breaking the stack on purpose: 14 October 2026 on Google Cloud and a home server, and the record's fuzzing run of 31 July 2026.

Each of the fourteen processes we killed on the home server came back by itself in under a second, and no event line was lost. The five-machine cluster was serving again 327 seconds after the reset, with no manual step and the same state as before: the same policies, the same approvals, 977 events on the bus and 977 in the console. A home server rebooted and was healthy 86 seconds later.

That is what a test day is for. Four of the defects it turned up were fixed in released versions before the next morning: the padded tool call, the streamed tool call that skipped the check a buffered one gets, a gateway that could admit calls before it had read its budgets after a restart, and a refused key that left no event behind. The padded call was re-tested live on two clouds the same day.

## What we built.

We build fifteen open-source services for running AI agents the way a company runs a workforce. Each one installs on its own, and all of them share one way of naming an agent and one event format, which is what lets a decision in one become evidence in another.

- **The gateway**, [TokenFuse](https://it-rat.com/services/tokenfuse.html), and **the policy point**, [Wardryx](https://it-rat.com/services/wardryx.html).

- **Delegation**, [Vouchryx](https://it-rat.com/services/vouchryx.html), and **an identity graph with its kernel sensor**, [Idryx](https://it-rat.com/services/idryx.html).

- **The egress gate**, [Scopyx](https://it-rat.com/services/scopyx.html), and **a cryptography inventory**, [Qryx](https://it-rat.com/services/qryx.html).

- **Key custody and a witness**, [Keyryx](https://it-rat.com/services/keyryx.html).

- **Memory**, [Engram](https://it-rat.com/services/engram.html); **quality grading**, [Verdryx](https://it-rat.com/services/verdryx.html); **typed answers**, [Typryx](https://it-rat.com/services/typryx.html).

- **The record**, [Trailryx](https://it-rat.com/services/trailryx.html); **alerts**, [Heraldyx](https://it-rat.com/services/heraldyx.html); **drills**, [Mockryx](https://it-rat.com/services/mockryx.html).

- **A FinOps crew**, [CostCrew](https://it-rat.com/services/costcrew.html), and **a console**, [Genaryx](https://it-rat.com/genaryx.html).

All of it is Apache-2.0 and self-hosted, with no seats, licence key or telemetry.

## Three things to try on Monday.

- Find one decision about an agent that today happens after the fact, in a report or a review, and **move it into the path of the call.**

- Write down what each control does when the thing it depends on is down. **Then switch that thing off and watch.**

- Give one agent its own identity, revoke it, and **time how long it takes until the next call is refused.**

[What changed in the stack from 1 to 15 October 2026](https://it-rat.com/changes-2026-10.html) lists the releases behind several fixes named here. [AI agent security](https://it-rat.com/ai-agent-security.html) covers the failure modes an agent introduces, and [the guides index](https://it-rat.com/guides.html) has the rest.

# How the numbers were produced

> The eight figures on the home page: how each was measured on real infrastructure, the bugs the live runs caught, and where the rest of the record is.

The [home page](https://it-rat.com/index.html#proof) shows eight figures from the validation campaign. This guide says how each one was measured, what the live runs caught along the way, and where the rest of the record is kept.

- [The eight figures](https://it-rat.com/stack-guide.html#proof)

- [What the campaign ran](https://it-rat.com/stack-guide.html#campaign)

- [What it caught](https://it-rat.com/stack-guide.html#caught)

- [Where the rest is recorded](https://it-rat.com/stack-guide.html#elsewhere)

- [Run it yourself](https://it-rat.com/stack-guide.html#run)

## Validated on real infrastructure. Then torn down.

Before this site existed, the stack ran on disposable boxes across Hetzner, AWS and GCP with a real Anthropic key: four physical machines holding one budget over a real network, a partition with no split-brain, and a kill switch cutting real spend. Then the same stack came up again as a five-node Kubernetes cluster on each of those three clouds, which is where the cost of the governance itself finally got measured.

- **8000/8000** · **Money, under load.** Requests admitted against one budget by 100 to 500 concurrent agents, on a stub provider. None dropped, and none over the budget.

- **$0.00042** · **Money, per unit of work.** The measured cost of one correctly resolved case, which is the number that changes a decision. Monthly spend is not.

- **2,449/s** · **Policy, throughput.** Decisions a single pod makes each second, with no cliff out to 256 concurrent callers on dedicated cores.

- **34** · **Policy, under concurrency.** Requests fired at once and sorted exactly right: 6/6 served, 6/6 oversteppers denied, differentiated rights holding.

- **426 B** · **Evidence, per decision.** Hash-linked audit written for every decision rather than a sample. This is the line item that grows on its own.

- **12/12** · **Portability.** Deliberate budget overruns blocked, identically on Hetzner, AWS and GCP. What differs between clouds is the price, not the behaviour.

- **25,586** · **Crypto inventory.** Real Linux binaries scanned by Qryx, stripped, static and truncated among them, with zero crashes.

- **0** · **Rehearsal.** Guardrail gaps across three hostile drills fired twice at a real gateway, with zero real spend behind it.

## What the campaign ran, and what it caught.

Every number above came from a run against real infrastructure, not a benchmark harness written to flatter us. The boxes were disposable, the model calls behind the cost and policy figures were real and paid for, and nothing from the campaign is still standing: the machines were deleted, the key revoked.

**Money.** Four nodes across two datacenters held one budget through a leader kill and a real network partition: the majority kept serving, the isolated node could not overspend, and the state stayed byte-identical on every node. Under 500 concurrent agents against a fixed budget, the ledger admitted exactly what the budget allowed and no more.

**Policy.** An enriched multi-agent campaign produced 176 real enforcement decisions with differentiated rights: an analyst agent refused a wire transfer that a treasury agent was allowed, an unattested agent refused until it attested, and shell execution refused for everyone regardless of identity. Fired as a 34-request concurrent burst, the decision point still sorted them exactly right.

**The rest.** Qryx scanned 25,586 real Linux binaries, stripped, static and truncated among them, without a crash. Engram's reflection ran against real Claude output three times on three topologies with zero contradictions. Verdryx priced a correctly resolved case at $0.00042. Mockryx fired three hostile drills against a real gateway twice, with zero gaps and zero real spend, because the provider behind that gateway was fake while every guardrail in front of it was live.

**At cluster scale.** The same manifests then came up as a five-node cluster on each of the three clouds, to answer the question the campaign above could not: what does the supervision itself cost. Several clusters went up in all: a quota ceiling capped the first GCP attempt at three nodes, and AWS was rebuilt twice, the last time a chip generation lower, once it turned out the first result had compared silicon rather than clouds. One policy pod peaks at about 2,449 decisions a second and answers in 3.2ms at p50 while the queue is short. On identical silicon the two hyperscalers land 1.2% apart, which makes choosing between them procurement rather than engineering. At full load the infrastructure under the control plane works out at EUR 0.024 per million governed decisions on Hetzner and about USD 0.21 to USD 0.23 on AWS and GCP. That is what the machines cost to run. What binds first is not the processor but the evidence: every decision is audited, not a sample of them, at 426 bytes each, which is 614 MB a day at a thousand calls a minute. Provability is measured in gigabytes and can be budgeted a year ahead from a single number.

The full ledger, every number and every bug, is public in each repository's `VALIDATION.md`. A validation write-up with no bug list is marketing.

## Live testing found real bugs.

**And what it caught.** Live testing found real bugs, which is the point of doing it. Two of them, both in the policy plane, were invisible to sequential test traffic: a request that merely declared a forbidden tool without calling it slipped past a deny rule, and a decision cache keyed without the attestation method let an unattested agent inherit a recently attested allow inside the cache window. Only the 34-agent concurrent burst surfaced the second one. Both were fixed, covered by regression tests, and re-verified live before any number here was taken as final.

## Where the rest of the record is.

- **On premises.** The 2026-09-17 run on a small box behind a home router, governing agents in AWS and GCP and then taking sixteen injected failures, is in [what is proven](https://it-rat.com/what-is-proven.html), under "Seven claims and what each one stops short of" and "Sixteen ways to break it, and what each one did".

- **What we withdrew.** The throughput cliff past 64 concurrent callers that turned out to be a shared-vCPU instance is in [what is proven](https://it-rat.com/what-is-proven.html), under "Three things we published and had to withdraw", and in [what runs where](https://it-rat.com/what-runs-where.html).

## You do not have to take our word for it.

You do not have to take our word for it: [install the stack](https://it-rat.com/install.html) in one command, on a box you own or on your laptop, and watch the money plane light up. The four that are not servers, Engram, Qryx, Verdryx and Mockryx, each carry a one-line try-it on their own page.

## Back to the home page.

The [home page](https://it-rat.com/index.html) has the eight figures and the people behind them, [the Stack page](https://it-rat.com/stack.html) has every service with its room and its guide, and [the guides index](https://it-rat.com/guides.html) has the field itself.

# Install the stack, all of it or one service at a time

> One command for the whole stack on a box you own, a cluster or your laptop, and how each service installs and runs on its own.

Every service is its own repository with its own releases, so nothing here has to be adopted whole. If you want all of it, one command brings it up on a box you own. If you want one piece, it installs and runs on its own. The exact commands, pinned to a version, live in each repository, because a second copy of an install procedure is a second thing to keep true.

- [Four ways in](https://it-rat.com/install.html#ways)

- [All of it, on one box](https://it-rat.com/install.html#all)

- [All of it, on Kubernetes](https://it-rat.com/install.html#cluster)

- [On your laptop](https://it-rat.com/install.html#laptop)

- [One service at a time](https://it-rat.com/install.html#one)

- [After it is up](https://it-rat.com/install.html#next)

## Four ways in.

one box

### All of it, on one machine

A Debian or Ubuntu machine you own, one command, every service pulled as a published image and nothing compiled.

a cluster

### All of it, on Kubernetes

The same services as plain manifests: one script for bare servers, or one apply on a cluster you already run.

your laptop

### A sandbox to look around

Built from source and run natively, with no Docker, bound to your own machine and gone when you press Ctrl-C.

one piece

### One service at a time

Any single service from its own repository. Most run on their own; the list says which lean on another.

## All of it, in one command.

You need a Debian or Ubuntu machine you control, root on it, and outbound internet. Everything else the installer brings: it adds Docker if the machine has none, pulls every service as a published image, and compiles nothing.

```
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TAIPANBOX/stack-single/main/install.sh | bash
```

It brings up the core: the gateway and the ledger behind it, policy, identity, key custody and its witness, alerts by mail, a check on the record's chain, the console, and the tunnel an operator uses to reach it. It ends by checking itself, and the last line it prints says whether every check passed.

**It comes up closed.** The gateway listens on the machine's loopback, so nothing faces the internet until you open it, and opening it is one word:

```
GATEWAY_BIND=0.0.0.0 ./install.sh
```

Then point an agent at the gateway, wherever that agent runs. Every call carries a client key, and the installer mints one for your agents when you bring none, in **/opt/agent-stack/agent-key**.

```
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://<your box>:4100
```

To check an installed box again without changing anything on it:

```
STACK_DIR=/opt/agent-stack ./install.sh status
```

### Add the rest when you want it

- **Delegation**, so an agent can prove whose authority it carries: `WITH_DELEGATION=1 ./install.sh`

- **Typed answers**, on a free, deterministic stub that makes no outbound call until you choose a model: `WITH_TYPED=1 ./install.sh`

- **Governed web access** for agents that fetch: `docker compose --profile egress up -d scopyx`

- **The FinOps console**: `docker compose --profile finops up -d costcrew`

Every flag, and what a second run does and does not change, is in the [stack-single repository](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/stack-single#readme).

## All of it, on Kubernetes.

The same services as plain YAML and a kustomization, with no Helm. On bare servers, one script builds the cluster and the stack together:

```
git clone https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/stack-k8s && cd stack-k8s
./deploy.sh --servers ip1,ip2,ip3 --agents ip4,ip5 --hcloud-token <token> \
  --trust-domain <your domain>
```

That script is written for Hetzner: it puts up the cloud firewall, a cluster with secrets encrypted at rest and network policy that is actually enforced, and storage, then applies the manifests and runs the stack's own checks and its containment tests. AWS and GCP have deploy scripts of their own, and on a cluster you already run the manifests apply with one command:

```
kubectl apply -k manifests/
```

Some services are opt-in on a cluster too, each one more manifest to apply. The [stack-k8s repository](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/stack-k8s#readme) names them, along with every trap found while building it.

## On your laptop, to look around.

A sandbox, not a deployment. It builds each service from source and runs it natively, with no Docker, binds everything to 127.0.0.1, and stops cleanly when you press Ctrl-C. If a toolchain or a port is missing, it says which.

```
git clone https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/stack-up && cd stack-up && ./up.sh
```

Delegation, the FinOps console and typed answers join with `--with-delegation`, `--with-finops` and `--with-typed`. The [stack-up repository](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/stack-up#readme) has the port map and the rest.

## One service at a time.

Nothing here has to be adopted whole. Each service is its own repository with its own releases, and most of them run alone. The list says how each one ships and what, if anything, it leans on; its repository has the command, pinned to a version.

| service | how it ships | on its own | install |
|---|---|---|---|
| the control room |  |  |  |
| Genaryx | The console of the one-box and cluster installs; built from source on its own. | Reads the stack it sits on. | [genaryx ↗](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/genaryx#readme) |
| money |  |  |  |
| TokenFuse | A container image: a proxy you start and point your agent at. | Yes, with a model provider behind it, or its stub for a dry run. | [tokenfuse ↗](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/tokenfuse#readme) |
| CostCrew | A Go binary, or the `finops` profile of the one-box install. | Yes. It listens on loopback and reads your bills. | [costcrew ↗](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/costcrew#readme) |
| TokenFuse Pocket | An iPhone app, not wired in yet, so there is nothing to install. | Not yet. | not yet |
| guardrails |  |  |  |
| Wardryx | A signed container image, or built from source with Go. | Yes. It answers policy questions over HTTP. | [wardryx ↗](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/wardryx#readme) |
| Idryx | A prebuilt binary for your platform. | Yes. It reads an event log. | [idryx ↗](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/idryx#readme) |
| Scopyx | A container image. | Asks Wardryx for every decision. | [scopyx ↗](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/scopyx#readme) |
| Vouchryx | A container image. | Needs an issuer, a signing key and the issuers it trusts. | [vouchryx ↗](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/vouchryx#readme) |
| proof |  |  |  |
| Qryx | A prebuilt binary, with checksums. | Yes. Point it at a path. | [qryx ↗](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/qryx#readme) |
| Keyryx | A container image whose build you can verify. | Holds the signing keys the others use; the one-box install includes it. | [keyryx ↗](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/keyryx#readme) |
| Verdryx | A Python package, installed from its repository. | Yes. A dry run uses a stub model, with no network and no key. | [verdryx ↗](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/verdryx#readme) |
| Typryx | A Go binary or a container image. An optional add-on. | Yes, on its stub backend until you choose a model. | [typryx ↗](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/typryx#readme) |
| Mockryx | A prebuilt binary. | Needs a pre-production gateway to fire its drills at. | [mockryx ↗](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/mockryx#readme) |
| Trailryx | Container images: a receiver and a store. No Rust toolchain needed. | Takes events from the stack and keeps the record. | [trailryx ↗](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/trailryx#readme) |
| ground |  |  |  |
| Heraldyx | A container image. | Reads an event file, and can write the mail to a file instead of sending it. | [heraldyx ↗](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/heraldyx#readme) |
| Engram | A Python package, `pip install engdbram`: a library in your own process. | Yes. | [engram ↗](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/engram#readme) |
| Platform | Agent Passport is a specification; agent-stack-go is a Go module with the `agent-conform` binary; the Terraform provider is on the Terraform Registry as `TAIPANBOX/taipan`. | Yes, each of them. | [agent-stack-go ↗](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/agent-stack-go#readme) |

## Where to go next.
