# TokenFuse guide

> How TokenFuse works, how to install and configure it, what changed from 1 to 15 October 2026, and what the default install does not do, in full.

The [TokenFuse room](https://it-rat.com/services/tokenfuse.html) keeps the simulation, the drawing and the common questions. This guide keeps the rest of what the room used to say: how a cap is enforced, where it sits, how to run it, what changed from 1 to 15 October 2026, and what the default install does not do.

- [At a glance](https://it-rat.com/tokenfuse-guide.html#overview)

- [How it works](https://it-rat.com/tokenfuse-guide.html#how-it-works)

- [Where it sits](https://it-rat.com/tokenfuse-guide.html#where-it-sits)

- [Running it](https://it-rat.com/tokenfuse-guide.html#run)

- [What changed](https://it-rat.com/tokenfuse-guide.html#changes)

- [What changed in November](https://it-rat.com/tokenfuse-guide.html#changes-november)

- [Limits](https://it-rat.com/tokenfuse-guide.html#limits)

## TokenFuse at a glance.

- **The breaker between your agents and your invoice.**

- **Release:** pinned tags · ghcr images (no :latest). **Core:** Rust.

- **Ledger:** in-process by default · raft cluster build optional.

- **Enforcement:** HTTP 402, in-line.

- **Proven on:** Hetzner · AWS · GCP.

- **Licence:** Apache-2.0.

### What it is

A fire in next month's bill is too late to fight. TokenFuse is the extinguisher: a drop-in gateway that gives every run a budget, watches its burn in real time, and cuts the circuit with an HTTP 402 the moment a run crosses its budget. Adoption is one base-URL change; no agent framework rewrite, no SDK lock-in.

## Not a dashboard. A set of hands on the wheel.

### Sixty seconds, one runaway

This is a simulation, but not a fantasy: it replays the exact shape of the live validation runs. An agent enters a retry loop against a $0.006 budget. Four calls land. The reserve for the fifth would cross the cap, so the ledger refuses it. [Watch it in the room](https://it-rat.com/services/tokenfuse.html#sim).

### One gateway in the path. One ledger everyone trusts.

Your agent's SDK points at TokenFuse instead of the provider. In the hot path: budgets, loop detection, a model router that downgrades routine calls, a semantic cache, DLP and the Wardryx policy hook. Behind it: the spend ledger, in one process by default; the optional cluster build replicates it with raft, so the gateways of one cluster still admit exactly what one budget allows.

### Per-run budgets

The run is the unit that pays. A sub-agent's run rolls up into its parent run, so its spend has to fit inside every ancestor's budget. Cross the cap and the answer is a clean 402 your framework already understands, not a Slack message at 9am. Since v1.5.0 an operator can also cap the budget a caller declares for its own run: `TOKENFUSE_MAX_RUN_BUDGET_USD` lowers a larger one to the ceiling and the answer says so in `x-fuse-budget-clamped`. The launchers set it to USD 5.00. It bounds each run, not an agent's total: a new run id gets a new ceiling.

### How a cap is actually enforced, and what it costs you

Budgets are hierarchical and checked all-or-nothing. A sub-agent's spend rolls up and is tested against every ancestor it belongs to, so a run cannot slip under its own cap while quietly breaking its parent's. The run is the unit that pays, because a per-key limit cannot tell one agent's afternoon of honest work from the same key looping on itself.

A business unit can also carry a monthly cap, the first budget above the run. It is set in the gateway's identity map, or overridden from the Cloud, and counts the calendar month in UTC; in enforce mode a call that would cross it is refused with a 402. Each gateway counts its own calls on top of a tally it reads from the Cloud when it starts, so that cap is not yet shared across a fleet of gateways.

Accounting is reserve then settle. Each call is priced before it happens, the reserve is taken, and the real cost settles afterwards; a call that would cross the cap is refused before the provider ever sees it. Models the price book does not recognise get a fallback price rather than passing through untracked, because untracked spend is exactly the failure mode this exists to remove.

Adoption is a one-line base-URL swap. Since v1.19.0 the default governed profile enforces budgets; set TOKENFUSE_MODE=shadow and the gateway prices and records everything while refusing nothing, so you can see what would have been blocked before anything is. Its own bookkeeping fails open: a telemetry push or an event write that fails never refuses a call. The one exception is the start: with a Cloud configured, a gateway answers 503 seed_pending (retryable) until it has read its money state, so a restart cannot hand a run its budget again. The one failure mode that is a choice is the policy hook, and the launchers make it for you: all three ship it fail-closed, so a policy plane that cannot be reached refuses every governed call rather than waving it through. That is measured, not read off a config file: on 2026-09-17 the policy plane was stopped under a box governing two clouds and every call came back 403 in 0.3 s until it was started again. The enforcement decision itself is in-process Rust, about 0.4 microseconds at p99. The thing standing between an agent and a four-digit night should not be the slow part.

### Loop detection

A retrying agent looks exactly like a compromised one from the budget's side. A sustained loop trips the breaker, and a fan-out explosion opens an incident in the Cloud, before either becomes a four-digit night.

### Burn forecast

Reserve-then-settle accounting prices each call before it happens, with a built-in price book of the vendors' rates as they read on 2026-10-13, long-prompt tiers included, and a deliberately high fallback rate for a model id it does not know, flagged on the response, so an unknown model is refused sooner rather than tracked never. The estimate is fast and honest about being an estimate.

### Model router

Routine calls ride a cheaper model that still clears your quality bar; hard ones stay on the frontier model. Both ship switched off: the router is off by default, and the cache is off in the gateway and in the launchers.

### Cluster build: a raft-replicated ledger

An optional build that ships as its own image tag (tokenfuse:<tag>-cluster). The default image does not run it. Four nodes on four machines held one shared budget through a leader kill and a real network partition: the majority kept serving, the isolated node could not overspend, nothing split-brained.

### What a budget survives: a crash, a restart, a partition

The images every launcher installs run one gateway with its ledger in memory, and a restart no longer starts every run at zero. Since v1.4.1 the gateway reads each run's spend back from the Cloud before it serves, for runs active in the last 31 days, and since v1.6.0 a gateway at a remote site does the same through a read scoped to its own site. With no Cloud configured there is nothing to read back, and a run starts from zero. The read-back is proven by tests, and the remote-site half on release binaries behind a stand-in for the hub entry, not yet on a live hub. A budget only means something if two gateways racing each other cannot both spend it, and that is what the cluster build is for, a separate build of the same binary: there the ledger is a raft state machine, and the affordability check is linearized across the whole fleet: four nodes on four machines admit exactly what one budget allows, not four copies of it.

In that build, with durable storage on redb, a budget outlives more than a node crash: it survives a full process restart, because a cap that resets when a process dies is a cap an unlucky deploy can hand back to a runaway.

That was tested rather than assumed. A four-node cluster across two datacenters took a leader kill and a real network partition: the majority side kept serving, the isolated node could not overspend, and nothing split-brained. Enforcement then held under a burst of 34 concurrent agents, and the cost accounting was run on the same protocol against Hetzner, AWS and GCP so the numbers could be compared honestly.

### FOCUS export

Agent spend lands in the same FinOps Foundation format as the rest of your cloud bill, so showback and chargeback reuse the pipes and dashboards finance already trusts.

### A label comes from the act, not from a name

A run carries labels for what it has read, the web label for one, and its next tool call is judged with them: after a page was read, a request to run a shell is refused. That label used to follow a tool name the agent reported. The gateway read the name from the conversation the caller sends, so a fetch reported under a name the policy trusts carried that name's labels, and a fetch left out of the conversation carried none. The label now comes from two witnesses that do not depend on that string.

**The MCP broker.** It made the connection, so it knows which server answered. `TOKENFUSE_MCP_UPSTREAM_LABELS="scopyx=web"` classifies an upstream by the server, not by the name a request chose. It needs `TOKENFUSE_MCP_TAINT_GATEWAY`, and the broker refuses to start on a name that matches no upstream or on a classification with no taint gateway. After a classified upstream answers a `tools/call`, and before the answer leaves, the broker reports to `POST /v1/fuse/observed-act` and the gateway puts the labels on the run. The report has no member for a tool name. A call that names no run is refused before anything is forwarded, and an answer whose label the gateway did not take is withheld.

**The provider's answer.** `server_tool_use` and `mcp_tool_use` blocks record a tool the provider ran, such as a built-in search. The gateway reads them, buffered and streamed, and labels the run before that answer's own tool calls are judged. The name map stays as the fallback, and a run carries the union of what the three say.

The event contract does not change: the same `taint_raised` event and the same `mcp_tool_call` and `model_tool_call` stages. A deployment that sets no classification sees no difference, apart from the provider's blocks, which now label.

### One incident per failing provider

A provider that is up but failing fails every call that reaches it, and each call is its own run. The gateway counts the `dependency_failed` events whose dependency is the provider and sends the Cloud one report every two seconds, with the Cloud key it already holds; a report it cannot deliver is dropped, not queued. A provider that has failed `TOKENFUSE_CLOUD_INCIDENT_PROVIDER_FAILURES` calls (three unless set) within ten minutes opens one incident per provider and reporting site, `dependency_failed:provider:NAME` (with `@SITE` appended for a key bound to a site), with severity high, the failures folded into its occurrences and a summary naming the provider and the last detail. It shows on `GET /v1/incidents`, on the stream and in push like any incident.

The route is `POST /v1/provider-failures`, for an admin or ingest key only, and it is held to a caller who may be hostile: the body is bounded, the label is cleaned, and providers past a bound fold into one visible `other` bucket instead of evicting a real one. The provider label is the host and port of `TOKENFUSE_UPSTREAM` with any `user:password@` removed. The per-call event on the bus is unchanged, and the incident names a provider and no agent or run, so it is not exported to the bus. [Heraldyx](https://it-rat.com/services/heraldyx.html) folds the same outage into one mail on its own side.

## The loud neighbor everyone listens to.

TokenFuse asks [Wardryx](https://it-rat.com/services/wardryx.html) before letting a declared tool through, and stamps the verdict on the response. Its Parquet traces are the raw material [Verdryx](https://it-rat.com/services/verdryx.html) prices outcomes from. [Mockryx](https://it-rat.com/services/mockryx.html) attacks it on purpose in pre-prod. [Idryx](https://it-rat.com/services/idryx.html) correlates its events into the identity graph. Everything travels as one envelope, the agent-event, and [Genaryx](https://it-rat.com/genaryx.html) lifts that same signed kill into a console you reach over your own tunnel, where it becomes a passkey break-glass ceremony.

Where this fits in the wider practice: [FinOps for AI](https://it-rat.com/finops-for-ai.html) on managing spend that creates itself, and [AI agent governance](https://it-rat.com/ai-agent-governance.html) on the rest of the runtime controls.

### It stops the spend. Two neighbours stop other things.

A breaker is the right answer to a runaway and the wrong one to a compromised delegation, where the money is affordable and the problem is that the agent may act for somebody at all. [Vouchryx](https://it-rat.com/services/vouchryx.html) ends that authority at every enforcement point at once. And a ceiling in the request path says nothing about the invoice that arrives a month later: [CostCrew](https://it-rat.com/services/costcrew.html) is where a bill gets taken apart, allocated and closed, by a crew of agents whose work a person stamps.

## Running it.

Run it from [the repository](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/tokenfuse#-get-started), where the one-line command lives beside the image tag it pulls.

Then point `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` at `localhost:4100` and give your next run a run id and a budget (the x-fuse-run-id and x-fuse-budget-usd headers). A call with no run id is refused with 400 metering_required. That's the whole migration. Behind a launcher, a header above USD 5.00 is lowered to the operator's ceiling unless the operator raises it.

Want more than the gateway? [Run the live services locally](https://it-rat.com/services/platform.html#run) in one command.

### TokenFuse ships as an image, and since v0.4.3 as binaries

The current release is v1.22.0. The image is the way to run it in front of traffic; the binaries, since v0.4.3, are for a laptop and a first look: one file, `TOKENFUSE_UPSTREAM` set, and it listens. Each address always serves the newest release: the asset names carry no version, so a link saved today still works after the next one. No Windows build yet, and saying so is cheaper than a broken link.

## What the gateway gained from 1 to 15 October

The whole stack's fortnight, TokenFuse among it, is in [the October changelog](https://it-rat.com/changes-2026-10.html#tokenfuse).

| shipped in | what it does |
|---|---|
| v1.7.0 | The price book holds a row for every Claude model Anthropic lists, at its list rate. Before this, a call to a model the book did not know was charged at a fallback rate several times too high. |
| v1.9.0 | A call whose outcome is unknown is kept as money owed. The reservation survives a restart, and a person closes it with evidence, using a short-lived token that the operator console mints after a passkey check. |
| v1.10.0 | A retained call and its closure are written to the event bus, so a notifier can tell a person that money is waiting. |
| v1.11.0 | Tool metadata is scanned for five warning signs: a credential, an order to run another tool, a path to local credentials, text addressed to the model, and hidden text. |
| v1.11.0 | With the scan set to block, a tool whose definition changed after it was pinned is refused on the call. |
| v1.11.0 | Tools a request declares are read for poisoning. A poisoned description marks the run as a suspected injection. The request itself is not refused. |
| v1.12.0 | Text recalled from an agent's memory is untrusted context. Under the starter policy, a run that carries it cannot then run a command, write a file or reach the network. |
| v1.12.0 | The compliance catalog cites the OWASP MCP Top 10, row by row, against the test that holds each control. |
| v1.13.0 | Prices for the current OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek, Kimi and GLM models are at their vendors' rates. A model sold at two rates by prompt length is priced by the tier each call falls in. A model the book cannot price exactly keeps a fallback rate, and the call says so. |
| v1.13.1 | Tool arguments up to 12 KiB reach the policy whole. Larger arguments are marked as truncated, so the policy still decides. |
| v1.14.0 | A tool call inside a streamed answer is judged like one in a buffered answer, and a denied call is cut before it reaches the agent. |
| v1.14.0 | Nothing a budget governs is admitted until the gateway has read its money state, so a restart cannot admit calls for a unit already over its cap. |
| v1.14.0 | A refused client key reaches the event bus with its reason and a fingerprint of the key, never the key itself. |
| v1.14.0 | IBANs are a kind of personal data the scanner finds, checked by country code, length and check digits. |
| v1.14.0 | Every FOCUS export row says whether it was priced from the price book or from the fallback. |

## What changed in November

| shipped in | what it does |
|---|---|
| v1.21.0 | A run's taint label comes from what an enforcement point saw: the MCP broker labels a call by the server that answered, and the provider's own tool blocks label the run before that answer's tool calls are judged. |
| v1.21.0 | A provider that keeps failing is one incident in the Cloud console and API, not one per call. |
| v1.22.0 | The MCP broker tells an upstream that labels a run which run is asking, and tells no other, so a read of the web is recorded under the run that asked for it. |
| v1.22.0 | The MCP broker follows no redirect, so the secrets it writes into a body cannot be carried to a host an upstream named, and a tool call in a stream's closing chunk is held like any other. |
| v1.22.0 | A call that searched on the OpenAI door labels its run, so a shell the run asks for afterwards can be refused. |
| v1.22.0 | A response that stopped short is charged the input as reported and the output at the request's cap, under the cost basis PartialUsage. |

## What the default install does not do, and what is not proven yet.

- **The cluster build is optional and ships as its own image tag.** The default image every launcher installs runs one gateway with its ledger in memory.

- A business unit's monthly cap: each gateway counts its own calls on top of a tally it reads from the Cloud when it starts, so that cap is not yet shared across a fleet of gateways.

- The model router and the cache both ship switched off: the router is off by default, and the cache is off in the gateway and in the launchers, so the saving seen in live runs arrives when you turn them on, not by default.

- With no Cloud configured there is nothing to read back, and a run starts from zero.

- The read-back is proven by tests, and the remote-site half on release binaries behind a stand-in for the hub entry, not yet on a live hub.

- The operator's run-budget ceiling bounds each run, not an agent's total: a new run id gets a new ceiling.

- A poisoned tool description marks the run as a suspected injection. The request itself is not refused.

- A label follows an act that passed through an enforcement point. A process with its own socket passes through none.

- A provider's built-in search is labelled and not controlled: nothing can refuse it, and no domain policy reaches it. The OpenAI wire carries its built-in search as annotations and no tool block, so it is not read.

- A deployment gets the broker half of the label by routing its fetch plane through the broker, which is separate wiring.

- No Windows build yet.

- The room's runaway is a simulation, but not a fantasy: it replays the exact shape of the live validation runs.

## Back to the room.

The [TokenFuse room](https://it-rat.com/services/tokenfuse.html) has the simulation, the drawing and the common questions, and [the guides index](https://it-rat.com/guides.html) has the field itself.

<!-- https://it-rat.com/costcrew-guide.html -->

# CostCrew guide

> How CostCrew works, how to install and configure it, what changed from 1 to 15 October 2026, and what it does not prove yet, in full.

The [CostCrew room](https://it-rat.com/services/costcrew.html) keeps the console, the drawing of one finding end to end, and the common questions. This guide keeps the rest of what the room used to say: how the work moves, how to run and configure it, what changed from 1 to 15 October 2026, and what is not proven yet.

- [At a glance](https://it-rat.com/costcrew-guide.html#overview)

- [How it works](https://it-rat.com/costcrew-guide.html#how-it-works)

- [Found, never saved](https://it-rat.com/costcrew-guide.html#found-not-saved)

- [Where it sits](https://it-rat.com/costcrew-guide.html#where-it-sits)

- [Running it](https://it-rat.com/costcrew-guide.html#run)

- [What changed](https://it-rat.com/costcrew-guide.html#changes)

- [Limits](https://it-rat.com/costcrew-guide.html#limits)

## CostCrew at a glance.

- **A crew of agents works your bill**, and a person stamps every deliverable and decides everything above a set amount.

- **Status:** pre-1.0, and main is supported.

- **Core:** one static binary. **Store:** SQLite, in a directory you name.

- **Reads:** FOCUS from TokenFuse, AWS and GCP billing exports, seats, recommendations; the Azure billing export is specified, not read yet.

- **Enforces:** nothing on your bill, by design. Every deliverable arrives as a draft.

- **Licence:** Apache-2.0.

### What it is

Analysts with named missions, budgets and owners take the cloud, SaaS and AI bill apart: allocation, chargeback, unit economics, anomalies and forecasts. Each one is hired into a desk, given a mandate and a monthly guard, and the work it does arrives as a draft. Nothing is published until a person stamps it. On your bill it enforces nothing at all: it watches spend, it does not spend, and it stops nothing out there. On its own crew it does enforce, because a mandate you cannot withdraw is not a mandate: suspend an analyst and it gets no rights, and no new work can be handed to it.

## A finding becomes a task, a task becomes a draft, a person stamps it.

The detector is two-sided and ranks by money: a fall matters as much as a rise, because a feed that stopped delivering and a workload switched off unnoticed both look like a drop. A Sunday is judged against Sundays, and the baseline is a median with a robust deviation, so last month's spike does not raise the bar for this month's.

### The finding names its rule

Every anomaly carries the rule that judged it, the baseline it was judged against and the day marked on its own series. A queue whose entries cannot be argued with is a queue nobody works.

### The task carries a guard

An analyst gets the task with a mandate, the rights that come with its skills and a spend guard on the row. What it may read follows from what it was hired to do, not from what is convenient.

### Only a person publishes

Work comes back as a draft. A person posts it or returns it, and the return is on the analyst's own card next to its first-pass rate, so a crew that produces confident noise is visible rather than merely busy.

### The path a number takes before anybody is charged for it.

Every screen in the room's gallery shows one station on this line. What no screenshot shows is the line itself, and the gate in the middle of it: an agent can carry a finding all the way to the stamp and no further. Returned work goes back up the dashed path and lands on that analyst's own card, next to its first-pass rate.

### A FinOps practice, staffed: what each frame shows

Every frame in the room's gallery is a fresh installation of the binary on its own seeded estate, with thirty-nine analysts. The figures are the fixture's, and the console says on each page which of its numbers are real money and which the estate generated.

- **The board.** Blocked and returned work sits first on purpose: it is the work that has stopped, and a board that buries it hides its own problems.

- **The crew.** Thirty-nine analysts, 3,871.35 of work across 310 tasks, and a first-pass rate left blank where nothing has been reviewed yet, because a rate over no reviews is not a rate.

- **One analyst.** Its desk and mission, three open tasks of the thirteen it has ever been given, and 173.97 of work against a 60.00 monthly guard.

- **Hiring.** Everything the form asks is a governance fact, asked once. The name becomes part of an agent://<host>/costcrew/<name> identity that other services parse, so one gateway key bound to agent://<host>/costcrew/* covers the crew and nothing else.

- **Anomalies.** Every irregularity ranked by money rather than by how far out it sits, 2,475.10 of it still unexplained. A four sigma move worth three dollars is real and is not worth your morning.

- **One finding.** 2,054.10 above baseline on Amazon EC2, the day marked on its own series, and the rule that judged it: 3.5 robust deviations from the median of the last 28 comparable days.

- **Allocation.** The part of the bill that arrived with nobody's name on it: 136,848.58 direct against 14,540.00 shared, placed by rules a team can argue with rather than by a number it must accept.

- **Chargeback.** Closing a period is what stops the numbers moving, because an allocation recomputed every time somebody opens the page cannot be charged to anybody. Out as a general ledger CSV.

- **Results.** Found, never saved. 1,254.35 found since the board opened against 3,871.35 the crew cost, and the word is load-bearing: nothing is saved until somebody acts.

- **KPIs.** Nine report a number, three refuse and four meet their target. The refusals are the important part: a library where everything reports is one where several of the figures are invented.

- **Connectors.** Every entry says which table it fills, what it needs, and whether running it costs money, because that last one is what decides whether an integration is a good idea.

- **Audit.** Everything the console did, in order, each entry hashed against the one before it. Tamper-evidence rather than tamper-proofing, and the page says which one it is.

- **Rightsizing.** What the providers' own exports say is paid for at a size nobody uses, ranked by the saving rather than by the instance name, and flagged where a fourteen day window would call a monthly job idle. A list, never something the console applies.

- **SaaS seats.** Sixty of 315 seats issued and not signed into in thirty days, 4,047.00 a month at what is actually paid, and one renewal inside ninety days whose notice deadline falls before it.

- **Cadence.** Thirty-one tasks are due today at a worst case of 2.3050, and not one of them runs: the switch is off and the ceiling is 0.00, and both of those are a person's own act.

- **The plan.** Sixty-seven items proposed under a 1,043.00 ceiling, and nothing exists until somebody approves it. A planner that writes straight to the board has spent the budget before anybody agreed to the work.

- **Owner and told.** Every finding carries the owner it belongs to, read from the team that pays for it or from the analyst that opened it. Telling that owner is its own logged step, so on a fresh install every row still reads not yet.

## Found, never saved.

One word is load-bearing throughout this console: money is found, never saved, because nothing is saved until somebody acts. A console that reports found money as saved is one whose numbers stop being believed the first time finance checks them against the invoice.

### Shared cost gets a defensible owner

Direct cost needs no product. This is about the part of the bill that arrived with nobody's name on it, placed by a rule a team can read and dispute rather than a figure it must accept.

### Closing a period stops the numbers

An allocation recomputed every time somebody opens the page cannot be charged to anybody: March's number is not April's, and the team is right to refuse it. A closed period freezes, and leaves as a general ledger CSV.

### A measure that cannot be computed refuses

The KPI library reports a number or says by name why it cannot. A practice that measures itself with invented figures is worse off than one that measures nothing.

## Genaryx governs agents. This is a crew of agents that works your bill.

They are floors, not alternatives. [Genaryx](https://it-rat.com/genaryx.html) is the control room over a fleet: it watches what is running now, demands a signature for anything destructive, and stops things. CostCrew's analysts are agents like any other, so Genaryx governs them too. This console runs the other way round: it reads last month's invoices, hands you drafts, and stops nothing. It emits its own work onto the same agent-event bus, so [Trailryx](https://it-rat.com/services/trailryx.html) can seal it and [Heraldyx](https://it-rat.com/services/heraldyx.html) can mail you about it. Optionally it asks [Typryx](https://it-rat.com/services/typryx.html) for a typed hint about each open anomaly, a suggestion an analyst may disagree with and never an action.

### Runtime is not the ledger

[TokenFuse](https://it-rat.com/services/tokenfuse.html) counts a run in micro-dollars while it happens and can kill it. CostCrew counts an invoice line in cents a month later and allocates it. Same money, two questions, and only one of them has a kill switch.

### Hiring is registration

The hire form collects what a Passport needs, so an analyst joins the crew and the estate in one act. In the original, those were two unrelated steps and the second one mostly did not happen.

### It says what it cannot do

Per-agent attribution of AI spend is not possible from an invoice: the charge carries a model and a workload, not an agent. It becomes possible when the calls go through TokenFuse, and until then the console does not pretend. It now reads a cloud bill too: of the eighteen connectors in its catalogue, twelve are built (the AWS and GCP billing exports as FOCUS folders, the TokenFuse FOCUS export, the Anthropic and OpenAI usage reports, SaaS seats, three rightsizing and three budget-recommendation readers) and six, the Azure billing export among them, are specified with their endpoint and not written. The catalogue says which is which, per entry, and so does this page.

## One binary, one directory.

No interpreter, no virtual environment, no second database engine in the process. It listens on loopback by default. From v0.10.0 it refuses to start on any other address unless a TLS proxy is in front and -behind-tls is set, or -insecure-http says plain HTTP is intended there. First account created at /signup becomes the admin of that installation, so make one before you hand anybody the address.

```
go install github.com/TAIPANBOX/costcrew/cmd/costcrew@latest
# then: costcrew -data ./local
```

```
# the whole local stack with the console on :8321, from TAIPANBOX/stack-up
./up.sh --with-finops
```

### A measured run

Measured on a box behind a home router on 2026-09-17: the crew ran beside the single-machine stack through a gateway door of its own, one real model call was settled at USD 0.05811 and the next was refused by a monthly cap set centrally, and the notifier mailed the crew's findings with the owner taken from a passport. The same run found the runner reporting its own estimate as spent, five times under the gateway's settlement, and an import of the box's real AI spend refused by an empty severity field; both were fixed in v0.2.1. No reader for a cloud bill existed then, so the crew worked the generated estate; the current release is v0.10.1, and it reads the AWS and GCP billing exports.

### The supervisor settles what it may

v0.3.0 lets the crew's supervisor settle what its job description already said it could. It now applies an analyst's own option by itself when its figure is at or under the anomaly threshold (for an option tied to an anomaly the figure is the excess the detector recorded, since v0.7.0, and an option whose figure differs goes to the owner with both numbers), and still sends anything larger, anything that is the owner's call and any disagreement between two analysts to the owner. That threshold, T.anomaly, is now USD 2,500, and the urgent one, T.urgent, USD 12,500: half the earlier figures, and recorded as decisions rather than defaults, so more requests reach the owner for the same work. An admin who answers for an owner has to give a reason, and it is recorded on the option, in the journal and on the bus. A task stopped partway keeps the charge the gateway already settled instead of showing zero. The supervisor pass is tested; the console buttons were not run end to end.

### Real money in, kept honest

v0.4.0 and v0.5.0 bring real money in and keep it honest. The console reads the AWS and GCP billing exports from a synced folder, exact to the micro-dollar, and reconciles the vendors' own usage reports against the gateway's rows. It can sign people in through the organisation's identity provider, run the whole crew on a model the organisation hosts itself, and decide how much of the bill a model is ever shown: everything, the names masked, or totals only; from v0.10.0 the default is masked. A re-exported gateway trace is counted once, and a call refused for identity is filed under the credential that made it, never under the agent it claimed. The AWS reader was proven on a real export, the GCP one only against a hand-written file, and sign-in only against an identity provider run inside the tests.

### Announced decisions

v0.6.0, released on 2026-10-13, lets a cost decision the crew recommends be announced before it lands. Only the owner can confirm an announcement. From its first day the anomaly queue and the forecast read it: a day that lands as announced is not raised, and one that lands short, late or in the wrong direction is, with the decision's name on it. A saving cannot be larger than the median daily spend it saves on, and the forecast carries an announced step before it lands. The Anthropic price rows are the vendor's list rates, as read on 2026-10-13. The release is plain about what it does not prove yet: every run in it used the generated estate, so detection quality and forecast accuracy on real spend are still open.

### What the repository gates

The repository gates more than its suite: every scenario written in the language of the request is bound to a named test in both directions, and each gate has a case that plants its own fault and requires the gate to go red.

## What the crew gained from 1 to 15 October

| shipped in | what it does |
|---|---|
| v0.4.0 | Provider usage is read from the vendors' own usage reports and reconciled against the gateway's rows, so the gap between the two is shown. |
| v0.4.0 | Sign-in through the organisation's identity provider, over OpenID Connect with signed tokens and PKCE. Session tokens are stored hashed. |
| v0.6.0 | A cost decision the crew recommends can be announced before it lands. Only the owner can confirm it, and a day that matches the announcement is not raised as an anomaly. |
| v0.7.0 | A FOCUS 1.1 file of agent spend, by agent, unit, model and credential, for a FinOps platform's custom ingress (the costcrew-cloudability binary in the image). No file has been accepted by a live tenant yet. |

## What it does not do, and what is not proven yet.

- **On your bill it enforces nothing at all:** it watches spend, it does not spend, and it stops nothing out there.

- Per-agent attribution of AI spend is not possible from an invoice: the charge carries a model and a workload, not an agent. It becomes possible when the calls go through TokenFuse, and until then the console does not pretend.

- Of the eighteen connectors in its catalogue, twelve are built and six, the Azure billing export among them, are specified with their endpoint and not written.

- The supervisor pass, which applies an analyst's own option by itself, is tested; the console buttons were not run end to end.

- The AWS reader was proven on a real export, the GCP one only against a hand-written file, and sign-in only against an identity provider run inside the tests.

- Release gates through v0.10.1 ran on the generated estate and on test fixtures, so detection quality and forecast accuracy on real spend are still open.

- The FOCUS 1.1 file of agent spend (costcrew-cloudability, in the image since v0.7.0) has not been accepted by a live tenant yet.

- The figures in the console frames are the fixture's, and the console says on each page which of its numbers are real money and which the estate generated.

- The audit chain is tamper-evidence rather than tamper-proofing, and rightsizing is a list, never something the console applies.

## Back to the room.

The [CostCrew room](https://it-rat.com/services/costcrew.html) has the seventeen frames, the drawing and the common questions, and [the guides index](https://it-rat.com/guides.html) has the field itself.

# TokenFuse Pocket guide

> How TokenFuse Pocket is designed to work, how it differs from Heraldyx, where it sits in the stack, and why it is not wired into a running stack yet.

The [Pocket room](https://it-rat.com/services/pocket.html) keeps the simulation, the live design mock and the drawing. This guide keeps the rest of what the room used to say: the screens in full, Pocket beside Heraldyx, where it sits, and the full account of why it is in the stack and not wired into one yet.

- [At a glance](https://it-rat.com/pocket-guide.html#overview)

- [How it works](https://it-rat.com/pocket-guide.html#how-it-works)

- [Pocket and Heraldyx](https://it-rat.com/pocket-guide.html#heraldyx)

- [Where it sits](https://it-rat.com/pocket-guide.html#where-it-sits)

- [Limits](https://it-rat.com/pocket-guide.html#limits)

## Pocket at a glance.

- **In the stack, and not wired into one yet.**

- **Watch the fleet burn live, and cut it from a device no attacker touched.**

- **Platform:** iOS · watchOS · SwiftUI. **Surfaces:** Dynamic Island · Live Activity · Watch complication.

- **Signing:** Secure Enclave, keys never leave the device.

- **Pairs with:** nothing today; genaryx-relay was removed.

- **Status:** no hardening pass, no whole-app security review. **Licence:** Apache-2.0.

### What it is

TokenFuse's gateway enforces the budget in the request path your agent runs on. Pocket asks what a control OUTSIDE that path should look like on a device you already carry: the fleet's burn rate live, and a kill signed by hardware the agent's host never touches. Both apps are built. The iPhone app's README says every screen was driven live against a real control plane on the simulator, and no run of ours is recorded for it yet. That is a long way from shipped: no production hardening pass, no security review, no App Store. The effort goes to the web console, and this moves when there is time for it.

## Not a bigger dashboard. A switch you can actually reach.

### Sixty seconds, one kill

This is a simulation, but it replays a shape the app is built for: a run drifts from baseline to 2.4x its burn rate, crosses a budget, and gets killed from an Apple Watch before anyone opens a laptop. The signature that authorizes the kill never leaves the Secure Enclave; the gateway only has to trust the result. [Watch it in the room](https://it-rat.com/services/pocket.html#sim).

### Do not watch it. Drive it.

An interactive design mock of the iPhone and Watch apps, running here as a web page. Seven iPhone screens, a Live Activity surface and five Watch screens, all live: the burn ticks and every screen is driveable. The ceremony the app implements is stricter than this mock: a kill is confirmed by name and signed on the device, and a killed run then leaves the pager, staying in the console and the audit trail. Drive it with the steps, the tab bar, or the Watch switch.

The mock runs [in the room](https://it-rat.com/services/pocket.html). Its seven steps, in full:

- **01 Runs, the deck.** Fleet burn up top, then the exception queue: the runs at or over their cap, worst first. The healthy fleet stays quiet.

- **02 Run detail, pull the breaker.** Spend against cap, model and steps. The kill wants you to mean it: slide to arm, then Face ID.

- **03 Budgets, the ladder above a run.** A cap on each run, and a monthly cap for each business unit, both enforced by the gateways. The org, team and agent ladder on this screen is a drawn design.

- **04 Agents, sorted by behaviour.** Not spend, conduct: a runaway agent, one reaching tools it never used, an orphaned key. Tap for why it fired and its blast radius.

- **05 Pairing, one scan and a key that stays.** As designed, your console would issue a one-time code, and scanning it would mint a signing key in the Secure Enclave that never leaves the phone. No console code issues one today.

- **06 Device, and how far it reaches.** The paired iPhone and the last action it signed. The mock draws a Default and a Strict peer mode for the Device screen. Neither is built.

- **07 Alerts that mean act.** Built for a relay that pushes the moment a cap breaks. Tap a banner to land on the run, or arm the kill from the wrist.

### One phone. One key. A path the gateway never sees.

As designed, the app pairs to a relay beside TokenFuse Cloud, never to the gateway your agent talks to, and no such relay runs today. A kill or a budget change is signed on-device by the Secure Enclave, forwarded byte for byte by the relay to Cloud, and pushed out to every gateway in the fleet from there. The request path and the kill path never share a wire.

### The fuse, everywhere

Mint under budget, amber warming, ember at the cap. The run list, the Dynamic Island, and the watch face all read the fuse the same way, so nothing needs translating between screens.

### Hardware-signed kill

The design signs every kill on-device, so a fully compromised server can neither forge that order nor change it. It can still refuse to pass the order on. The same property is what the web console reaches for with a passkey, which is why this became the direction we are building first.

### The fleet at a glance

Every run with its spend, its burn rate in dollars per minute, and how close it sits to a budget break, sorted hottest first, red once it's over.

### Pairing in seconds

Scan the QR code a Genaryx relay issues. No relay runs today, so nothing can be paired yet. The key is generated inside the Secure Enclave and never leaves it, not even to the app.

## Heraldyx mails you. Pocket buzzes. They are not the same control.

Both answer one question, how a human finds out, and they answer it from the same events. The difference is what each one is allowed to do about it, and that difference is the reason both exist rather than one replacing the other.

### The same four signals

Pocket surfaces `budget_exhausted`, `sustained_loop`, `fanout_explosion` and `spend_spike`. All four are in [Heraldyx](https://it-rat.com/services/heraldyx.html)'s catalogue too, with a sentence each for what happened, what the box already did, and what happens if nobody acts.

### One arrives here and never there

`spend_spike` is about a whole organisation, and the shared envelope requires an agent id, so its producer skips it rather than inventing a subject. It was built to reach this phone through the relay's own read slice, and it never reaches the mail. An operator who only reads mail does not learn about it.

### Mail cannot act. This can

Heraldyx reads a file and speaks SMTP, holds no credential for any plane, and its link is a view with no action in it, because mail gateways prefetch links. Pocket is the opposite by design: it pairs to a relay and the kill is signed on the device. That is a bigger blast radius, and it is why it needs a Secure Enclave and a per-device pairing rather than an address.

### Different routes, on purpose

Heraldyx reads the planes' shared event log directly, on the box, and needs nothing else running. Pocket reads `relay/v1/exceptions`, so it needs a relay up and the phone paired. Two paths that fail apart: the night the relay is down, the mail still goes out, and while no relay runs at all, the mail is the only one of the two that does.

### And Trailryx?

Nothing connects them. Pocket reads the control plane's own replay, not the record store, and neither knows the other exists.

## The human end of a machine decision.

Pocket is the human end of [TokenFuse](https://it-rat.com/services/tokenfuse.html): the gateway enforces the budget in the request path, Pocket lets you watch it happen and pull the kill switch from somewhere else entirely. A kill is written as a run_killed event on the same agent-event bus the rest of the [Platform](https://it-rat.com/services/platform.html) reads. What actually gets enforced was decided upstream, by [Wardryx](https://it-rat.com/services/wardryx.html) and the budgets you set. Pocket doesn't make that call; it gives you a fast, honest way to see it and override it.

### What it pairs with

Pocket was designed to pair through [Genaryx](https://it-rat.com/genaryx.html) to a TokenFuse plane you host yourself. That relay was removed from Genaryx on 2026-07-28, so nothing pairs today. Both apps are built and open, and neither is connected to a running stack: the console is what an operator uses today.

The plane it reads is open today: [stand up the stack's live services locally in one command](https://it-rat.com/services/platform.html#run) and see the same money plane on your own machine.

## In the stack, and not wired into one yet.

**Where this sits today, stated rather than implied.** Pocket is listed in the stack registry as not wired into a running stack yet. It is designed as the out-of-band control for TokenFuse, the way to pull the Breaker when the machine running the gateway, or the machine running your console, is itself the thing that has gone wrong. That is why the signature comes from the Secure Enclave on a device the agent's host never touches.

**How it is meant to work, and what it lacks today.** The phone pairs once, by QR, to a relay beside the stack. The one it was built against, genaryx-relay, was removed from genaryx on 2026-07-28, so today there is nothing to pair with and none of this runs end to end. The relay pushes only what needs a human, an over-cap run, straight into the signed-kill flow; the kill is signed on the device and the gateway has only to check the signature. The watch pairs on its own and carries the same flow, so a deauthorized device says it was deauthorized rather than pretending.

**What is actually true today.** The interface is finished. The iPhone app's repository records every screen as driven against a real control plane on a simulator, and no run of ours is recorded for it yet. It is not connected to anything you are running: there is no App Store build, no real push delivery, and no hardening pass or whole-app security review; a narrower review on 2026-09-06 led to one transport-security fix. Treat it as the shape of the control rather than a control you have. The console you run today is the [Genaryx](https://it-rat.com/genaryx.html) web app.

### Everything the room says is not done

- That is a long way from shipped: no production hardening pass, no security review, no App Store. The effort goes to the web console, and this moves when there is time for it.

- The relay it was built against, genaryx-relay, was removed from genaryx on 2026-07-28, so today there is nothing to pair with and none of this runs end to end. No relay runs today, so nothing can be paired yet.

- The live screens on the room are an interactive design mock of the iPhone and Watch apps, running as a web page. The ceremony the app implements is stricter than this mock.

- The org, team and agent ladder on the Budgets screen is a drawn design.

- No console code issues a pairing code today.

- The mock draws a Default and a Strict peer mode for the Device screen. Neither is built.

- `spend_spike` never reaches the mail. An operator who only reads mail does not learn about it.

- The kill from the wrist on the room is a simulation, but it replays a shape the app is built for.

## Back to the room.

The [Pocket room](https://it-rat.com/services/pocket.html) has the simulation, the live design mock and the drawing, and [the guides index](https://it-rat.com/guides.html) has the field itself.

<!-- https://it-rat.com/wardryx-guide.html -->

# Wardryx guide

> How Wardryx decides allow, deny or hold, how to run it, what changed from 1 to 15 October 2026, and what is open by default or not proven yet.

The [Wardryx room](https://it-rat.com/services/wardryx.html) keeps the simulation, the drawing and the common questions. This guide keeps the rest of what the room used to say: how a hold is resolved, the modes and the outage choice, where it sits, how to run it, what changed from 1 to 15 October 2026, and its limits.

- [At a glance](https://it-rat.com/wardryx-guide.html#overview)

- [How it works](https://it-rat.com/wardryx-guide.html#how-it-works)

- [Where it sits](https://it-rat.com/wardryx-guide.html#where-it-sits)

- [Running it](https://it-rat.com/wardryx-guide.html#run)

- [What changed](https://it-rat.com/wardryx-guide.html#changes)

- [What changed in November](https://it-rat.com/wardryx-guide.html#changes-november)

- [Limits](https://it-rat.com/wardryx-guide.html#limits)

## Wardryx at a glance.

- **Deterministic allow, deny or hold, with a human on the expensive actions.**

- **Status:** v2.5.1, surface frozen at 1.0 · main is supported.

- **Core:** Go 1.27 · deterministic PDP. **API:** POST /v1/decide on :8090.

- **Rules:** deny_tool · allow_tool · allow_models · allow_domains · max_steps · deny_if_unattested · require_identity_source · max_chain_depth · require_root_principal · deny_if_chain_unproven · deny_above_usd · require_human_above_usd · hold_if_signal.

- **Lineage:** PDP/PEP · XACML's good ideas.

- **Licence:** Apache-2.0.

### What it is

Your gateway asks one question before an agent acts: POST /v1/decide. Wardryx answers allow, deny or hold in one deterministic pass. No LLM sits in the decision path, so the same policy and the same request always return the same verdict, and a big spend waits for a human who signs off with a short-lived token. The pattern is old and good: PDP/PEP, XACML's good ideas, pointed at what agents do.

## Rules in one fixed order. No moods.

### Sixty seconds, thirty-four requests

This is a simulation, and it says so. It replays the shape of the live validation record: a 34-request concurrent burst, different agents, budgets and policies, all hitting /v1/decide at once. In the real run the filtering came back exact: 6/6 permission oversteppers denied with 403, unattested calls denied until attested, 176 decisions across the full campaign. [Watch it in the room](https://it-rat.com/services/wardryx.html#sim).

### One question in. One of three answers out.

The PEP posts the proposed action: agent, tools, declared domains, step count, estimated cost, attestation. Wardryx matches policies by agent:// glob and applies the rules in a fixed order, where deny_above_usd outranks every approval and the hold check comes after it. The verdict returns with a cacheable flag, the caller's cache keys on agent, tool set and attestation, and every decision leaves as an event.

### Three verdicts, zero improvisation

Every answer is allow, deny or hold. No LLM sits in the decision path, so the same policy set and the same request return the same verdict, every time. A decision you can replay in a test is a decision you can defend in an audit.

### Hold means a human

A big spend becomes a hold, not a guess. A human grants it out of band and the agent resubmits with a signed token; nothing parks a connection waiting for a signature.

### A hold that holds nothing open

The agent asks, Wardryx answers `hold` with an approval id, and the call ends there. A human decides out of band, Wardryx mints an approval token, and the agent asks again with the token in hand; that second answer is `allow`. No connection is parked waiting for a signature, and Wardryx does not have to remember an open request: the grant is proven by the token, not by anyone's memory of it.

The token is bound to what was actually approved. Its claims name the agent, the run and the exact sorted set of tools, and carry an expiry, ten minutes by default; verification checks the signature over the still-encoded payload before reading any claim, then checks that what is being asked matches what was granted. A token for one run does not quietly authorise another.

Since v1.2.0 an approval is also bound to the tool call a person read, when the held request carried one. The person is shown the tool and its target, and the token carries a digest of the name, the target and the exact arguments, so it is refused for any other call, the same JSON re-spaced included. A call whose arguments were too large to send binds only its name and target.

The signing is fail-closed. The token is signed by Keyryx custody (ES256) when WARDRYX_APPROVAL_SIGNER=keyryx, which the stack-single and stack-up launchers set (and stack-k8s sets it by default from 1.6.0, tagged 2026-10-19, unless it is deployed with --without-keyryx), and with an HMAC secret otherwise. With neither a signer nor the secret, Wardryx refuses to mint or verify rather than accepting anything, because there is no such thing as an unsigned or always-valid approval. Since 1.0 a token works once by default: the first redemption is recorded atomically, so presenting the same token twice falls back to a fresh hold instead of silently allowing the action again. Setting `WARDRYX_APPROVAL_SINGLE_USE=false` makes it reusable within its window. With no shared database that single-use guarantee is per process, and the server says so at startup rather than letting you assume otherwise.

### A spent error budget is a reason to hold

The quality plane, [Verdryx](https://it-rat.com/services/verdryx.html), writes an `slo_burn` event to its event file when an agent's error budget is exhausted or burning fast. With `WARDRYX_SIGNAL_EVENTS` pointing at that file, Wardryx adds one standing signal named `slo_burn` to the agent's decisions, and a `hold_if_signal` rule on it holds the call. A granted approval lets that one call through, as for any hold. It is off unless the setting is set, and it changes nothing without a rule that reads the signal: same answer, same policy version.

```
name: hold-while-the-budget-is-spent
target: "agent://acme.example/support/*"
hold_if_signal:
  name: slo_burn
  values: [exhausted, fast_burn]
  min_probability: 1
```

The signal takes four values, `exhausted`, `fast_burn`, `unmeasured` and `none`, always at probability 1. An unmeasured zero is not evidence of health: a fast burn whose `burn_events_seen` is missing, zero, negative, fractional or not a number reads as `unmeasured`, never as `none` and never as `fast_burn`. An exhausted event stands on the budget, so its `burn_events_seen` does not matter. While the file is sound the signal is present for every agent, because `when_absent: hold` holds every call with no signal of the rule's name, and a signal only for agents with an event would make that setting hold the healthy ones too. Absence therefore means one thing: the file cannot be believed, and the policy's `when_absent` decides.

The reader sits outside the decision code, so the signal can add a hold and nothing else, and a recorded decision replays with the file gone. A caller's own `slo_burn` signal is dropped, so it cannot end an absence hold. An event signals for `WARDRYX_SIGNAL_EVENTS_MAX_AGE` after its time (48 hours unless set), the newest event of an indicator replaces its older ones, and the quality plane writes no event on recovery, so recovery is a weaker event or the age running out.

The file is checked before it is believed. The hash chain is verified, and a broken chain, a malformed line, a restart, a start in the middle of a chain, a time in the future or a file past its size bound reads as `broken`; a missing file, or one that is not a plain file, reads as `unreadable`. `/readyz` says which in `signal_events` without changing its status code, and the log names the file and the reason once per change.

### A hard ceiling that outranks approvals

deny_above_usd is the rule no token can talk past. It is checked before the hold logic ever runs, so even a granted approval cannot authorize a spend over the ceiling. Some numbers should end the conversation, and this one does.

### Attestation as a first-class gate

deny_if_unattested demands a live attestation before an agent touches the sensitive rules. Methods are trimmed and lowercased on the way in, so a literal “None” string reads as no attestation instead of sneaking past as a value.

### A proof is accepted once, on every instance

When a decide carries an agent's DPoP proof, Wardryx accepts that proof once. With `WARDRYX_DB` set, the record of accepted proofs is the table `agent_proof_replays`, shared by every instance on that database. A proof presented at a second instance, or again after a restart, is refused with `403 agent_token_proof_invalid`. The claim is one atomic insert and the last step of the check, so only a proof that passed every other check reaches the database, and the key is a hash over the holder's key thumbprint and the proof's id, so no client byte reaches SQL and one holder cannot spend another's id. A row is kept until the longest proof window has closed, and a purge removes the rows after that.

A record that cannot be asked refuses. A proof nobody could check for replay may be a replay, so a store that is gone answers `503 agent_token_proof_unrecorded`, a store that failed with an error of its own answers 500, and the process does not stand in with a memory of its own. TokenFuse treats any answer outside 2xx as its fail mode, closed under enforce unless an operator set it open. A request with no proof decides from memory as before. Without a database the record stays in the process, and serve says so at start.

### Fail-open or fail-closed, your call

When the decision point is unreachable, the enforcement point picks the failure mode per deployment. The TokenFuse gateway closes under enforce when its failure mode is unset, and stays open in shadow mode, where it blocks nothing; all three launchers set it closed on purpose. The egress point fails closed with no override. Every default is documented, and so is the tradeoff.

### Three modes at the call site, and one honest choice about outages

Wardryx itself never acts. It answers; the enforcement point, a gateway or a proxy, decides how much weight to give the answer. There are three settings at that call site.

Two enforcement points ask this plane, and the answer lives at the call site rather than here. **TokenFuse**'s binary closes under enforce when its failure mode is unset, and stays open in shadow mode, where it blocks nothing. It was open under enforce until 2026-10-17, for the reason a money plane gives: a call refused on every policy blink costs production traffic during a network partition. All three launchers set it closed, because on a box that exists to govern, policy wins. That is not a reading of the configuration. On 2026-09-17 the policy plane was stopped under a box governing two clouds, and every call came back `403 wardryx unreachable` in 0.3 s, none reaching the provider, until it was started again. **Scopyx** fails closed with no override: an egress point that failed open is an unrestricted fetch proxy wearing a governance label, and that failure would be silent.

**off** never calls the decision point at all: local development, or an environment with no policy loaded. **shadow** asks on every call and records the answer while the action always proceeds, which is how a new policy set is validated against real traffic before it can block anything. **enforce** makes the answer binding: a deny stops the call, a hold pauses it until a signed approval token is presented.

Then the question everyone postpones: what happens when the decision point cannot be reached. Fail-open treats it as allow, so availability wins and an outage silently disables policy. Fail-closed treats it as deny, so policy wins and an outage blocks every governed action until it recovers. There is no clever third answer; there is only choosing on purpose and writing the choice down.

Wardryx applies the same rule to itself. Started with no policy configured, it starts anyway and allows, and it says so in the log rather than pretending to enforce something it was never given.

### Policy admin API + Terraform

PUT, GET and DELETE /v1/policies/{id} manage a runtime policy layer with validate-then-apply semantics; the file-loaded set stays a permanent floor no API write can erase. A PUT whose body holds a key the policy does not declare is refused with 400 and stores nothing (since 1.3.2). The taipan_wardryx_policy resource drives the same API from Terraform.

## The desk every expensive idea stops at.

[TokenFuse](https://it-rat.com/services/tokenfuse.html)'s PEP hook asks Wardryx on every request and stamps the verdict on the response. Each decision lands on the bus as a source: wardryx event, which [Idryx](https://it-rat.com/services/idryx.html) correlates into the identity graph. [Mockryx](https://it-rat.com/services/mockryx.html) rehearses the denials in pre-prod, so the first real no is never the first no ever. And the policies themselves are code: the [Platform](https://it-rat.com/services/platform.html) page's Terraform provider creates, changes and destroys them like any other resource. A typed risk signal from [Typryx](https://it-rat.com/services/typryx.html) can turn an allow into a hold for a person and never into a deny: since v1.2.0 a decision reads `signals` and the pending `tool_call`, a `hold_if_signal` rule can only hold, and Typryx's `wardryx-proxy` adds the signal on the way in. The launchers offer it as an opt-in, off by default.

The policy point is one control among several: see [AI agent security](https://it-rat.com/ai-agent-security.html) for the failure modes it answers, and [AI agent governance](https://it-rat.com/ai-agent-governance.html) for how the planes fit together.

### A decision is only as good as the identity under it.

This plane answers about an action. What it cannot answer is whether the caller really holds the delegation it claims, which is a different question with a different mechanism: [Vouchryx](https://it-rat.com/services/vouchryx.html) mints a short-lived token bound to the caller's own key and lets a person end it, and a hold resolved by a signed approval token is the same idea pointed at one action rather than at a delegation.

## Running it.

```
make serve
```

Boots on `127.0.0.1:8090` with an in-memory store. `serve` refuses to start without `WARDRYX_KEYS`, so `make serve` opts in to the dev key on loopback only: allow-all until you load a policy, and it logs that choice. Then dry-run a policy offline against a directory of Agent Passports:

```
./bin/wardryx check ./passports ./policies/finance.yaml
```

## What the policy plane gained from 1 to 15 October

The whole stack's fortnight, Wardryx among it, is in [the October changelog](https://it-rat.com/changes-2026-10.html#wardryx).

| shipped in | what it does |
|---|---|
| v1.3.0 | A policy can name the only tools its agents may use. A requested tool the list does not name is denied, and no approval can lift that. |
| v1.3.1 | Every document of a YAML policy file, and every value of a JSON policy file, is loaded. A file that does not load stops the service at start, and the error names the part that failed. |
| v1.3.2 | A policy write with a field the policy does not declare is refused with a 400, and nothing is stored. Before, the field was dropped and the write still answered 200. |
| v1.4.0 | A policy can hold a tool call whose risk signal never arrives (when_absent: hold), for a person to decide. |
| v1.5.0 | A policy can name the only models its agents may use. A request for any other model is denied on that call. |

## What changed in November

| shipped in | what it does |
|---|---|
| v2.5.0 | With a database set, the record of accepted DPoP proofs is shared by every instance and survives a restart: a proof is accepted once, and a record that cannot be asked refuses the decide with a 503. |
| v2.5.0 | A spent error budget can put an agent's tool calls to a person: with WARDRYX_SIGNAL_EVENTS set, a hold_if_signal rule on slo_burn holds the call. |
| v2.5.1 | The policy archive is created with directory mode 0750 and file mode 0640, so the account that runs wardryx replay can read it from the group of the account that writes it. An archive written before keeps its modes until an operator widens it. |

## What is open by default, and what is not proven yet.

- When the decision point is unreachable, the enforcement point picks the failure mode per deployment. The TokenFuse gateway closes under enforce when its failure mode is unset, and stays open in shadow mode, where it blocks nothing; all three launchers set it closed on purpose. The egress point fails closed with no override.

- Started with no policy configured, it starts anyway and allows, and it says so in the log rather than pretending to enforce something it was never given.

- With no shared database the single-use guarantee of an approval token is per process, and the server says so at startup rather than letting you assume otherwise. Setting `WARDRYX_APPROVAL_SINGLE_USE=false` makes a token reusable within its window.

- A call whose arguments were too large to send binds only its name and target.

- An outage of the store behind the proof record stops every decide that carries a proof. Every instance must run this build, because an older one keeps its own record, and two clocks more than five minutes apart can accept a proof twice.

- The chain behind the budget signal shows that a line was not edited or removed from the middle. It does not say who wrote the file and cannot see lines cut from the end, so the file is as trustworthy as its permissions. An event is matched by exact agent id, in no org, and a crash mid-write leaves the file broken until it is moved aside. Under `when_absent: hold`, a file that cannot be read holds every tool call of the agents the rule matches.

- The typed risk signal from Typryx: the launchers offer it as an opt-in, off by default.

- The room's stampede is a simulation, and it says so: it replays the shape of the live validation record.

## Back to the room.

The [Wardryx room](https://it-rat.com/services/wardryx.html) has the simulation, the drawing and the common questions, and [the guides index](https://it-rat.com/guides.html) has the field itself.
