# Idryx guide

> How Idryx builds one identity graph and what its detectors look for, how to run it, what it answers, and what it does not do or prove yet.

The [Idryx room](https://it-rat.com/services/idryx.html) keeps the simulation, the drawing and the common questions. This guide keeps the rest of what the room used to say: what the graph is made of, what the detectors look for, what it answers, where it sits, how to run it, and its limits.

- [At a glance](https://it-rat.com/idryx-guide.html#overview)

- [How it works](https://it-rat.com/idryx-guide.html#how-it-works)

- [What it answers](https://it-rat.com/idryx-guide.html#what-it-answers)

- [Where it sits](https://it-rat.com/idryx-guide.html#where-it-sits)

- [Running it](https://it-rat.com/idryx-guide.html#run)

- [What changed](https://it-rat.com/idryx-guide.html#changes)

- [What changed in November](https://it-rat.com/idryx-guide.html#changes-november)

- [Limits](https://it-rat.com/idryx-guide.html#limits)

## Idryx at a glance.

- **Every identity on one graph, every unused grant on notice.**

- **Release:** latest · prebuilt binaries. **Core:** Go 1.27 · 27 detectors.

- **Connectors:** Okta · Entra · AWS · GCP · Azure.

- **Output:** CycloneDX 1.6 Agent-BOM.

- **Posture:** read-only, proposes diffs.

- **Licence:** Apache-2.0.

### What it is

Your IdP counts the humans. Nobody counts the keys, the service accounts, or the agents acting on their behalf. Idryx reads what Okta, Entra, AWS, GCP and Azure already log, adds the agent-event bus, stitches all of it into one identity graph with delegation chains and blast radius, and runs 27 deterministic detectors over the result. Read-only by design: it proposes Terraform diffs, it never applies.

## Five identity kinds. One set of answers.

### Sixty seconds, one graph

This is a simulation, but it replays the shape of the live validation run: TokenFuse agent-event NDJSON and Agent Passports land in a Postgres-backed graph, the detectors read the state back, and findings fire. The same three detectors fired against a real Postgres 16 during validation: runaway_agent, attestation_missing, orphaned_nhi. [Watch it in the room](https://it-rat.com/services/idryx.html#sim).

### Sources in. Findings out. Nothing written back.

Read-only connectors for Okta, Entra, AWS, GCP and Azure describe the humans, keys and service accounts; the agent-event bus streams what TokenFuse, Wardryx, Mockryx, Verdryx and Scopyx watched the agents do. One core resolves the graph, walks delegation chains root-first, and runs the 27 detectors. Everything that leaves is an alert, a BOM, a proposed diff a human applies, or an identity_finding event on the bus.

### One graph, every identity

Humans, service accounts, keys, MCP servers and AI agents: five node kinds in one graph, not five tools. Agents are first-class, keyed name@url, with owner, runtime and attestation pinned to the node instead of lost in a generic service-account bucket.

### Delegation chains

on_behalf_of edges record who acts for whom: agent to sub-agent to service account to human. The walk is cycle-safe and resolves root-first, so the question audits stall on for weeks gets answered in one query.

### Five kinds of identity, five kinds of edge, one question answered

Every identity is one of five kinds: a human, a service account, a key, an AI agent, or an MCP server exposing tools. Putting them in one graph is the whole point, because the interesting failures live in the joins, not inside any single directory.

They are connected by a deliberately small set of edges. `on_behalf_of` is the dynamic delegation chain, ordered root first: who this identity is acting for right now. `owner` names the human or team accountable for rotating and revoking it. `has_scope` carries each grant along with whether it is admin-equivalent and whether it has ever been used. `calls_tool` joins an agent to the tools an MCP server exposes, which is how a poisoned tool is traced back to the agent that can call it. And a separate parent edge records the static provisioning relationship, which is an org chart, not an act of delegation, and is kept apart from one.

Resolving those edges is what makes blast radius computable: an identity's reach is the union of every permission along its chain, not the list of grants attached to its own name. That distinction is the difference between a key that looks harmless and a key that reaches admin two hops away.

### 27 deterministic detectors

Statistics and rules over the graph, in four families. The LLM is never in the detection path, so every finding is reproducible and auditable.

### What the 27 detectors look for, and why none of them ask a model

Detection is deterministic: statistics and rules over the graph. The model is an interface for asking questions in English and getting explanations back, and it is never in the detection path, so a finding can be reproduced, argued with and defended in an audit. A baseline engine learns what is normal per identity and stays quiet during its learning period rather than opening a week of false positives on day one.

**Identity threats.** Impossible travel, MFA fatigue, a privileged identity on an unseen device, and logins that deviate from that identity's learned country, device and active hours.

**Non-human identity hygiene.** Service accounts unused past ninety days, non-human identities holding admin-equivalent permissions or no owner at all, and the quiet escalation permissions that grant a path to admin without holding admin: `iam:PassRole` on AWS, `actAs` on GCP, role-assignment writes on Azure. A credential seen from many countries, IPs or devices is flagged for what it usually is: shared or leaked.

**Agents and AI.** An agent that reaches admin through its delegation chain; egress to a known external LLM API; an MCP server in use but missing from the sanctioned registry, and an agent whose declared tools are exposed by that unsanctioned server; a spend runaway correlated with the agent's privilege, delegation depth and blast radius; a privileged agent with no attestation on record; DLP-blocked actions accumulating within a day; a taint-tracked action stopped; an MCP server whose tooling changed under an agent; an agent whose passport declares one set of model providers while its egress reaches another; connections to one destination on a regular cadence (beaconing); a process that names itself an agent identity which no Passport, IAM record or event knows (claimed_agent_unknown), or that reaches an LLM provider its Passport does not declare (claimed_agent_drift); an agent whose Passport binds it to a workload while its only runtime carrier is a process that named itself (claimed_agent_unattested); and an agent whose web egress an enforcement point governs but which opened its own connections to public addresses (unrouted_egress).

**Least privilege.** Permissions granted and never exercised, with a revocation to propose. It fires only where usage data exists, so a source with no observed-usage signal produces no recommendations rather than confident nonsense.

### The Agent-BOM

When the auditor asks what agents you run, the answer is a CycloneDX 1.6 document: owner, runtime, attestation, tools and delegation chain for every agent identity. Its companion detector, bom_incomplete, flags the agents the BOM cannot yet prove.

### Blast radius

What does this key reach, transitively? Idryx computes the union of every permission reachable through an identity's delegation chain. excessive_agency fires when an agent reaches admin-equivalent power through that chain (OWASP LLM06).

### eBPF network sensor

A Linux-only sensor on a kprobe on __sys_connect_file, run on arm64 and x86_64 kernels, captures real outbound connections and flags egress to known LLM APIs. unmanaged_egress fires for identities the sensor is the only evidence of: no IAM record, no passport, just traffic. Pointed at a real agent on an x86_64 box, it labelled every one of the agent's flows with the passport the agent claimed, showed its model calls leaving through the gateway, and caught the one thing that did not: the agent connecting straight to the PyPI package hosts when it started. That was one agent turn on one lab node, on 2026-09-27; it has not yet run on a fleet or a cloud host.

### AI usage: declared, seen, in the code

`idryx ai-inventory` compared its sources provider by provider. It now also says, for each agent or service, what was declared, what was seen and what the code can reach, and it names every disagreement. Nothing in it is scored or ranked, and nothing in it is a detector.

**One row per source.** The report is built from up to five sources: `declared`, `bus`, `egress`, `ebpf` and `code`. A source nobody supplied is a row that says what its absence means. Code not scanned is not nothing in the code, and an absent capture is not a capture that saw nothing.

**One row per subject and provider, with the disagreement named:** `declared_not_seen`, `declared_bus_only`, `seen_not_declared`, `seen_no_declaration`, `declares_no_models` and `no_declaration`, and on provider rows `in_code_not_seen`. The bus names no provider, so an agent active there through an enforcement point is shown as `bus_only`, which is a different statement from not seen: a governed agent's provider connection is made by the gateway's process, where only a capture of that host sees it. A source scan finds a file and a line, and no field binds a repository to an identity, so the code column stays per provider for the whole estate.

It joins on the provider vocabulary `ai-inventory` already used, with no second vocabulary and no change to any shared contract. The JSON document gains `sources` and `subjects`, each provider row gains `gaps`, and the schema string `idryx.ai-inventory/v1` stays. There is no new subcommand and no new flag.

The report agrees with the detectors, and a test holds it. The agents it names `seen_not_declared` are exactly the agents `undeclared_llm` fires for, and the processes it names `seen_no_declaration` are exactly the ones `unmanaged_egress` grades as having reached a model API. The qryx document it reads is untrusted input: its size and the number of providers and labels are bounded, every kept string is escaped and cut, and names from a passport, a bus envelope or a capture are escaped before they reach a terminal. Three monitoring limits travel with every report: attribution is self-declared, the eBPF sensor is Linux-only, and a process with code execution can open a socket of its own.

## Built for the identities that never log in.

Your IdP counts the humans. The keys, service accounts and agents acting on their behalf are what this is built around: an agent is a node kind here, not a field bolted onto a user record. It reads Okta, Entra, AWS, GCP and Azure as sources of truth and proposes changes back as Terraform, never applying them itself.

| Question you ask | What answers it |
|---|---|
| What is acting in my estate, and on whose behalf | One graph of humans, service accounts, keys, agents and MCP servers |
| Who let this agent do that | Delegation chains, resolved root-first to the human at the top |
| What breaks if this credential is taken | Blast radius, computed over the graph |
| What is wrong right now | 27 deterministic detectors, each one named and separately testable |
| What reached an LLM API that nobody provisioned | The eBPF sensor, and unmanaged_egress for identities it is the only evidence of |
| Prove it to an auditor | A CycloneDX Agent-BOM, generated from the graph rather than typed up |
| Change something | It proposes a Terraform diff. Applying it stays your decision |
| Start today | Point it at logs you already keep. Apache-2.0, on hardware you own |

## The one that reads everything and touches nothing.

Idryx consumes the same envelope [TokenFuse](https://it-rat.com/services/tokenfuse.html), [Wardryx](https://it-rat.com/services/wardryx.html), [Mockryx](https://it-rat.com/services/mockryx.html), [Verdryx](https://it-rat.com/services/verdryx.html) and [Scopyx](https://it-rat.com/services/scopyx.html) write: the agent-event. It validates Agent Passports against the [platform contract](https://it-rat.com/services/platform.html), and the loop closes at the policy plane: Wardryx's deny_if_unattested policy refuses an agent with no live attestation, and the gateway answers that refusal with a 403 instead of your production data. Idryx's attestation_missing detector reports those agents in the graph.

Blast radius, shadow tooling and unattested agents are covered as failure modes in [AI agent security](https://it-rat.com/ai-agent-security.html), the graph's place among the planes in [AI agent governance](https://it-rat.com/ai-agent-governance.html), and what an agent identity has to be in [agent identity and authentication](https://it-rat.com/agent-identity.html).

### It records who acts for whom. It does not prove it.

The delegation chain here is a record: each identity lists the on_behalf_of chain it acts under, root first, and the graph walks that chain to show what the identity can reach. [Vouchryx](https://it-rat.com/services/vouchryx.html) is the other half, proof of possession per request and a revocation an incident can actually use, and every finding it produces lands on the same bus this graph is folded from.

## Running it.

```
idryx detect events.ndjson
```

```
idryx serve events.ndjson
```

Download [the latest release binary](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/idryx/releases) (SHA256SUMS ships next to it), run detect against a log, then serve for the read-only dashboard on `:8080`.

### idryx, every platform

Every one of those addresses always serves the newest release, so a link saved today still works after the next one. The asset names carry no version, which is what makes that true; the version lives inside the binary, where `idryx version` reads it back.

## What changed.

Idryx's releases from 1 to 15 October 2026 are listed in [the October changelog](https://it-rat.com/changes-2026-10.html#idryx), beside the rest of the stack's.

## What changed in November

| shipped in | what it does |
|---|---|
| v1.4.0 | idryx ai-inventory reports, for each agent or service, what was declared, what was seen and what the code can reach, and names every disagreement. Additive to the idryx.ai-inventory/v1 schema. |

## What it does not do, and what is not proven yet.

- **Read-only by design:** it proposes Terraform diffs, it never applies. Applying a diff stays your decision.

- The delegation chain here is a record. Proof of possession per request, and a revocation an incident can use, are [Vouchryx](https://it-rat.com/services/vouchryx.html)'s half.

- A baseline engine learns what is normal per identity and stays quiet during its learning period rather than opening a week of false positives on day one.

- Least privilege fires only where usage data exists, so a source with no observed-usage signal produces no recommendations rather than confident nonsense.

- The companion detector bom_incomplete flags the agents the BOM cannot yet prove.

- The eBPF network sensor is Linux-only. It has attached and captured live flows on two kernels: a Docker Desktop Linux VM on a Mac (2026-09-08, arm64 kernel 7.0.12; a 12-second capture in a container, not against an agent: 3 flows on the fixed build, after 16 of the first run's 21 flows turned out to be the sensor's own traffic) and one x86_64 lab node (2026-09-27, one agent turn, 349 flows in 70 seconds). It has not yet run on a fleet or a cloud host.

- The bus carries a model only in `call_retained`, which the AI usage report does not read, so it compares no model names with anything: the egress side names a host, never a model. Whether an identity has a declaration is read from its source or from a declared model or attestation, which is a reading of the graph and not an attested fact.

- The room's runaway is a simulation, but it replays the shape of the live validation run.

## Back to the room.

The [Idryx room](https://it-rat.com/services/idryx.html) has the simulation, the drawing and the common questions, and [the guides index](https://it-rat.com/guides.html) has the field itself.

# Scopyx guide

> How Scopyx decides an agent's web egress, how to run its two images, what changed from 1 to 15 October 2026, and what it will not do, in full.

The [Scopyx room](https://it-rat.com/services/scopyx.html) keeps the request in flight, the two mechanisms you can switch off, what the record keeps, and how to start it. This guide keeps the rest of what the room used to say: the measured run behind the gates, redirects, the backends it decides over, what a result admits, how to run and configure it, what changed from 1 to 15 October 2026, and what it will not do.

- [At a glance](https://it-rat.com/scopyx-guide.html#overview)

- [How it works](https://it-rat.com/scopyx-guide.html#how-it-works)

- [Redirects](https://it-rat.com/scopyx-guide.html#redirects)

- [What it decides over](https://it-rat.com/scopyx-guide.html#backends)

- [Two mechanisms in a browser](https://it-rat.com/scopyx-guide.html#mechanisms)

- [What the answer admits](https://it-rat.com/scopyx-guide.html#fidelity)

- [What is kept](https://it-rat.com/scopyx-guide.html#record)

- [Running it](https://it-rat.com/scopyx-guide.html#run)

- [Behind the broker](https://it-rat.com/scopyx-guide.html#broker)

- [What changed](https://it-rat.com/scopyx-guide.html#changes)

- [What changed in November](https://it-rat.com/scopyx-guide.html#changes-november)

- [Limits](https://it-rat.com/scopyx-guide.html#limits)

## Scopyx at a glance.

- **Shipped:** v1.3.0, two images (default and -chromium).

- **Core:** Go 1.27 · one direct dependency.

- **One way out:** http and https, and nothing else.

- **Fails:** closed, and says which refusal.

- **Keeps:** the origin and a hash, not the URL unless you opt in.

- **Licence:** Apache-2.0.

### What it is

Every other plane in the stack governs what your agents do to your own services: what they spend, what they may call, who they are. None of them watches the one direction that leads outside. An agent reads a page, and the page tells it what to do next. An agent posts a customer list to an address it found in a prompt. Scopyx sits between an agent and whatever fetching tool you already run, and adds the four things that were missing: a decision before the request, a decision on every redirect, a bound on what comes back, and a record of the fetch and of the refusal.

## Five gates, in this order, and the order is the claim.

The verdicts run in this order: the scheme, the host, every address that name resolves to at the moment of the fetch, your policy plane, and last the site's own `robots.txt`. Before the first verdict the plane resolves the name and asks your policy plane once per host, so a refused destination costs one lookup and one policy question. It is never fetched, and its `robots.txt` is never requested. The [room](https://it-rat.com/services/scopyx.html#flight) runs four requests through the gates; pick one and watch where it stops.

### The diagram argues. This is the receipt.

Four real requests, one container, the published image against a fixture policy and the live internet. Watch where each stops: a name pointing inside your own deployment is refused before any policy runs, and the request that never became a request is the last row.

The third row is the one worth reading twice. The fixture policy said **allow**, and it was refused anyway. Policy languages talk about domains an agent may reach, and none of them was written with the cloud metadata endpoint in mind: an agent that can be talked into fetching that address reads the credentials of whatever it runs on. The fourth is not a fetch at all. A free-form header parameter is a credential-laundering channel straight past a broker's inspection, so the tool has no field for one, and an unknown argument is refused by name rather than ignored.

## A redirect is a destination the caller never named.

An allowed host answering 302 to a denied one is the oldest allowlist bypass there is, and it is invisible to any check that reads only the URL the caller passed. The same argument applies one layer down, to the name itself.

### It refuses to follow

The fetcher it ships with returns the redirect instead of following it. Following inside the fetcher would be a second request that no decision preceded, which is exactly the bypass. Most HTTP clients follow redirects by default, which is why this is written down rather than assumed.

### Every hop is resolved again

The target's name is looked up at the moment of the hop, never from anything remembered. An address resolved a minute ago would satisfy the check while the fetch reached something else.

### And the socket goes where the decision looked

Every HTTP client resolves the name again, inside the dialer, with no memory of what was checked, and a hostile zone answers differently between the two lookups for nothing. So the checked addresses are pinned and the transport refuses to dial a host no decision covered, which makes it the floor under everything above it: a code path that reached out without asking cannot open a socket.

### And bounded twice

Your configured depth, and a ceiling the plane keeps regardless. Two servers pointing at each other is a fetch that never returns, and a fetch that never returns is worse than one that is refused, because nothing reports it.

## It is not a browser, and that is the whole design.

Scopyx supplies no capability you do not already have. Point it at the fetching service you already run, through an HTTP endpoint that speaks scopyx's external contract (SCOPYX_EXTERNAL_ENDPOINT). A vendor API needs an adapter in front of it, and this repository ships none. Either way, the tool you own gains a decision, a bound and a record. Anyone proposing a feature here should ask whether it makes the fetch better or the fetch more governed. The first belongs in somebody else's product.

### The one that needs nothing

The default fetcher wants no account, no API token and no browser on the host, so a box is governed on the day it is installed rather than the day somebody arranges a fetching service. It runs no JavaScript, and the result names its backend as passthrough-http, which is how you can tell, because a page assembled in a browser arrives as the shell that assembles it.

### The one your invoice already covers

Wrapping a service you already run is the commercially important case and the least impressive code in the repository. A destination your policy refuses never reaches that service, so it never appears in your bill for it either.

### And a browser you installed

It runs the page's own JavaScript, so a document assembled in the browser arrives assembled. Nothing is bundled and nothing is downloaded: the image stays small, and a missing browser is refused at startup with a message about the browser rather than at the first fetch with a message about the network.

## A page is forty requests nobody named. Here is what stops them.

A rendering backend is the first one that fetches things the caller never asked for: fonts, images, scripts, each potentially a different host. Two separate things stop a refused one, and they are not redundancy for its own sake. Switch either off and the refused server is still never reached; switch both off and it is reached once, and the chromium test that asserts otherwise goes red.

The two switches are on the [room](https://it-rat.com/services/scopyx.html#mechanisms).

## Governed at the navigation is not governed per request.

A fetch through a service you already run is decided before it is made, and then that service loads the page's images, fonts and scripts with nothing in between. The navigation was governed. The requests it caused were not. Every result says which of the two guarantees was in force, so a partial answer is visible as one rather than read as a complete one.

### A count nobody can supply is null

Zero says the page asked for nothing. Null says nobody knows. Reporting the second as the first claims perfect fidelity for exactly the backend that can see the least, and an agent that does not know it read half a page will report confidently on the half it got.

### Nothing extracted with a failure is not an empty page

It is an error. For a person, degrading to a blank frame is right. For an agent it is the worst failure available, because the model cannot tell the difference and you cannot either.

## A URL is personal data, and the record is built around that.

`https://crm.example/customers/12345?email=jane@example.com` is an address and also a name, an identifier and a contact detail. The path and the query string, which is exactly where an identifier or a session token lives, are never assembled into the event at all. What is kept is the origin and a SHA-384, so two records can be compared without either holding the address.

### Its own journal, its own volume

A component that can write the shared log can, once compromised, corrupt the trail it was adding to. This is the one part of the box that reaches the public internet on purpose, which makes it the last one that should be able to rewrite anybody else's record.

### Chained, so a deletion shows

Every line names its predecessor, in the same envelope the rest of the stack speaks. A journal that did not chain would look identical until somebody tried to verify it, which is the moment it matters and the moment it is too late.

### No identity, no record, and the skip is counted

A fabricated subject makes every downstream count wrong and puts a name on an alert that did not do the thing. A fetch with no authenticated agent behind it is not written, and the number of times that happened is reported rather than hidden.

## Two images: default and -chromium.

```
# full command, environment and volume: https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/scopyx#run-it
# it refuses to start bound wide with no credentials, deliberately
```

```
# the -chromium image, the same service with a browser: https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/scopyx#backends
# 267 MB to pull against 3.5 MB (measured on v0.1.2, 2026-08-10)
```

### Configuration the room names

- **SCOPYX_EXTERNAL_ENDPOINT:** point it at the fetching service you already run, through an HTTP endpoint that speaks scopyx's external contract. A vendor API needs an adapter in front of it, and this repository ships none.

- **SCOPYX_RETAIN=payload:** turning retention on is a decision, and the field it writes is called url_unprotected rather than url. There is no subject-keyed payload plane here, so a field called url would imply one and a reader would assume a protection that does not exist.

- **SCOPYX_ACCEPT_KEY_IN_META=1:** read a tools/call credential from the call's own metadata instead of the header, for a plane that sits behind the TokenFuse MCP broker. Off by default.

## The key can come through the TokenFuse MCP broker.

Scopyx knows an agent by the key it presents in the `X-Scopyx-Key` header. The TokenFuse MCP broker forwards a call with nothing of the caller's, so a plane behind it never sees that header, and an agent that holds the key can go round the broker. Letting the key come through the broker means the broker can put a run's label on the act itself rather than on a tool name the agent reported; the [TokenFuse guide](https://it-rat.com/tokenfuse-guide.html#how-it-works) has that half.

With `SCOPYX_ACCEPT_KEY_IN_META=1` the door reads a `tools/call` credential from `params._meta["scopyx/key"]`. The agent writes a `{{secret:NAME}}` handle, the broker fills it in on the last hop, and the agent never holds the key. The header wins when both are sent, the entry is taken out of the request at the door so nothing past it holds the key, and a `tools/call` with no id still needs a credential: this server dispatches on the method, so a missing id is not read as a notification.

It is off by default, and then the door is the header, checked before the body, as it was. Nothing in Scopyx turns the broker on; that is deployment wiring. With the switch on, the door reads a bounded request body from whoever reaches the port, so the port belongs on a network only the broker reaches.

## What changed from 1 to 15 October

No release in the window, still 1.0.1. The same entry, beside every other service's, is in [what changed in the stack](https://it-rat.com/changes-2026-10.html#scopyx).

- Documentation and toolchain only: the Go toolchain moved to 1.27.2, the shared library pin moved to 1.3.0, the secret scan runs on every pull request, and the README was corrected against the code.

## What changed in November

| shipped in | what it does |
|---|---|
| v1.2.0 | The key can come through the TokenFuse MCP broker: SCOPYX_ACCEPT_KEY_IN_META=1 reads a tools/call credential from the call's metadata, as a handle the broker fills in. Off by default. |
| v1.3.0 | A fetch through the TokenFuse MCP broker carries the run that asked for it, so the record names that run. |

## What it will not do, stated rather than discovered.

No stealth, no CAPTCHA solving, no TLS-fingerprint matching, no bulk crawl, no image harvesting, and `robots.txt` is honoured. It identifies itself as scopyx to robots.txt and on the default fetcher. A browser you installed sends its own user agent to the page, because the plane does not set one.

### Because of what this is for

Defensive tooling for an operator governing their own agents. A component that defeated a third party's controls would be the first thing here useful to somebody attacking a stranger, and that is a different product.

### And because of Article 5

The EU AI Act prohibits untargeted scraping of facial images to build recognition databases. A bulk-crawl mode is the feature that turns a governance tool into that, so there is not one.

### The one that needed code

Every other line above holds because no code path exists to do it, and an absence enforces itself. Honouring `robots.txt` is the only one that had to be written: group boundaries, longest match, Allow beating Disallow at equal length, and both wildcards. It reads as one item in a list and it is not one.

### What it claims under the AI Act

Scopyx applies rules you wrote and infers nothing, so we do not treat it as an AI system under Article 3(1). Whether a system you run is one is for your own legal review. Used beside one, it supplies evidence for Article 12 record-keeping and Article 14 human oversight. The wording here is "covers the requirements of Article 12", never "AI Act compliant", because there is no certification and no auditor behind those words, and a claim nobody can hold is worse than no claim.

### What is not proven or not shipped

- A vendor API needs an adapter in front of it, and this repository ships none.

- The default fetcher runs no JavaScript: a page assembled in a browser arrives as the shell that assembles it.

## Back to the room.

The [Scopyx room](https://it-rat.com/services/scopyx.html) has the request in flight, the two switches and the record, and [the guides index](https://it-rat.com/guides.html) has the field itself.

# Vouchryx guide

> How Vouchryx proves and ends an agent's delegation, its seven endpoints, how to run and configure it, what changed in October and November 2026, and its limits.

The [Vouchryx room](https://it-rat.com/services/vouchryx.html) keeps the loop drawn end to end, the two kill switches, how to start it, and the common questions. This guide keeps the rest of what the room used to say: the gap it closes in full, the seven endpoints, the configuration it will not start without, a measured revocation run, what changed from 1 to 15 October 2026, and what is not proven yet.

- [At a glance](https://it-rat.com/vouchryx-guide.html#overview)

- [How it works](https://it-rat.com/vouchryx-guide.html#how-it-works)

- [The endpoints](https://it-rat.com/vouchryx-guide.html#surface)

- [Two kill switches](https://it-rat.com/vouchryx-guide.html#two-switches)

- [Configuration](https://it-rat.com/vouchryx-guide.html#configuration)

- [Running it](https://it-rat.com/vouchryx-guide.html#run)

- [What changed](https://it-rat.com/vouchryx-guide.html#changes)

- [What changed in November](https://it-rat.com/vouchryx-guide.html#changes-november)

- [Limits](https://it-rat.com/vouchryx-guide.html#limits)

## Vouchryx at a glance.

- **Status:** pre-1.0 · main is supported.

- **Core:** Go 1.27 · ES256, one runtime dependency.

- **API:** POST /v1/token on :4310.

- **Tokens:** 300s by default, capped at 3600.

- **Standards:** RFC 8693 · RFC 9449 DPoP.

- **Licence:** Apache-2.0.

### What it is

An RFC 8693 token exchange that mints a short-lived token carrying nested `act`, sender-constrained with RFC 9449 DPoP so a lifted token is useless to whoever lifted it. A revocation list enforcement points poll, and public keys anybody can verify against offline. Revoking a delegation ends the right to act on somebody's behalf at every enforcement point on its next poll of the list, 12 seconds by default at the gateway, whatever the token still says about its own expiry; a call admitted before that poll is not pulled back. The TokenFuse gateway polls that list, and so does Wardryx from 2.3.0; no other enforcement point does yet.

## The record said who acted for whom. Nothing proved it.

The Agent Passport spec disclaims two things on purpose. It is not an authentication protocol: the Passport names an agent, it does not prove possession. And it is not a freshness claim: the delegation chain records who acted on behalf of whom, not when. So the estate held the record of a delegation and pointed at a mechanism that did not exist. This is that mechanism, and it does not replace `on_behalf_of`; it makes it provable and lets it be ended.

### Proof of possession, per request

The minted token carries `cnf.jkt`, the thumbprint of the caller's own key. Spending it needs a fresh DPoP proof from that same key on every call, so a token copied out of a log buys nothing.

### Revocation an incident can use

By one token id, or by subject for every token an agent already holds. The list carries `as_of`, so an empty answer and an unreachable service are never the same answer to a machine reading it. Run end to end on a cluster: an agent revoked by subject mid-run was refused at the gateway 2.2 seconds later, with the gateway polling every second rather than its default of every 12.

### Verification without a round trip

Public keys at a JWKS endpoint, so an enforcement point verifies offline. That is also why there is no introspection endpoint, on purpose: it would put this service on the request path of every enforcement point at once.

## Seven endpoints, and one that deliberately does not exist.

| POST /v1/token | The exchange. A `subject_token` and an `actor_token` in, plus a DPoP header. Out comes a short-lived JWT with nested `act` and `cnf.jkt`. Since 2026-09-24 the same route also runs Cross App Access's jwt-bearer grant (RFC 7523, an ID-JAG in), closed unless VOUCHRYX_CLIENTS is set. It also runs the `client_credentials` grant: an agent enrolled in VOUCHRYX_AGENTS gets its own five-minute credential, bound to a key it proves with DPoP, closed while VOUCHRYX_AGENTS is unset. |
|---|---|
| POST /v1/revoke | By `jti` for one token, or by `subject` for every token an agent holds. Both `actor` and `reason` are required, because a revocation nobody can attribute is an outage rather than a decision. With `"ban": true` on a subject it is also a ban: nothing names that party again until the ban is lifted. |
| POST /v1/revoke/lift | Ends a ban. `subject`, `actor` and `reason` are required, and the subject must be banned. It never un-revokes: what the party held when it was banned stays revoked. |
| GET /v1/revocations | What enforcement points poll, carrying `as_of`. Each entry holds only what a verifier needs, `jti`, `subject`, `issued_before` and `expires`; who revoked a token and why stay in the operator's record. |
| GET /.well-known/jwks.json | Public keys. Verification is offline and stays offline. |
| GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server | RFC 8414 metadata for this service's own endpoints and grants. |
| GET /healthz | No credential. Answers 200 once the process is listening; with `VOUCHRYX_SIGNER=keyryx` it answers 503 until a working key is certified, so there it reads as readiness. |
| no introspection | Refused by design. Wardryx answers at a 3.2 ms p50 and nothing here is going to sit in front of that. |

## One stops the money. This one stops the authority.

[TokenFuse](https://it-rat.com/services/tokenfuse.html) refuses a call with a 402 before the provider bills, which is the right answer to a runaway. It is the wrong answer to a compromised delegation, where the spend is affordable and the problem is that the agent may act for somebody at all. Revoking ends that at every enforcement point on its next poll, and the token's own expiry has no say in it.

## It refuses to start rather than start permissive.

Three values are required and have no default: VOUCHRYX_ISSUER, VOUCHRYX_SIGNING_KEY (for the file signer; the Keyryx signer needs its own four values instead) and VOUCHRYX_TRUSTED_ISSUERS (unless VOUCHRYX_AGENTS enrols an agent). The listen address and the token lifetime have defaults, and the others switch optional features on. A missing or malformed value aborts the process and names the variable. The reason is the shape of the two failures: a token service that came up trusting nothing would issue nothing and look healthy, and one that came up trusting a default would issue everything.

In the stack-single launcher from 1.3.0 (released 2026-10-19), vouchryx starts on every default box. From 1.6.0 (released 2026-11-05) it signs with a working key that Keyryx certifies, checked against a delegation root the box pins, and the gateway and the MCP broker poll its key set. Restarting it stops new tokens for two minutes, until the new key is valid. VOUCHRYX_SIGNER=file in .env keeps the file key, VOUCHRYX_SIGNING_KEY.

The key sets of the trusted and workload issuers are read from files, and they are read again while the service runs, every `VOUCHRYX_JWKS_RELOAD_SECONDS` (thirty unless set, 0 never, a day at most). A file that cannot be used, because it is unreadable, gone, not JSON, an error page, empty of keys or holding a key with no `kty` or `kid`, never replaces the keys held: a failure is logged once while it lasts and the recovery once. A key removed from a readable file stops verifying. The service still fetches nothing: a refresh job writes the file, and the service reads it.

## Mint it, prove it, then end it.

An RFC 8693 exchange takes two signed input tokens and a DPoP proof whose public key travels in the JWS header, which is a JOSE client before it is a curl command. So the client ships with the service: `vouchryx-demo` makes the keys, performs the exchange and prints a proof.

```
# the whole local stack with the delegation door open, from TAIPANBOX/stack-up
./up.sh --with-delegation
```

```
# prints the token, its nested act and the key thumbprint bound to it
vouchryx-demo exchange -url http://127.0.0.1:4310 -idp-key idp.pem -kid idp-1 -iss https://idp.local -aud http://127.0.0.1:4310 -subject user://acme/ada -actor agent://acme/triage -holder-key holder.pem
```

### A measured run

Measured on 2026-09-27 on the forge lab, with a lab image of vouchryx rather than a published release: a call 0.9 seconds after the subject was revoked was still answered, and one 2.2 seconds after it was refused, and every call after that was refused too. 359 tests, and the repository gates that number against its own suite.

### A run against a real provider

The loop was run against a real OpenID provider, in throwaway realms with generated credentials: the exchange, the DPoP binding, hostile tokens, revoke, ban and lift, agent credentials, the hand-off, and a workload token the provider issued. A provider's token was exchanged once the provider wrote a `user://` or `agent://` URI into `sub`, and a service account's token from the provider was presented as an RFC 7523 assertion.

One phase of the run failed, rotation. The provider's new key was in its published set the second it was created, and a token signed by it was refused with `invalid_grant` (no key in the set has that kid) for the life of the process, because a key set file was read once, at start. Against the image published at the time the rotation phase failed; with the key set files followed while running, the whole run passes. The record and its commands are in `docs/live-oidc-run.md` in the repository.

## What changed from 1 to 15 October

0.1.0 to 0.2.0, one release. The same entry, beside every other service's, is in [what changed in the stack](https://it-rat.com/changes-2026-10.html#vouchryx).

| shipped in | what it does |
|---|---|
| v0.2.0 | The public revocation list no longer says who revoked a token or why. |

## What changed in November

| shipped in | what it does |
|---|---|
| v0.7.0 | Key set files are read again while the service runs (VOUCHRYX_JWKS_RELOAD_SECONDS), so a provider that rotates its signing key is followed without a restart. Found by a run against a real OpenID provider. |

## What it does not do, and what is not proven yet.

- The TokenFuse gateway polls that list, and so does Wardryx from 2.3.0; no other enforcement point does yet.

- Revoking a delegation ends the right to act on somebody's behalf at every enforcement point on its next poll of the list, 12 seconds by default at the gateway; a call admitted before that poll is not pulled back.

- The revocation timing on this page was measured on 2026-09-27 on the forge lab, with a lab image of vouchryx rather than a published release.

- The cluster run that refused a revoked agent 2.2 seconds later had the gateway polling every second rather than its default of every 12.

- The exchange takes only `user://` or `agent://` subjects, so a provider's opaque `sub` is refused; the provider has to write the URI into `sub`, which the live run did. A mapping for other providers is a naming decision, described in `docs/live-oidc-run.md`.

- There is no introspection endpoint, on purpose: it would put this service on the request path of every enforcement point at once.

- **Status:** pre-1.0, and main is supported.

## Back to the room.

The [Vouchryx room](https://it-rat.com/services/vouchryx.html) has the loop drawn end to end and the common questions, and [the guides index](https://it-rat.com/guides.html) has the field itself.

<!-- https://it-rat.com/qryx-guide.html -->

# Qryx guide

> How Qryx finds every key and grades its post-quantum risk, the risk model, how to run it, what changed in October 2026, and what it leaves out.

The [Qryx room](https://it-rat.com/services/qryx.html) keeps the sixty-second sweep, the drawing of the one graph, how to start it, and the common questions. This guide keeps the rest of what the room used to say: what it holds in full, the risk model, how it counts honestly, where it sits in the stack, downloads for every platform, what changed from 1 to 15 October 2026, and what it leaves out.

- [At a glance](https://it-rat.com/qryx-guide.html#overview)

- [How it works](https://it-rat.com/qryx-guide.html#how-it-works)

- [What it holds](https://it-rat.com/qryx-guide.html#holds)

- [The risk model](https://it-rat.com/qryx-guide.html#risk-model)

- [Counting honestly](https://it-rat.com/qryx-guide.html#counting)

- [What it reads](https://it-rat.com/qryx-guide.html#reads)

- [In the stack](https://it-rat.com/qryx-guide.html#in-the-stack)

- [Running it](https://it-rat.com/qryx-guide.html#run)

- [What changed](https://it-rat.com/qryx-guide.html#changes)

- [Limits](https://it-rat.com/qryx-guide.html#limits)

## Qryx at a glance.

- **Release:** latest · prebuilt binaries.

- **Core:** Go 1.27 · ML-DSA (FIPS 204).

- **Scans:** binaries · containers · TLS · cloud KMS · source · certs.

- **Output:** CBOM · NCSC report · signed evidence.

- **Milestones:** NCSC 2028 · 2031 · 2035.

- **Licence:** Apache-2.0.

### What it is

A crypto audit tells you what your architecture documents say you run. Qryx tells you what is actually running: it scans binaries, containers, live TLS, certificates, dependencies and cloud KMS, and comes back with a cryptographic asset graph instead of a slide deck. Every asset gets a post-quantum grade against the NCSC's 2028, 2031 and 2035 milestones, and CI fails the day a new weak key ships, not at the next audit cycle.

## One graph. Every report reads the same one.

Five kinds of sources feed one scan engine: binaries, containers, live TLS, cloud KMS, and source plus Terraform. Findings dedupe into an asset graph keyed on algorithm, key size and risk class, so a certificate that is both expired and quantum-vulnerable gets two nodes, not one silently overwriting the other. CBOM, the CNSA audit, the NCSC readiness report and the migration plan all read that same graph, so they cannot disagree with each other.

The [room](https://it-rat.com/services/qryx.html#sim) replays a live run against 25,586 ELF binaries, a container image and a live TLS endpoint. A quantum-vulnerable cert turns up mid-sweep.

## Not a PDF audit. A graph that grades itself.

### CBOM

CycloneDX 1.6, one component per unique asset and risk class, every occurrence attached. It plugs into the same supply-chain tooling that already tracks your SBOMs, so cryptography stops living in its own isolated report.

### Harvest now, decrypt later

Data encrypted with a quantum-vulnerable algorithm today can be captured now and decrypted once a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists. The migration clock is already running.

### Post-quantum signing

Evidence attestations sign with ML-DSA (FIPS 204) straight from Go's stdlib, crypto/mldsa, no cosign dependency. All three security levels, ML-DSA-44/65/87, live-verified end to end against real openssl-generated keys.

### Context beats compliance

The asset graph keys on risk class as well as algorithm and key size, so a certificate that is both expired and quantum-vulnerable gets two findings instead of one silently overwriting the other.

### CI drift gate

Snapshot the graph, then fail the build the moment a new weak or quantum-vulnerable asset appears: a baseline diff exits 2 on new high-risk findings. The policy engine exits 3 on a standards violation; a regressed compliance trend exits 3 too.

### Agent-aware

The agents connector inventories the governance stack's own trust surface: Agent Passport attestation crypto and the agent-event hash chain's prev_hash integrity. Identity stays Idryx's job; this connector stays strictly on the crypto axis.

## Six risk classes, and a clock that started without you

### How an asset is scored

Every asset Qryx finds is scored against a post-quantum and hygiene model, not a single pass-or-fail line.

| Class | Examples | Why it is called that |
|---|---|---|
| quantum-vulnerable | RSA, ECC, DSA, DH | breakable by Shor's algorithm on a capable quantum computer |
| weak | MD5, SHA-1, DES, RC4, RSA under 2048 | broken or deprecated already, no quantum computer required |
| misconfig | TLS 1.0 and 1.1, unsafe cipher suites | a sound primitive used unsoundly |
| expired | past-due certificates | the validity window has elapsed |
| hardcoded | private keys in source or config | a secret committed into the tree |
| safe | ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA | the post-quantum standards, FIPS 203, 204 and 205 |

The timeline is not ours to argue with. NIST standardised the replacements in 2024, and the NCSC clock runs discovery by 2028, the highest-priority systems by 2031, and everything by 2035. The first of those dates is about knowing what you have, which is the part that takes longest and cannot be bought late.

## Two findings, not one, and why test crypto is not debt

### What the count leaves out

Keying the graph on risk class as well as algorithm and key size sounds like a detail until a certificate is both expired and quantum-vulnerable and you only hear about one of them. That exact bug turned up scanning a real endpoint, and it is fixed: an asset in two risk classes produces two findings, because they need two different fixes on two different clocks.

The opposite failure is inflation. Cryptography in test code is scanned and counted, then kept out of the production inventory: out of the asset graph, the compliance verdict, the policy gate, the saved baseline and every export. One line on stderr says how much was set aside and how much of it exists nowhere else, and a flag counts it as production if that is what you want.

This is not cosmetic. Scanning Qryx's own repository, 8 of 13 assets existed only in test fixtures, and 21 of 40 occurrences were test code. In a sibling repository a hardcoded-key finding reported three occurrences, two of them fixtures. Counting those inflates the number an operator is trying to drive to zero, and buries the findings they actually have to migrate.

The classification is not merely path-based either: Rust's in-file test modules are recognised, so an inline test block inside a production file is set aside while the production code around it still counts.

## You cannot migrate what you cannot see.

Qryx reads binaries, container images, live TLS endpoints, certificates, dependencies, cloud KMS and source code, and puts them into one graph graded against the CNSA 2.0 and NCSC milestones.

## The inventory the rest of the stack borrows from.

Qryx can write its agent-passport findings, drift, policy violations and signed-evidence records as agent-events onto the shared bus that [Platform](https://it-rat.com/services/platform.html) defines and every service writes to (opt-in, with --events). Only a finding that names a real agent emits an event, which today means the findings of qryx agents; scans of code, binaries, TLS and cloud KMS carry no agent and emit none. It watches the same estate [TokenFuse](https://it-rat.com/services/tokenfuse.html) spends against, the binaries, endpoints and keys underneath the calls TokenFuse meters. [Mockryx](https://it-rat.com/services/mockryx.html) can demand a crypto reaction in its drills too: an expect.event assertion that a fire drill actually produced a crypto_finding, not silence.

Crypto posture is one plane of a wider practice: [AI agent governance](https://it-rat.com/ai-agent-governance.html), and the defensive picture in [AI agent security](https://it-rat.com/ai-agent-security.html).

## One binary, any platform.

```
qryx scan .
```

```
qryx tls api.anthropic.com:443
```

Grab the latest binary from the [releases page](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/qryx/releases) (Linux, macOS, Windows, SHA256SUMS included), or build from source with Go 1.27; the pinned go1.27.3 toolchain downloads itself on the first build.

### Download, any platform

Every one of those addresses always serves the newest release, so a link saved today still works after the next one. The asset names carry no version, which is what makes that true; the version lives inside the binary, where `qryx version` reads it back.

## What changed from 1 to 15 October

No release in the window, still 1.0.0. The same entry, beside every other service's, is in [what changed in the stack](https://it-rat.com/changes-2026-10.html#qryx).

- Documentation, tests and toolchain only: the Go toolchain moved to 1.27.2, the shared library pin moved to 1.3.0, the secret scan runs on every pull request, and a test now checks every environment read against the component manifest.

## What it leaves out, on purpose.

- Identity stays Idryx's job; the agents connector stays strictly on the crypto axis.

- Cryptography in test code is scanned and counted, then kept out of the production inventory: out of the asset graph, the compliance verdict, the policy gate, the saved baseline and every export. A flag counts it as production if that is what you want.

- The sixty seconds on the room are a simulation, but the shape is real: they replay a live run against 25,586 ELF binaries, a container image and a live TLS endpoint.

## Back to the room.

The [Qryx room](https://it-rat.com/services/qryx.html) has the sweep, the drawing and the common questions, and [the guides index](https://it-rat.com/guides.html) has the field itself.

<!-- https://it-rat.com/keyryx-guide.html -->

# Keyryx guide

> How Keyryx signs, publishes and witnesses keys and the record, its routes, how to configure, run and verify it offline, its releases, and its limits.

The [Keyryx room](https://it-rat.com/services/keyryx.html) keeps the picture of the two roles, the common questions and the short version of each part. This guide keeps the rest: the routes, the configuration it refuses to start without, the witness's findings, how to run it and verify it offline, the releases so far, and the limits an operator meets. The README's NOT PROVEN section has the full list.

- [At a glance](https://it-rat.com/keyryx-guide.html#overview)

- [How the roles work](https://it-rat.com/keyryx-guide.html#how-it-works)

- [The routes](https://it-rat.com/keyryx-guide.html#surface)

- [Configuration](https://it-rat.com/keyryx-guide.html#configuration)

- [The witness](https://it-rat.com/keyryx-guide.html#witness)

- [Running and verifying it](https://it-rat.com/keyryx-guide.html#run)

- [Releases](https://it-rat.com/keyryx-guide.html#changes)

- [Limits](https://it-rat.com/keyryx-guide.html#limits)

## A key service and a witness, in one binary that runs as two processes.

Keyryx is a service of its own: public, Apache-2.0, written in Go, and off every request path. It has two roles, **custody** and **witness**. The binary has one command for each role and a third for offline checks. The roles never share a process, a key or a data directory, the launcher gives each its own uid (stack-single does), and the witness refuses to start if it is given custody's directory or root key.

Custody holds signing keys and signs low-rate statements for consumers that were granted a key: approval tokens, record seal roots and audit manifests. It certifies the short-lived keys that high-rate signers generate for themselves, and it publishes each key set with an overlap so that a rotation is never an outage.

The witness reads the record without writing to it. It checks that every byte it saw before is still there, reads each Trailryx store's sealed manifests, and keeps its own append-only log. Each head of that log is signed with ECDSA P-384 and ML-DSA-65 side by side.

## What custody keeps, and what a consumer receives.

### The key store

Each key is one file under the data directory. Its private half is wrapped with AES-256-GCM under a key derived by HKDF from the root key, and the derivation is bound to the key's name, id and algorithm, so a record moved or swapped refuses the start. The root key is 64 hex characters in a file that no group or other account can read. Every key and statement record carries a state MAC under a second derived key: a record whose MAC does not hold is treated as revoked, is never published or used, and raises an alarm until an admin revokes the key it names.

### Algorithms

ES256 and ES384 keys use fixed-width R and S over SHA-256 or SHA-384. ML-DSA-65 follows FIPS 204 through Go 1.27's standard library. Key ids are RFC 7638 thumbprints for elliptic keys and `mldsa65:` plus the base64url SHA-256 of the public key for ML-DSA. Custody never publishes a private member, and a route that tried to would fail its own test.

### Delegated keys

A high-rate signer keeps its own key in memory and asks custody to certify it in three steps: it asks for a challenge, it signs the challenge with the key being certified, and it sends its public key, the challenge, that proof and the life it wants. Custody answers with a key statement: a JWS with one payload and exactly two signatures, ES384 and ML-DSA-65, made by the two halves of the delegation root. The key is published until its end plus the name's overlap. A key id is certified once, and a revoked one is never published or certified again. At most four keys of one name are live at once.

### The use log

Custody writes one line per signature, statement, rotation and revocation to `use.ndjson`, each line naming the SHA-256 of the line before it. A signature or statement is answered only after its line is on disk, and the log holds the digest of what was signed, never the statement itself.

### Consumers and their one way in

Each consumer in the policy authenticates exactly one way: a unix socket of its own, a bearer key held as a digest and compared in constant time, or a Kubernetes projected service-account token checked against the cluster's keys for this service's audience. A consumer signs only with a key it was granted. The policy file is read whole and strictly, and an unknown field, a duplicate, or a grant of an undeclared key refuses the start.

## Custody and witness HTTP surfaces.

### Custody

| Route | Who | What |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /healthz` | anyone | liveness |
| `GET /v1/state` | anyone | the role, the version, each key's active and next id, and the alarms: every state on disk custody could not vouch for |
| `GET /v1/keys` | anyone | the inventory, revoked keys included; never a private member |
| `GET /v1/jwks/{name}` | anyone, cacheable | the key set a verifier caches; for the delegation root, both halves |
| `GET /v1/statements/{kid}` | anyone, cacheable | the statement that certified a delegated key, and when it was revoked |
| `POST /v1/keys/{name}/sign` | a consumer granted sign | signs a statement of at most 4 KiB |
| `POST /v1/keys/{name}/challenge` and `/delegate` | a consumer granted delegate | the proof-of-possession steps for a delegated key |
| `POST /v1/keys/{name}/rotate` | an admin key | creates the next key, published before it signs |
| `POST /v1/kids/{kid}/revoke` | an admin key | takes a key id out of every key set at once |

A refusal answers its status and a word, and the reason goes to the operator's log. Admin routes answer 403 when no admin key is configured and 401 for a wrong one.

### Witness

| Route | What |
|---|---|
| `GET /healthz` | liveness |
| `GET /v1/witness/head` | the latest signed tree head |
| `GET /v1/witness/keys` | the key set the witness's heads and attestations verify under |
| `GET /v1/witness/inclusion` and `/consistency` | RFC 9162 proofs for a leaf, or between two sizes of the tree |
| `GET /v1/witness/entries` | the entries in a range, at most 1000 per answer |

The witness routes take no credential and only read. Its listener is on the loopback address by default, and its compose service in the stack-single launcher has no network at all.

## What it will not start without.

Anything missing or malformed refuses the start with exit code 2, and the message names the variable. Custody needs its data directory (mode 0700), its root key file, and a policy file of at most 1 MiB. Its listen address defaults to `127.0.0.1:4340`, and `KEYRYX_PUBLISH_AHEAD` sets how long a next or renewed key is published before it signs, 15 minutes by default.

The witness needs its own data directory (mode 0700, never custody's), its own root key file, and the bus directory it reads. The rest are optional: `KEYRYX_WITNESS_CHECKPOINTS` with a custody URL and a stream-key list, a records list for Trailryx data directories, a pin for the delegation root, an alert path, an interval (one minute by default), and an RFC 3161 time-stamping authority. Nothing calls an authority unless `KEYRYX_WITNESS_TSA_URL` is set.

Nothing has a default that signs. A key service that came up holding nothing would answer and sign nothing and look healthy, and one that came up with a default key would sign anything. Both refusals are deliberate.

## What it reads, and what it reports.

Every interval the witness reads, without writing to what it reads. It keeps the count of lines and bytes it has read and their SHA-256, not the bytes, in the prefix form of agent-passport SPEC 6.5.1, and it hashes each stream again from byte zero (hourly for a stream over 256 MiB). The prefix matters: the SPEC chain hash leaves `prev_hash` out, so a line rewritten with its successor re-linked would pass a chain check alone.

- **Streams.** A changed byte is `witness_stream_rewritten`. A stream holding fewer bytes than it was seen to hold is `witness_stream_truncated`. A new chain in the middle of a stream is `witness_chain_restarted`.

- **Checkpoints.** When a checkpoint directory is set, each record is checked by the steps of SPEC 6.5.1 against a key custody certifies for the stream's key name. A record that does not hold is `witness_checkpoint_invalid`; an unsigned one is `witness_checkpoint_unsigned`. While custody does not answer, a record waits.

- **Trailryx records.** For each store root it computes, the witness writes an ES384 attestation of trailryx's witness statement to its own volume. A sealed manifest that is rewritten or gone is `witness_root_equivocated`; a record that grows past a seal's worth with no new root is `witness_root_missing`.

Every finding is an agent-event in the alert file (by default `keyryx.ndjson` in the events directory), with counts and clipped hashes and never record content. Every observation is an entry in the witness's own RFC 9162 log over SHA-384, and each interval ends with a tree head signed by both halves of its key. The witness does not read custody's use log.

The witness pins the delegation root the first time it reads it, unless an operator sets `KEYRYX_WITNESS_DELEGATION_ROOT_PIN` beforehand. A different set served later is a high-severity finding and is not used until an operator pins it.

## Build, run, and check the outputs offline.

Build with `go build -o keyryx ./cmd/keyryx`, then start custody and the witness with their own variables, each as its own process and under its own account:

```
KEYRYX_DATA=/var/lib/keyryx KEYRYX_ROOT_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/keyryx-root \
  KEYRYX_POLICY=/etc/keyryx/policy.json ./keyryx custody
KEYRYX_WITNESS_DATA=/var/lib/keyryx-witness KEYRYX_WITNESS_ROOT_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/keyryx-witness-root \
  KEYRYX_WITNESS_EVENTS=/var/lib/agent-stack/events ./keyryx witness
```

The health checks are `/healthz` on the two listeners. Outputs can be checked with no service running:

```
# the witness log, against the key set it published
keyryx verify log --dir /var/lib/keyryx-witness --keys witness-keys.json
# streams and their checkpoints, against saved statements and the delegation root
keyryx verify streams --events events/ --checkpoints checkpoints/ \
  --statements statements/ --stream-keys 'wardryx.ndjson|wardryx-stream' \
  --roots delegation-root.json
```

Each check prints ok, weak or broken for each item and ends with VERIFIED (exit 0) or NOT VERIFIED (exit 1). A directory with nothing in it is reported as measured nothing, never as verified.

The image is published as `ghcr.io/taipanbox/keyryx` for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64, with no moving tag. The stack-single Compose file pins v0.1.3 by digest.

## What each release is.

- **v0.1.0**, tagged 2026-10-18: the first release. Custody and the witness, both roles, the offline checks, an SBOM and a build-provenance attestation. Its image carries no cosign signature.

- **v0.1.1**, tagged 2026-10-19: a patch on v0.1.0. It moves the shared wire-type import to agent-stack-go v2 and signs the image in the legacy `.sig` format that the cluster admission controller reads; that signature has not yet been checked with cosign. Nothing an operator sets moves with it, with one exception below.

- **v0.1.2**, tagged 2026-10-19: a patch on v0.1.1. The witness writes each attestation with mode 0640, in directories of mode 0750, so a record plane in the witness's group can read it; v0.1.1 wrote them 0600. It also moves agent-stack-go to v2.0.1, which changes no code. Attestations written by v0.1.1 keep their mode until an operator changes it once, as the release notes say.

- **v0.1.3**, tagged 2026-10-26: a patch on v0.1.2. The binary and the image are built with Go 1.27.3, which fixes GO-2026-6809 in crypto/x509 (reached through the time-stamping client, only when KEYRYX_WITNESS_TSA_URL is set). No key, statement, log, route or variable changes.

**An operator-visible change in v0.1.1.** Since agent-stack-go v2, a stream file this service creates is mode 0640, not 0644, so only its owner and its group can read it. A new stream is created only in a directory this service's account owns. A bus directory shared with other services, and not owned by this account, gets no new stream unless each file is created beforehand by the uid of the service that writes it. Check the owner of the bus directory and the mode of each stream before upgrading.

## What is not proven yet, stated here.

- The cosign signatures of v0.1.1, v0.1.2 and v0.1.3 have not been verified. The build-provenance attestation of each release has (gh attestation verify, 2026-10-19 for v0.1.0 to v0.1.2, 2026-10-26 for v0.1.3).

- No admin key is set, so custody refuses every rotation and revocation (403) until an operator sets one.

- Trailryx reads the witness's attestations into a pack only when its attestations folder is set to the witness's output. stack-up has set it by default since 2026-10-19, stack-k8s since v1.6.1, tagged on 2026-10-20, and stack-single since v1.6.0, tagged on 2026-11-05. At keyryx v0.1.1 the witness wrote each attestation readable only by its own user, so a record plane running as another user could not open it; stack-up runs the witness and the record plane as one user, so it could. keyryx v0.1.2, tagged on 2026-10-19, writes them readable by the group, and stack-single, stack-up and stack-k8s now pin v0.1.3; stack-k8s and stack-single run the witness in the record plane's group. On a stack-single box on 2026-11-05, a pack of 1024 records verified with the root signature and the witness on it.

- The store root is rebuilt by hand in the tests from trailryx's construction. It is checked against trailryx's source, not against a store that trailryx itself sealed in this repository.

- No public time-stamping authority has been asked. The client is tested against an authority the tests build.

- The first root is taken on first use unless the operator pins it. A real rotation of the delegation root reads as a changed root until an operator pins the new set, and no rotation has been run against a witness.

- The witness reads the bus and the record, not custody's use log, and custody writes no key rotation or revocation event yet.

- Vouchryx consumes key statements from 0.5.0 and, from 0.6.0, checks each one against a pinned root, and stack-single switches that on by default from v1.6.0. TokenFuse consumes them for its checkpoint key from 1.18.0, which is opt-in: no launcher switches it on, and no producer in a launcher writes signed checkpoints yet.

- The state MAC proves custody wrote a state, not that it is the latest. Whoever can write the data directory can restore an earlier copy of a record whose MAC still holds.

- Challenges live in memory, so a restart drops the outstanding ones.

- No consumer has yet authenticated with a projected service-account token on a real cluster; that path is tested against tokens the repository mints. On a kind cluster custody has served a bearer-key consumer and refused a wrong key (stack-k8s, 2026-10-18).

- No cloud key management. The root key is a file, and a KMS adapter would be a metered dependency, which is the operator's decision and not a default.

- In stack-single the witness is a separate user and volume; in stack-up both roles run as the user that started them. Either way, on one machine, it is not a separate trust domain. An off-host anchor closes that, and it is the operator's to switch on.

- Post-quantum signatures come from Go's standard library. Vouchryx from 0.6.0 checks the ML-DSA-65 half of a key statement; the shared verifier in agent-stack-go checks the classical half only. The key set's AKP form follows a JOSE draft, not an RFC.

## Back to the room.

The [Keyryx room](https://it-rat.com/services/keyryx.html) has the picture of the two roles and the common questions, and [the guides index](https://it-rat.com/guides.html) has the rest of the field.
