<!-- https://it-rat.com/verdryx-guide.html -->

# Verdryx guide

> How Verdryx turns agent spend into cost per resolved case, its six graders, how to run it offline, what changed in October 2026, and its limits.

The [Verdryx room](https://it-rat.com/services/verdryx.html) keeps the sixty-second shift, the drawing of the graders, how to start it, and the common questions. This guide keeps the rest of what the room used to say: what it grades in full, how a case gets a price, the six graders, where it sits in the stack, how to run it, what changed from 1 to 15 October 2026, and its limits.

- [At a glance](https://it-rat.com/verdryx-guide.html#overview)

- [How it works](https://it-rat.com/verdryx-guide.html#how-it-works)

- [What it grades](https://it-rat.com/verdryx-guide.html#grades)

- [Cost per outcome](https://it-rat.com/verdryx-guide.html#cost-per-outcome)

- [The six graders](https://it-rat.com/verdryx-guide.html#graders)

- [In the stack](https://it-rat.com/verdryx-guide.html#in-the-stack)

- [Running it](https://it-rat.com/verdryx-guide.html#run)

- [What changed](https://it-rat.com/verdryx-guide.html#changes)

- [What changed in November](https://it-rat.com/verdryx-guide.html#changes-november)

- [Limits](https://it-rat.com/verdryx-guide.html#limits)

## Verdryx at a glance.

- **Version:** 0.2.0 · Python 3.11+.

- **Tests:** fully offline suite.

- **Core deps:** one, rfc8785 (+ optional extras).

- **Reads:** tokenfuse Parquet traces · NDJSON · CSV.

- **Exports:** agent-events v0.2 · OTLP spans.

- **Licence:** Apache-2.0.

### What it is

Verdryx grades each case by exact match, regex, a production outcome tag, the order of its tool calls or an LLM judge, and prices the result that matters: cost per resolved case, not cost per call. On the live run in VALIDATION.md, a resolved case cost $0.00042, and each abandoned attempt cost $0.00025 for nothing.

## Six graders in, one honest number out.

Traces and eval sets go in. Exact match, regex, an outcome tag straight off the gateway or the order of the tool calls decide what happened, and where a rule cannot, an LLM judge or a typed verdict from Typryx does, with its own cost counted like everything else. What comes out: a cost-per-outcome report, a drift verdict against a stored baseline, a SQLite file, and an event or a span for whatever is already watching your stack.

### Sixty seconds, one shift

This is a simulation, but shaped by the real run: a live, Claude-backed support workload whose outcome-tagged traces were read back and graded. A shift's worth of support cases gets graded, a real cost per resolved case comes out the other side, and a drift check runs against a stored baseline before one OTLP span closes the loop. It runs on the [room](https://it-rat.com/services/verdryx.html#sim).

## Not a bigger number. A truer one.

### Cost per outcome

Resolved, abandoned, escalated: real outcome tags straight off the TokenFuse gateway turn into a dollar figure per case, not a total nobody can act on.

### Drift with statistics

A flat threshold catches the obvious drop. A two-sample significance check beside it, Welch's t plus a bootstrap interval, catches the small, consistent regression a threshold tuned for noise would miss. Point it at a baseline whose source run is gone and it fails loudly, not silently.

### The LLM judge is metered

An llm_judge case's cost is a real dollar figure, priced against the same book TokenFuse uses, not the zero placeholder the deterministic graders leave behind.

### One-dependency core

The graders and drift maths use only the standard library. The one runtime dependency is rfc8785, which canonicalises the JSON the event chain is hashed over. Anthropic and Parquet support are opt-in extras, not a tax on the common path.

### Offline test suite

The suite runs against a deterministic StubLLMAdapter, with no network and no API key. It's what Verdryx's own CI runs, and what --model stub gives you too.

### Findings

drift and slo used to print a verdict and forget it. A drift regression, or an SLO breach the interval establishes (the bar the bus already uses), is now stored as a finding: the agent, the window, the kind (`drift`, `slo_exhausted` or `slo_fast_burn`), the evidence (run ids, the lowest scoring cases, the gateway runs that failed an indicator) and a suspect model or version. The suspect says which of three things it is: a change, no change across the runs compared, or too few runs to compare. `verdryx eval` can record an `--agent-version` on a run. The same failure seen again is one finding seen again, and `verdryx findings list` and `show` read them back.

### Fix verification

`verdryx findings fix ID --note ...` registers a fix, with an optional `--version`. The next drift or slo decides it from the runs that started after it. Measured and clean is `verified`, and the finding closes. Measured and still failing is `failed`: the finding reopens and the attempt is kept with its numbers. Anything short of a measurement stays `pending` with its reason: no run since, too few runs, runs of another version, or an interval that still covers the target. A fix draws a line in time. Runs from before it neither verify it nor undo it, and a closed finding is not reopened by the runs it was closed over. Unmeasured is never a pass.

### Human grades

`verdryx grade RUN CASE VALUE --author NAME --key-file PATH` writes a person's grade. It replaces the model's value in a run's mean, in drift and in the quality floor, and the model's own value stays beside it. A later grade supersedes an earlier one, and both stay on record. Every grade carries its author, a principal registered with `verdryx principal add`, whose generated key is written once (mode 0600) and stored as a hash. The role `reviewer` can grade; the role `uploader` cannot. `eval` needs no credential and has no path to a grade: a gate reads the package for exactly one place that writes a grade and exactly one caller of it.

All of it is deterministic: no model, no network and no new event type on the bus.

### Defensive by design

Grades an operator's own agents against an eval set or a production outcome tag. The README puts it plainly: it “never manipulates outputs, never crafts adversarial prompts, and never attacks anything.”

## How a case gets a price, including the calls nobody tagged

### How the figure is built

The input is the gateway's own trace, not a second pipeline built to agree with it: run id, step, outcome tag, decision, and cost in microdollars, read straight from TokenFuse's Parquet segments, NDJSON or CSV. Verdryx reduces it the same way TokenFuse itself does, so the two never quietly disagree about what a run cost.

Rows are ordered by run and step, and the last non-empty tag a run carries is the one that counts: a case that escalated after two failed attempts is an escalation, not three separate stories.

Then the parts most reports lose. Every call in a run folds into that run's bucket, not only the tagged one, so an untagged intermediate call's cost is not dropped on the floor. A run nobody ever tagged still appears, under an explicit untagged label, rather than vanishing from the report and making the average look better than it is. And a call the breaker blocked is still counted, but at no cost: the figure recorded for it is an avoided estimate, never a settled charge, so it stays out of what the outcome cost.

The result is one row per outcome tag, with count, total and mean, plus an overall row pooling everything. A dollar figure per resolved case is a number an operator can act on; a monthly total is not.

## Six graders, and which two of them can cost money

### What grades a case

Every case resolves to a score between zero and one, whichever of the six graders it asks for, so a case simply names the one it needs.

**Exact** and **regex** score a literal or a pattern: deterministic, free, and the right tool far more often than people expect. **Outcome tag** reads a production tag instead of an expected answer, scoring a resolved case at one, an escalation at a half and an abandonment at zero, with the whole table overridable; an unrecognised tag scores zero rather than raising, so one odd tag cannot take a report down. **Tool trace** scores the model's ordered tool calls against the calls it was supposed to make, which is the difference between a right answer and a right answer reached by touching things it should not have. **LLM judge** grades against a written rubric where those four cannot. **Typed** asks a separate [Typryx](https://it-rat.com/services/typryx.html) service a typed question about the output, a yes or no or a graded level, and scores the probability it returns; a case Typryx cannot answer is counted apart with its reason, never scored as a zero.

Only the judge and the typed grader can spend money, neither runs by default, and both say so: the judge’s cost is priced against the same book the money plane uses, and a typed verdict carries whatever cost Typryx reports for it, rather than the zero a deterministic grader honestly leaves behind. The typed grader runs only when a run is given a Typryx address with `--typed-url`. An eval suite is itself an agent workload; a quality tool that hides its own bill has no business auditing anyone else's.

The judge takes an injected adapter, so the same suite runs against a deterministic stub with no network and no key, which is what Verdryx's own tests use, or against a real model when you want the real verdict.

## The line that turns spend into a verdict.

Verdryx prices the traces [TokenFuse](https://it-rat.com/services/tokenfuse.html) writes: outcome tags and spend data share the same request path, so cost and quality can never quietly drift apart. Its `quality_drift` events ride the same bus as [Platform](https://it-rat.com/services/platform.html)'s Agent Passport contract. [Mockryx](https://it-rat.com/services/mockryx.html) can require an off-path reaction from Verdryx as part of a pre-prod drill. A typed grader from [Typryx](https://it-rat.com/services/typryx.html) sits beside its LLM judge, opt-in per run with `--typed-url`.

Cost per resolved case sits inside a wider practice: [FinOps for AI](https://it-rat.com/finops-for-ai.html), and the controls around it in [AI agent governance](https://it-rat.com/ai-agent-governance.html).

## Grade with a stub, then price the traces.

```
git clone https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/verdryx && cd verdryx
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e '.[traces]'
```

Into a virtual environment: system Python is usually externally managed. There is no PyPI package, so the version you run is the commit you can read. The traces extra adds pyarrow, which reads TokenFuse's Parquet traces; the stub run needs only the base install.

```
verdryx eval evalset.json --model stub --db verdryx.db
```

No network, no key: `--model stub` is deterministic. Then price the traces it left behind.

```
verdryx cost-per-correct --traces $TOKENFUSE_DATA_DIR
```

## What changed from 1 to 15 October

No release in the window, nine pull requests merged. The same entry, beside every other service's, is in [what changed in the stack](https://it-rat.com/changes-2026-10.html#verdryx).

- **Shipped in v0.1.0, released 19 October:** its price book mirrors the gateway's, row for row: every listed Claude id, the Gemini rows on Vertex AI, the vendors' prices of 13 October with their long-prompt tiers, and the `openai/...` rows.

## What changed in November

| shipped in | what it does |
|---|---|
| v0.2.0 | drift and slo failures are stored as findings, with their evidence and a suspect model or version. verdryx findings list and show read them. |
| v0.2.0 | A fix is registered against a finding and decided by the runs that follow: verified, failed, or pending with its reason. |
| v0.2.0 | A person's grade replaces the model's value in a run's mean, in drift and in the quality floor, and the model's value stays beside it. |
| v0.2.0 | drift writes its quality_drift event under the agent stored with the newest run when no --agent-id is given, and eval and drift say on stderr how many events were not written, to which file and why. |
| v0.2.0 | eval has --typed-timeout for a slow Typryx, and the error now says "did not answer within Ns" instead of "could not reach". |
| v0.2.0 | slo_burn carries burn_events_seen, the number of runs behind burn_rate, so a rate nobody measured is told apart from a measured zero. |
| v0.2.0 | The price book mirrors gpt-6.1-terra and its openai/ twin from TokenFuse's default price book. |

## What runs only when you ask, and what is not proven.

- Only the judge and the typed grader can spend money, and neither runs by default. The typed grader runs only when a run is given a Typryx address with `--typed-url`.

- A case Typryx cannot answer is counted apart with its reason, never scored as a zero.

- The store file is the trust boundary for grades. A console build that reads scores directly shows the model's value, not a person's, until it reads `human_grades` too.

- There is no PyPI package, so the version you run is the commit you can read.

- The sixty seconds on the room are a simulation, shaped by the real run: a live, Claude-backed support workload whose outcome-tagged traces were read back and graded.

The [Verdryx room](https://it-rat.com/services/verdryx.html) has the shift, the drawing and the common questions, and [the guides index](https://it-rat.com/guides.html) has the field itself.

# Typryx guide

> How Typryx works, its measured runs in full, how to choose a data mode at install, what changed, and what it does not prove yet.

The [Typryx room](https://it-rat.com/services/typryx.html) keeps the measured replay, the drawings and the widgets, and the common questions. This guide keeps the rest of what the room used to say: how an ask moves and what it holds to, the three data modes, your own model, the speed and calibration runs with their tables, where it plugs into the stack, how to choose a mode at install, what changed, and what is not proven yet.

- [At a glance](https://it-rat.com/typryx-guide.html#overview)

- [How it works](https://it-rat.com/typryx-guide.html#how-it-works)

- [Three modes](https://it-rat.com/typryx-guide.html#modes)

- [Your own model](https://it-rat.com/typryx-guide.html#own-model)

- [The measurements](https://it-rat.com/typryx-guide.html#measured)

- [Where it plugs in](https://it-rat.com/typryx-guide.html#plugs)

- [Where it sits](https://it-rat.com/typryx-guide.html#where-it-sits)

- [Running it](https://it-rat.com/typryx-guide.html#run)

- [What changed](https://it-rat.com/typryx-guide.html#changes)

- [Limits](https://it-rat.com/typryx-guide.html#limits)

## Typryx at a glance.

- **A typed answer with a probability**, never a guess.

- **Status:** an optional add-on. Off is the default, and the rest of the stack runs as it did before.

- **Shapes:** choice, score or yes/no, asked through a versioned template.

- **Deps:** one direct dependency.

- **Spend cap:** 1,000 calls an hour, by default.

- **Licence:** Apache-2.0, public on GitHub.

### What it is

Agents already ask each other, and their models, questions that have exactly one shape: choice (which option), score (how good, on an ordered scale) or yes/no. Typryx takes a question from a versioned template and returns a typed answer read off a probability distribution, or refuses with a named reason instead of inventing one. Only the fields the template names leave the box unless an operator switches freeform questions on (TYPRYX_ALLOW_FREEFORM=1, off by default). Every answer, refusal or timeout lands on a hash-chained journal.

## The path of one ask.

An agent reaches typryx over MCP, most often through tokenfuse's broker, both built. Inside, a call crosses the door, the template lookup, the egress filter and the hourly cap before it reaches a swappable backend; the answer is read off the probability distribution, never taken as the backend's own claim. Everything is journaled. On the right of the room's drawing: the calibration loop that scores a later truth, and the consumers, all still planned, that would read the journal.

### A probability, never an enforcement decision.

**No deny from a probability.** Not here, and not in a consumer. Wardryx's `hold_if_signal` rule may turn a signal into a hold, which a person releases; nothing turns a probability into a deny. It is built and released, and measured on the stub backend only.

**Calibration, never pooled.** `typryx calibration` groups by template, template version, backend and model, never averaged across any of the four. Two models under the same question with opposite calibration would otherwise cancel out on paper while neither is fine.

**A later truth, scored honestly.** An outcome posted later is scored against the exact template version an answer was asked under, read from the ledger's own record, never against whatever the live template says today. A second outcome for the same answer is refused.

**One direct dependency.** agent-stack-go, the stack's shared envelope library, is the only import beyond the standard library. A hostile-input sweep runs against the backends that parse bytes from outside the process, and the ledger survives a torn write mid-crash without losing the record after it.

**Spend capped by default.** 1,000 calls an hour by default, counted only against calls that got past the door, the template lookup and the egress filter. Disabling it logs a warning at boot rather than doing it quietly.

**Offline by default.** The stub backend is deterministic and free, for tests and demos, and every answer it gives says so. The suite itself runs against httptest fakes; nothing in the test run reaches a live network.

### Never invents an answer

A backend error, a timeout, missing or malformed probabilities, a cap hit: the answer is unanswered with a named reason, and the wire shape omits `answer` and `probabilities` entirely. No renormalizing, no fallback guess.

The served answer is always read back off the probability distribution itself: the argmax for a choice, the level for a score, `probabilities["true"]` for a yes-or-no, never from a claim the backend states alongside a disagreeing distribution.

### Where Jev meets the stack.

Three question shapes are the whole contract: `choice`, `score`, `noul` (yes/no). A template goes to any backend unchanged, because the templates are the contract and the backend is swappable. Switch the backend and watch what is sent and what comes back change; the typed-answer shape at the far right never does.

| template | type | options | who would ask it | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| eval.outcome_met | noul (yes/no) | n/a | Verdryx's grading; the calibration run below used it | measured 2026-09-25 |
| eval.answer_quality | score | 4 ordered levels | Verdryx grader | README example, 2026-09-25 |
| request.complexity | choice | cheap / default / hard / reasoning | TokenFuse router, shadow mode only | planned, shadow only |
| action.risk_class | choice | read_only / reversible_change / destructive / external_send / financial | Wardryx, through `wardryx-proxy`, from the tool, its arguments and its target only | released in v0.4.0, run on the stub only |

### What leaves the box

Only `task` and `final_answer` are in the template's `fields`, so on a template ask they are the only two that reach the backend, whatever else sits in the state. The type a backend receives for a template ask is constructible only inside the template package, so a map or raw state cannot reach one on that path, even by an implementation mistake. The one exception is a freeform question, which sends the whole state when TYPRYX_ALLOW_FREEFORM=1 is set (off by default).

Measured (undated, see the typryx README): a five-field state carrying `user_email` and, separately, `customer_iban`, neither ever reached the backend or the record. Through Claude Code over MCP, an extra `api_token` field never reached the record either (`held_back_fields: 1`).

## Three modes: where your data goes.

You pick one when you install typryx, and you can change it later. With Jev, the fields a question names go to TypeSafe AI. With your own model, nothing leaves your hardware. With it off, the stack runs as it did before. All three were run on the same 434 questions, in the room's chart.

### Jev run live 2026-09-30

A hosted service from TypeSafe AI. Only the fields a template names leave the box, to a third party that handles them under its own terms. Of the three modes it was the most accurate and the best calibrated on the test in the room's chart.

Whether that is worth sending those fields out is a decision for whoever answers for your data. It is never the default.

### Your own model measured 2026-09-30

Any OpenAI-compatible server you run yourself, such as Ollama or vLLM. Nothing leaves your hardware. You choose the model, and you can tune it on your own questions (next section).

The one measured here is a small 7B model on a machine with no GPU. A model you have tuned, or a machine with a GPU, is not measured.

### Off the default

typryx is not started. The rest of the stack runs exactly as it did before, and this is what every launcher does until you choose another mode.

Without typryx, an agent that needs a typed answer gets one fixed default. That is the bottom row of the room's chart.

### How the accuracy chart reads

ECE is expected calibration error: lower means the confidence a backend states matches how often it is right. The fixed answer states certainty every time, so its ECE is one minus its accuracy. The questions are synthetic and frozen, each label follows from how its question was built, and an independent re-label agreed on every one of the 434 questions. The benchmark and its runner are public: [github.com/TAIPANBOX/typryx-evalset](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/typryx-evalset).

## Your own model, on your own questions.

typryx does not train, fine-tune, host or ship a model. It keeps the two records a tune needs, the question as the template let it through and the truth a person posted, and it measures the result against the model it replaces. The tuning is yours, on your hardware.

### What it keeps

One line per answered, templated question, in a file on your own disk that only its owner can read: the template and its version, the answer's id, which backend and model answered, and the state as the template let it through. A field the template holds back is on your disk nowhere.

### What it never keeps

The backend's answer or its probabilities. The record has no field for them, and the package that writes it cannot reach the code that knows them. Nothing is written for a question that was refused, unanswered or free-form.

It is off by default: with no directory set, nothing is written and no directory is created.

### Why labels are human truths only

The export labels a question with the truth a person posted and with nothing else. A hosted model's answer never becomes a training label, which matters because TypeSafe's agreement forbids using Jev's output for model distillation or to build a similar or competing product.

What typryx cannot see is how a person reached a truth. A label copied from a model's answer would get through, and the poster's own word is the only record of where it came from.

Decided 2026-09-30: a customer picks one of three data modes for typed answers, typryx does not train or ship models, and a customer can tune their own model on their own questions and measure it with typryx.

## The replay, the speed run and the calibration run.

### Every real judgement from one run, replayed in the same order.

Not an illustration: the room's replay plays the 60 real arithmetic judgements from the calibration table below, qwen2.5:7b run locally on Ollama, wording v2, in the order they were asked (the real run took 9.44 seconds; this replay plays it about 2× slower). Watch the resolved probability, the verdict, and how often "confident" and "right" turn out to be different things.

### The one-token shortcut is not always faster.

Decision speed, measured 2026-09-25. Same 60 items, seed 1, timed end to end from the caller (`go run ./examples/speed`, typryx f4045e0, one run each, so read the medians as indicative rather than final).

| way of deciding | model | median | p95 | accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| typed, one token, through typryx | gpt-4.1-mini | 538 ms | 795 ms | 71.7% |
| text judge, short verdict | gpt-4.1-mini | 723 ms | 1,012 ms | 100% |
| reasoning judge | gpt-5.4-mini (current, reasoning) | 562 ms | 896 ms | 100% |
| typed, one token, through typryx | qwen2.5:7b | 148 ms | 159 ms | 66.7% (3 of 60 unparsed, counted wrong) |
| text judge, short verdict | qwen2.5:7b | 1,509 ms | 2,103 ms | 100% |

Against a hosted API the network dominates: on gpt-4.1-mini the shortcut was about 1.3× faster than a short text verdict and gave up 28 points of accuracy (71.7% against 100%), and gpt-5.4-mini, a current small reasoning model, was right on all 60 in about the same time as the shortcut. Locally, on qwen2.5:7b, the shortcut is about 10× faster. A typed decision earns its place by the probability it carries and where it runs, not by speed; vendor speed claims are not on this page. Jev is not on this chart: it was measured on a different set of questions, the 434 in [Three modes](https://it-rat.com/services/typryx.html#modes), and the two sets are never mixed.

### Stated confidence and actual accuracy are not the same number.

Calibration, measured 2026-09-25. Eight groups, 480 judgements, never pooled: `typryx calibration --min-n 30 --json` over durable ledgers, 60 arithmetic judgements per group, seed 1, template `eval.outcome_met`, backend openai-logprobs, half the items right and half wrong. Five models: three OpenAI models of the previous generation over the hosted API (gpt-4.1-mini, gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1-nano, each with two template wordings) and two open-weight Qwen 2.5 models run locally on Ollama (3B and 7B). Every group was 96% to 100% confident on average and right 50% to 73% of the time.

Every group was 96% to 100% confident on average, right 50% to 73% of the time, and the errors do not lean one way: three groups (gpt-4.1-nano in both wordings, and qwen2.5:3b) said "correct" to every one of 60 items, right exactly half the time, the base rate. gpt-4.1-mini passed half of the wrong answers as right (15 of 30 in each wording); gpt-4o-mini erred both ways; qwen2.5:7b never passed a wrong answer but failed two-thirds of the right ones (20 of 30). Rewording (v1 to v2) barely moved accuracy, because a one-token judge has no room to work anything out before answering: it suits classification, not verification. OpenAI's current models, gpt-5.x and gpt-6, refuse token probabilities outright (the typryx README records this probe: "'logprobs' is not supported with this model"), so this backend reaches only earlier hosted models and open models.

| model | wording | n | stated | accuracy | ECE | Brier | right | lenient | strict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| gpt-4.1-mini | v1 | 60 | 0.990 | 0.733 | 0.267 | 0.525 | 44 | 15 | 1 |
| gpt-4.1-mini | v2 | 60 | 0.958 | 0.733 | 0.243 | 0.505 | 44 | 15 | 1 |
| gpt-4o-mini | v1 | 60 | 0.987 | 0.583 | 0.414 | 0.823 | 35 | 11 | 14 |
| gpt-4o-mini | v2 | 60 | 0.983 | 0.633 | 0.358 | 0.716 | 38 | 5 | 17 |
| gpt-4.1-nano | v1 | 60 | 0.99999 | 0.500 | 0.500 | 1.000 | 30 | 30 | 0 |
| gpt-4.1-nano | v2 | 60 | 0.9995 | 0.500 | 0.500 | 0.999 | 30 | 30 | 0 |
| qwen2.5:3b | v2 | 60 | 0.998 | 0.500 | 0.498 | 0.995 | 30 | 30 | 0 |
| qwen2.5:7b | v2 | 60 | 0.965 | 0.667 | 0.298 | 0.597 | 40 | 0 | 20 |

Exact models: gpt-4.1-mini, gpt-4o-mini and gpt-4.1-nano over OpenAI's API; qwen2.5:3b and qwen2.5:7b on Ollama on a development Mac. Wording v1 is the example template (`2d3ecbdc`), v2 asks plainly whether the answer is exactly correct (`781efaaf`); the local models ran v2 only. Every figure here is one run of 60 items, reproducible with `examples/calibration` in the repository.

**stated confidence**
The probability the model's own answer carried when it was given, averaged over the group.

**ECE**
Expected calibration error: the average gap between stated confidence and actual accuracy across the bins, 0 is perfect.

**Brier**
Mean squared error between the stated probabilities and the true outcome; here, multi-class, 0 is best and 2 is worst.

## What each part of the stack would get.

Three edges are built and wired in, and each has been run: Claude Code as an MCP client and TokenFuse's MCP broker with typryx as a named upstream, both measured on 2026-09-25, and Verdryx's typed grader, run end to end against typryx v0.5.1 with a local model. The Wardryx edge is built and released and runs only against stand-ins; the rest are what a later integration would read, not something built.

|  | what typryx gives it | status |
|---|---|---|
| MCP clients (Claude Code and others) | a typed answer with a probability, per call, over MCP | built |
| TokenFuse, as broker | a named upstream; one tool_call recorded against the agent | built |
| TokenFuse, router shadow mode | the class it would have routed to, alongside cost, recorded only | planned |
| Verdryx | a typed grader beside the existing LLM judge, opt-in per run with `--typed-url` | built, and run end to end against a local model |
| Wardryx | an `action.risk_class` signal a `hold_if_signal` rule may turn into a hold, never a deny; opt-in in the launchers, off by default | built and released, run only against a loopback stand-in (v0.4.0 release notes) |
| CostCrew | a suggested anomaly class at triage; a person still decides | built and released in costcrew v0.4.0, opt-in via COSTCREW_TYPRYX_URL, not run live |
| Genaryx | a panel, live only when `GENARYX_TYPRYX_URL` resolves | planned |
| Engram | an optional importance score | planned |
| Journal readers (Trailryx, Idryx) | the four event types reach the shared events volume; heraldyx renders them; Idryx lists typryx as a source and never calls it; Trailryx refuses them by design | on the shared bus |

## Optional, and it changes nothing when it is absent.

Typryx sits behind [TokenFuse](https://it-rat.com/services/tokenfuse.html)'s MCP broker as a named upstream, so a call an agent makes is priced and recorded there before it ever reaches typryx's own door; the `request.complexity` template maps directly onto that router's own task classes, in shadow mode only, planned rather than built. [Verdryx](https://it-rat.com/services/verdryx.html) can ask typryx for a typed verdict beside its existing LLM judge, opt-in per run, and post a person's label back as the truth; built, and run end to end against typryx v0.5.1 with a local model. A typed answer is a single number a policy can threshold, calibrated against real outcomes rather than assumed honest, and it does not replace the judgement Verdryx already makes. [Wardryx](https://it-rat.com/services/wardryx.html) can read one: `typryx wardryx-proxy` sits in front of it, asks `action.risk_class` about a pending tool call, and adds the answer to the decision request, where a `hold_if_signal` rule may turn it into a hold, which a person releases. Nothing here or in a consumer turns a probability into a deny. The launchers carry it as an opt-in, off by default, from stack-single v1.1.17 and stack-k8s v1.1.23, and it was measured on the stub backend only, never with a real model behind it.

Without it, the rest of the stack behaves exactly as it does today: nothing here is consumed by anything else unless an operator wires it in.

## How to choose it at install.

```
# stack-single
TYPED_MODE=jev|own-model|off
# stack-k8s and stack-up
--typed-mode jev|own-model|off
```

`TYPED_MODE=jev|own-model|off` for stack-single, and `--typed-mode jev|own-model|off` for stack-k8s and stack-up. Off is the default. A key is only ever a file you point at, never an environment value. released in stack-single v1.1.16 and stack-k8s v1.1.22; stack-up runs from main

## What changed, release by release.

Released as v0.6.0 on 2026-11-06, which reaches OpenAI's current models through three request variables, after v0.5.1 on 2026-10-26, built on Go 1.27.3, v0.5.0 on 2026-10-19, v0.4.1 on 2026-10-14, v0.4.0 on 2026-10-04 (which added the `action.risk_class` template and `wardryx-proxy`), v0.3.0 on 2026-09-30 and a first tag, v0.1.0, on 2026-09-25: a signed image on ghcr.io for amd64 and arm64, and a release page with SBOMs; public on GitHub, with the release run for v0.6.0 green. From v0.5.0 a new event stream file is created with mode 0640, and only in a directory the service's account owns. Built and tested: the HTTP and MCP surfaces, the stub, openai-logprobs and jev backends, the journal and ledger, calibration, and the opt-in training log and export. Jev ran live on 2026-09-30, and all three data modes were measured on the same 434 questions.

The releases from 1 to 15 October 2026, with what each one shipped, are in [the stack's changes for October](https://it-rat.com/changes-2026-10.html#typryx).

## What it does not do, and what is not proven yet.

- **Not yet:** a model tuned from an export and measured against the one it replaces, the Wardryx signal with a real backend behind it, and the deeper consumers in the tables above.

- The Wardryx edge is built and released and runs only against stand-ins.

- The launchers carry the Wardryx signal as an opt-in, off by default, and it was measured on the stub backend only, never with a real model behind it.

- CostCrew's suggested class is built and released in costcrew v0.4.0 and not run live; the TokenFuse router, Genaryx and Engram readers are planned.

- In the loop from a question to a tuned model, steps 1 to 5 are built, tested and run on the stub backend; steps 6 to 9 are not run end to end, and no tuned model is measured yet.

- The own model measured is a small 7B model on a machine with no GPU. A model you have tuned, or a machine with a GPU, is not measured.

- OpenAI's current models, gpt-5.x and gpt-6, refuse token probabilities outright, so the openai-logprobs backend reaches only earlier hosted models and open models.

- A freeform question sends the whole state when TYPRYX_ALLOW_FREEFORM=1 is set (off by default).

- What typryx cannot see is how a person reached a truth. A label copied from a model's answer would get through.

- The speed figures are one run each, so read the medians as indicative rather than final.

## Back to the room.

The [Typryx room](https://it-rat.com/services/typryx.html) has the measured replay, the path of one ask, the widgets and the common questions, and [the guides index](https://it-rat.com/guides.html) has the field itself.

<!-- https://it-rat.com/mockryx-guide.html -->

# Mockryx guide

> How Mockryx fire drills work, how to run and download it, the drills added since v0.2.1, and what it does not prove yet.

The [Mockryx room](https://it-rat.com/services/mockryx.html) keeps the fire drill, the drawing of one target URL and three exit codes, and the common questions. This guide keeps the rest of what the room used to say: what a scenario names, how a reaction is proven, how a skipped guardrail is told from a gap, where it sits in the stack, how to run and download it, the drills added since v0.2.1, and the limits.

- [At a glance](https://it-rat.com/mockryx-guide.html#overview)

- [How it works](https://it-rat.com/mockryx-guide.html#how-it-works)

- [What it proves](https://it-rat.com/mockryx-guide.html#what-it-proves)

- [Where it sits](https://it-rat.com/mockryx-guide.html#where-it-sits)

- [Running it](https://it-rat.com/mockryx-guide.html#run)

- [What changed](https://it-rat.com/mockryx-guide.html#changes)

- [What changed in November](https://it-rat.com/mockryx-guide.html#changes-november)

- [Limits](https://it-rat.com/mockryx-guide.html#limits)

## Mockryx at a glance.

- **Prove every guardrail holds**, against your own gateway, before real traffic.

- **Status:** pre-1.0, and main is supported.

- **Core:** Go, an outbound-only CLI. **Scenarios:** YAML, one file each.

- **Target:** your own gateway, at /v1/messages.

- **Verdicts:** exit 0 held, 1 a real gap, 2 broken.

- **Licence:** Apache-2.0.

### What it is

A guardrail nobody has ever fired is a guess. Mockryx replays hostile scenarios (a fake secret in a prompt, a budget burn, a denied tool, a forged delegation chain, an unapproved action, an injected page, a quality drift, a reaction chain that has to reach the mail, a token flood, personal data in a prompt, a poisoned tool description, a respelled allow-listed tool, and a provider outage) against the URL you hand it: your own pre-production gateway, with a fake provider behind it. The enforcement path is the real one; the spend is not. CI reads the verdict as an exit code.

## One gateway URL. One report. Three exit codes.

A scenario file names a request in the Anthropic Messages shape, the status it must be answered with, the headers that must ride the response and, optionally, the off-path event that must follow. A step is one of three kinds: a request to /v1/messages (which can carry tool history), a tool_check that asks the gateway whether a tool may run and expects allow or deny, or an mcp step that sends one JSON-RPC request to your MCP broker, named with --mcp-broker. The runner sends it at your gateway's /v1/messages, reads the gateway's own answer, polls the NDJSON event logs the off-path services write, and folds everything into a report and an exit code a CI gate can act on. It talks only to the URLs you name on the command line: your gateway and, for the optional broker drills, your MCP broker.

### Watch every guardrail answer for itself.

The room's simulation replays five of the drills, and the shape is the real record: three of those five ran live against a real gateway on disposable boxes, twice, and held both times, 0 gaps, $0 real spend. The other two are the Wardryx scenarios that ship in the same set. The provider behind the gateway is fake, so the burn the runaway drill attempts never reaches an invoice.

## Not a mock of your gateway. Your gateway.

### Scenarios are YAML, not code

One drill is one file: the request to send, the status the guardrail must answer, the headers it must stamp. It reads like the real call it imitates. A malformed file fails the whole load, because a safety check that vanishes silently is worse than one that fails loudly.

### In-path checks, on the real path

Assertions read the gateway's own answers: the breaker's 402, DLP's 403, the deny or hold riding the x-fuse-wardryx header. No mocked gateway in the middle, so the code you rehearse is the code production traffic meets.

### Async reaction checks

A drill can demand that the off-path services actually react, not only that the gateway answered. A gateway that blocks while nobody downstream notices is half a defence.

**Proving the services that answer later answered at all.** The gateway's own status and headers can only speak for the guardrails standing in the request path. Verdryx, Idryx and Qryx never touch that response: they react off path, on their own schedule, and record what they did as an agent-event envelope in the same NDJSON format everything else in the stack writes.

So a scenario can assert on that too. Name the source and the event type it expects, optionally how long to wait, and after the synchronous check passes the runner polls those event logs for a matching event correlated by the exact run id it put on the wire. Not "an event appeared", but "the event this request should have caused appeared".

Order matters here. A synchronous mismatch is never followed by an event check: chasing a downstream reaction to a request that did not even trigger the guardrail would turn one clear failure into two confusing ones. The drill reports the thing that actually broke.

### A provider that is up but failing

Three game-day drills rehearse it against a stub provider: `provider-5xx`, `provider-rate-limited` and `provider-timeout`. A fourth, `provider-outage`, needs no stub: point the gateway's upstream at an address that refuses the connection. They live in `scenarios/game-day/`, and a plain `mockryx run ./scenarios` never loads them: a failing provider sends no `x-fuse-*` header, so a routine CI run would show a false gap on any ordinary day. Each of the three sends the operator's own gateway a call and checks the chain in order. The call comes back with the provider's own status, 503, 429 or 504. The gateway puts a `dependency_failed` for the run on the bus, from source tokenfuse. And the run reaches a person: an `alert_sent` from heraldyx. The drills use the existing event check only, add no scenario capability and declare no `requires`, so a miss is a finding and never a skip.

The provider is a local stub, `internal/providerstub`, started by `scripts/provider-stub.go` with `go run`. The script is excluded from the build, so the repository still builds one binary. The stub listens on loopback only and refuses any other address before binding, exiting 2. It makes no outbound call, and it holds a timeout for at most ten seconds, under Mockryx's own fifteen-second client timeout.

Each drill is run through a model of the chain: the stub, a gateway that passes the status through and writes `dependency_failed` to a hash-chained file, and a notifier that writes `alert_sent`, read back by the real event watcher. All three pass with the chain whole. Each fails on the status when the gateway hides the failure, on `tokenfuse/dependency_failed` when the bus is silent, and on `heraldyx/alert_sent` when nobody is told. The self-test runs every drill against a gateway that answers 200 to everything, and every run comes back failed.

### A skip cannot hide a gap

A guardrail that is off looks exactly like one that is broken. The runner insists on evidence before it calls a miss either one.

**The difference between a gap and a feature you never turned on.** A finding means the guardrail was supposed to hold and did not: something to fix today. A scenario that declares an optional guardrail is telling the runner something narrower, that a miss counts as a real gap only if there is other evidence the feature is actually wired in.

The evidence is the gateway's own response headers. If the header for that feature appears even once anywhere in the run, whatever its value, the feature is clearly live and a mismatch is a genuine finding. If it never appears across every attempt, the gateway plainly does not have it configured, and the scenario reports itself as not configured, with its raw mismatches dropped: they describe an absent feature, not a broken defence.

Three things can never be excused this way. A scenario with no optional guardrail declared, the budget breaker, is core and always on, so a miss there is always a finding. A transport error, where the gateway could not be reached at all, is always a finding too: being unreachable is never evidence that a feature is merely switched off. So is a gateway that refuses the drill's own credential (a 401, or a 403 identity_mismatch): that is a finding, never a skip.

When you know a guardrail must be there, one flag turns even a skip into a failure. That is the honest way round: the tool refuses to claim a pass it cannot prove, and it refuses to cry gap it cannot prove either.

### CI-native exit codes

Exit 0: every drill held. Exit 1: a real defensive gap, fail the build. Exit 2: the harness itself is broken (bad flag, unreadable scenarios), so nothing was proven. Gate on 1, fix the pipeline on 2, and never let the two blur.

### Zero real spend by design

The provider behind the gateway is fake, so the runaway scenario can burn all it wants: the meter it trips is real, the invoice is not. And every hostile input stays inside your perimeter; Mockryx only talks to the URLs you hand it: the gateway and, for the broker drills, your MCP broker.

## It picks fights with the rest of the stack. On purpose, in pre-prod.

In the request path, Mockryx rehearses [TokenFuse](https://it-rat.com/services/tokenfuse.html): the breaker's 402 and the DLP's 403, provoked deliberately and expected to answer. It does the same to [Wardryx](https://it-rat.com/services/wardryx.html), asserting that deny and hold verdicts land in the x-fuse-wardryx header. Off path, expect.event demands that [Verdryx](https://it-rat.com/services/verdryx.html), [Idryx](https://it-rat.com/services/idryx.html) and [Qryx](https://it-rat.com/services/qryx.html) visibly react to what just happened. And when MOCKRYX_EVENTS_PATH (or --events) is set, it also writes sim_run, sim_finding and blast_radius_measured events in the same agent-event format as everything else on the bus: [the shared contract](https://it-rat.com/services/platform.html).

Why rehearsal belongs in CI, and what else it sits beside: [AI agent security](https://it-rat.com/ai-agent-security.html) and [AI agent governance](https://it-rat.com/ai-agent-governance.html).

## Two commands, one gateway URL.

```
./bin/mockryx run --gateway http://127.0.0.1:8080 ./scenarios
./bin/mockryx report out/report.json
```

Add `--save out/report.json` to keep the evidence. Point it at pre-prod, never at prod: the URLs you pass are the only places it will ever send traffic.

### Download, any platform

Every one of those addresses always serves the newest release, so a link saved today still works after the next one. The asset names carry no version, which is what makes that true; the version lives inside the binary, where `mockryx version` reads it back.

## Four drills added in v0.2.2

These four drills shipped in v0.2.2. The current release is v0.4.0.

| drill | what it rehearses |
|---|---|
| Token flood | One request asks for a very large completion on a one-cent run budget. The gateway must refuse it before it is forwarded. |
| PII in a prompt | A support prompt carries a customer's email address and phone number. With PII blocking on, the call must be refused before any model sees it. |
| Poisoned tool description | A request declares a tool whose description orders the model to call another tool first and not to mention it. The gateway must answer the request, then deny a dangerous action in the same run. |
| Respelled allow-listed tool | A policy allows a tool by its exact name. A request that declares the same tool under a respelled name must be refused by the allow-list. |

What changed from 1 to 15 October 2026, release by release, is in [the stack's changes for October](https://it-rat.com/changes-2026-10.html#mockryx).

## What changed in November

| shipped in | what it does |
|---|---|
| v0.4.0 | Three game-day drills for a provider that is up but failing (a 5xx, a rate limit and a timeout), and a loopback-only local stub they run against. |

## What it does not do.

- The game-day drills (scenarios/game-day/) and the MCP broker drills (scenarios/mcp/) are not loaded by a plain mockryx run ./scenarios, on purpose: a failing provider sends no x-fuse-* header, so a routine CI run would show a false gap, and a broker drill needs --mcp-broker.

- Of the five drills the room replays, three ran live against a real gateway on disposable boxes, twice; the other two are the Wardryx scenarios that ship in the same set.

- It is pre-1.0, and main is supported.

- A gateway response can only speak for the guardrails standing in the request path; off-path services are proven by their own events, and a synchronous mismatch is never followed by an event check.

- A scenario that declares an optional guardrail reports itself as not configured when the gateway never shows that feature's header; one flag turns even a skip into a failure.

- It only talks to the URLs you hand it: your gateway and, for the broker drills, your MCP broker. Point it at pre-prod, never at prod.

## Back to the room.

The [Mockryx room](https://it-rat.com/services/mockryx.html) has the fire drill, the drawing and the common questions, and [the guides index](https://it-rat.com/guides.html) has the field itself.

# Trailryx guide

> How Trailryx proves an answer complete, how erasure leaves the chain intact, the durability runs, the offline verifier, and its limits.

The [Trailryx room](https://it-rat.com/services/trailryx.html) keeps the replay of two questions and one erasure, the drawing of how a query is classified, and the short version of each part. This guide keeps the rest of what the room used to say: where it sits today, how erasure leaves the trail intact, the durability runs and what a sealed pack does and does not prove, the verifier and its downloads, what it seals lately, and the limits.

- [At a glance](https://it-rat.com/trailryx-guide.html#overview)

- [Where it sits](https://it-rat.com/trailryx-guide.html#where-it-sits)

- [How it works](https://it-rat.com/trailryx-guide.html#how-it-works)

- [Measured, not asserted](https://it-rat.com/trailryx-guide.html#proof)

- [Running it](https://it-rat.com/trailryx-guide.html#run)

- [What it seals lately](https://it-rat.com/trailryx-guide.html#sealing-lately)

- [What changed](https://it-rat.com/trailryx-guide.html#changes)

- [Limits](https://it-rat.com/trailryx-guide.html#limits)

## Trailryx at a glance.

- **A record of what your agents did** that nobody can quietly change, or quietly shorten.

- **Core:** Rust, no unsafe, and no third-party code in the core or the verifier.

- **Ingest:** OTLP protobuf, JSON, or a collector's file.

- **Proves:** record, time, agent, run and type.

- **Erasure:** crypto-erasure, per subject.

- **Licence:** Apache-2.0.

### What it is

Tamper-evident is the easy half, and most audit stores stop there: you can tell if a record was edited. The hard half is the answer. Ask "everything agent X did in March" and an ordinary store hands you rows with no way to know whether it handed you all of them. Trailryx answers with a completeness proof when it can, and says partial with the reason named when it cannot. And its store is built to erase one person on request without breaking the trail; the shipped node does not expose that yet.

## Where this sits today, stated rather than implied.

Trailryx reads the shared agent-event bus and seals it. That was the open gap on this page until 2026-08-27 and it is closed: a dedicated crate maps the envelope the other planes write, `stack-up` runs the sealing routine at 06:57 by default, and the Kubernetes install has a nightly job that packs the ledger and verifies the pack before it exits. It still takes plain OTLP as well, from a collector or straight over the wire, so it stays useful to somebody who has traces and no TAIPANBOX. **Two gaps are left.** The console has no panel for the record plane, so what is sealed is read with the CLI rather than in a browser. Erasure is a library and the demo path today: trailryx-node has no erase command and keeps no payload plane, so an operator cannot yet erase one subject through the shipped binary.

## The auditor asks. One answer carries a proof, the other admits it cannot.

Records arrive and chain. Then a question lands on one of the five dimensions the index can prove, and the matching records are a contiguous range: that contiguity is the mechanism, not a picture of it. The second question is about something nothing sorts by, so the rows are still right and the answer says so. At the end, one subject is erased and the chain still verifies.

### Erase one person in the library, and the trail still verifies.

An audit store that cannot forget anybody fails the first request it gets in Europe. One that forgets by deleting rows breaks every proof it ever issued. Trailryx separates the two planes so neither has to give way.

**Typed metadata, encrypted payload.** The plane the proofs are built on holds identifiers, enums, hashes, numbers and timestamps, and nothing else. Any prose lives in the encrypted payload under the subject's own key. A mapper that does not know where an attribute belongs puts it in the encrypted plane rather than guessing, because guessing the other way is how personal data ends up outside the erasure boundary.

**The record commits to the payload it no longer has.** Forgetting drops the key. The record keeps its hash, size, class and key id, so what it committed to is still checkable and the chain around it is untouched. The answer to "was anything removed here" stays yes-and-here-is-where, rather than becoming unanswerable.

## The number that makes the other number mean something.

A durability sweep reporting zero violations proves nothing on its own: a check that cannot fail reports zero forever. So the same harness is run against a disk that lies about its writes, and it is required to fail.

### With a disk that keeps its word

As recorded, undated, in the repository's VALIDATION.md: 400,000 seeds, roughly 800 million shard ticks, about 12 million crashes injected, nine days and six hours of simulated time in ten minutes and forty seconds of real time. Zero durability violations.

### With a disk that lies

The same harness, the honest-disk assumption removed (as recorded, undated, in VALIDATION.md): 17,869 of 20,000 seeds fail, each naming its own seed and digest. That is what makes the zero above worth reading.

### What the installed profile seals today

What the installed profile seals today, stated beside the verdict rather than under it: the `record-seal` job the launchers run keeps the typed metadata plane and writes down that it declined the payload, because a node cannot choose an operator's custody for them. Its pack verifies as self-consistent, and `trailryx-verify` says in plain words when a pack carries no root signature and no witness. All three launchers sign each sealed root through Keyryx by default and attach the witness's attestations: stack-up since 2026-10-19, stack-k8s since v1.6.1, tagged on 2026-10-20, and stack-single since v1.6.0, tagged on 2026-11-05. No witness is an outside party, since stack-up's runs on the same host as the same user, stack-k8s's in the same cluster and stack-single's on the same box, each of those two as its own user in the record plane's group, and trailryx-verify does not warn about that. So a pack's verdict proves the chain was not altered and which key signed it. A date an outside party can vouch for takes an anchor off the box.

## The offline verifier.

```
trailryx-verify incident-4471.trxevid
```

Zero third-party dependencies, because an auditor reads it rather than trusting it. A download on [GitHub releases](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/trailryx/releases) with a SHA256SUMS file signed keyless by Sigstore, so nobody has to build it first.

### Download the verifier

Each address always serves the newest release: the asset names carry no version, so a link saved today still works after the next one. These are the offline verifier; `trailryx-ingest` sits beside them on the releases page. No Windows build yet, and saying so is cheaper than a broken link.

## The newest thing on the bus is a crew of agents.

[CostCrew](https://it-rat.com/services/costcrew.html) writes twenty-three event types about money and about its own analysts. This plane seals the two about money with everything else and refuses the other twenty-one by name, because they record a practice rather than an agent's run. The rest were refused by design rather than dropped, which is the distinction this store exists to keep.

## Releases from 1 to 15 October 2026.

What changed from 1 to 15 October 2026, release by release, is in [the stack's changes for October](https://it-rat.com/changes-2026-10.html#trailryx).

## What it does not do, and what is not proven yet.

- The console has no panel for the record plane, so what is sealed is read with the CLI rather than in a browser.

- Erasure is a library and the demo path today: trailryx-node has no erase command and keeps no payload plane, so an operator cannot yet erase one subject through the shipped binary.

- SQL is a facade in the tree and not yet a port in the shipped node: today you read the records through `read`.

- The `record-seal` job the launchers run keeps the typed metadata plane and declines the payload. All three launchers sign each sealed root through Keyryx by default and attach the witness's attestations: stack-up since 2026-10-19, stack-k8s since v1.6.1, tagged on 2026-10-20, and stack-single since v1.6.0, tagged on 2026-11-05. No witness is an outside party: stack-up's runs on the same host as the same user, stack-k8s's in the same cluster and stack-single's on the same box, each of those two as its own user in the record plane's group. trailryx-verify does not warn about that. So the verdict proves the chain was not altered and which key signed it; a date an outside party can vouch for takes an anchor off the box.

- The durability figures are as recorded, undated, in the repository's VALIDATION.md.

- No Windows build of the verifier yet.

## Back to the room.

The [Trailryx room](https://it-rat.com/services/trailryx.html) has the replay, the drawing and the short version of each part, and [the guides index](https://it-rat.com/guides.html) has the field itself.
