# Heraldyx guide

> How Heraldyx decides what reaches a human, what its mail may carry, what its dispatch record proves, what changed from v0.7.0 to v0.9.0, and its boundaries.

The [Heraldyx room](https://it-rat.com/services/heraldyx.html) keeps the burst replay, the drawing of the four checks, the sample mail and the short version of each part. This guide keeps the rest of what the room used to say: why the checks run in that order and what changed in them, what a mail may carry and who it names, what the dispatch record proves, who else writes to the log it reads, what shipped from v0.7.0 to v0.9.0, and the boundaries in full.

- [At a glance](https://it-rat.com/heraldyx-guide.html#overview)

- [How it works](https://it-rat.com/heraldyx-guide.html#how-it-works)

- [What actually arrives](https://it-rat.com/heraldyx-guide.html#the-mail)

- [The dispatch record](https://it-rat.com/heraldyx-guide.html#the-record)

- [Running it](https://it-rat.com/heraldyx-guide.html#run)

- [Who else writes to the log](https://it-rat.com/heraldyx-guide.html#sources)

- [What changed in November](https://it-rat.com/heraldyx-guide.html#changes-november)

- [What changed](https://it-rat.com/heraldyx-guide.html#changes)

- [Limits](https://it-rat.com/heraldyx-guide.html#limits)

## Heraldyx at a glance.

- **Your agents run on your infrastructure.** This is the part that writes to you.

- **One way out:** it reads the log, speaks SMTP, and nothing else.

- **Limits:** a severity floor, a dedup window of 10 minutes, and 20 mails an hour.

- **Leaves behind:** a hash-chained dispatch record.

- **Core:** Go, with two direct dependencies (the shared agent-stack-go contract and a JSON canonicaliser).

- **Licence:** Apache-2.0.

### What it is

Every other plane in the stack records what happened. None of them wakes anybody. Heraldyx reads the shared event log the others already write, decides which of those events a human should hear about tonight rather than tomorrow, and sends one mail. It comes from your own box, and it carries links into your own console. It reads a file and sends mail: that narrowness is the design, because this is the one component of the box allowed to open a connection to anything outside it.

## Four checks, in this order, and the order is the point.

The decision layer is a pure function over an event and a few counters. It performs no I/O at all, which is what makes the awkward cases (a burst, a restart, a clock that moved) testable without a mail server. The last cell of the room's drawing was redrawn after a run on 2026-09-17: the v0.2.3 image sent one notice at the ceiling and then nothing for 28 minutes of high and critical events. Since v0.2.4 a critical passes the ceiling and whatever is held is summarised every ten minutes until the hour turns; the launchers pin v0.8.2 on their main branches.

### A provider that is down is one mail, not one per call

For `dependency_failed` the dedup key is the dependency that failed and what the gateway did about it, not the run. A provider that is down fails every call that reaches it, and every call is its own run, so keyed on the run an hour of outage was one mail per call up to the hourly ceiling and a summary of the rest. Keyed on the dependency it is one mail per window. The key is read from the event's own `data.dependency` and `data.effect`, for a provider that fails calls it reads `dependency_failed:dependency/provider/call-failed`, and it is what an acknowledgement is made against and what the mail prints, so acknowledging a provider outage holds the whole storm.

The effect is part of the key because the outcomes want opposite responses. A gateway that fails open lets calls through with no policy on them, and that must not hide behind an earlier mail about calls that were refused. Only the type `dependency_failed` and only the event contract's own words qualify. No data, an unknown dependency, a value that is not text, a path-like or oversized value, or another type carrying the same field keeps the key of its run, so a field read from a log this process does not own can never fold anything into anything. The event contract does not change, no data key is added to what the mail may print, and the link in the mail points where it did.

The Cloud side of the same outage is [TokenFuse](https://it-rat.com/services/tokenfuse.html)'s one incident per failing provider. The two are independent: this one changes only what is mailed.

### A hundred and twenty events arrive. Twenty-one messages leave.

The room's replay is a scripted scenario: `scripts/burst-demo.sh` in the repository feeds 120 events to the real binary with the default limits and counts what comes out. Watch where the other hundred stop. An alerting system that forwards everything teaches its operator to filter the sender to trash, and then the one that mattered is in trash too.

## Four short paragraphs, and three links that are views.

What happened with its numbers, what the box already did about it, what happens if nobody acts, and where to look. Nothing in it is text a model wrote.

### The links are views, never actions

A link that acts is an unauthenticated capability held by anyone who sees or forwards the message. Mail gateways also prefetch links, which would fire the action before a human read the sentence next to it. You sign in at the console, and a destructive action asks for your passkey there.

### Identifiers and numbers, never content

An event's data can hold anything a producer put there, and some producers sit next to prompts, model output and matched secrets. Mail leaves your perimeter through a server nobody here controls, so the renderer allows twenty-two named keys and then checks the shape of every value on top. A live secret is perfectly identifier-shaped, so the key list is what stands between it and your inbox.

### Who is answerable comes from a passport

Not from the event, which carries the agent and who it acted for, and neither of those is the owner. No passport means no owner line rather than a guess: naming the wrong team at three in the morning is worse than naming nobody at all.

## Every message it sent, sealed, on a volume the planes cannot reach.

"We wrote to you at 03:14, and your mail server took it at 03:14:02" is a claim somebody eventually has to prove, in an argument they did not choose. So every message leaves one hash-chained record behind it, in the same envelope the rest of the stack speaks.

### "Accepted", never "delivered"

What the process observes is a mail server taking the message. Whether it reached a mailbox, a spam folder, or a filter that drops it silently is not knowable from here, so the record does not say it.

### A chain of one is not "verified"

The first record has no predecessor to hash, so editing it is undetectable. The tool says so instead of reporting a good chain. A check that cannot fail is worse than no check, because it is louder.

### It reports, and never repairs

A tool that could mend the chain would be a tool that could forge it. It exits non-zero on a break, so a deployment check can use it directly.

## Reading the dispatch record.

```
heraldyx --journal
```

The image is distroless: there is no shell in it to read the file with.

Since v0.3.0 a line counts as the source it claims only when the file it came from may carry that source. Each plane's file carries its own name, `HERALDYX_STREAMS` declares anything else, and a line in the wrong file is refused, counted and raised once as `foreign_source`; a file nobody declared is raised once as `unknown_stream`. It does not stop a process that creates a plane's file before that plane does, or a writer forging its own stream. The checkpoint gate, from v0.8.0, answers that for streams a producer signs, and it is off by default.

## Twelve planes write the log it reads.

This plane mails about what other planes wrote, so its reach grows when theirs does. Twelve planes write the shared log, and the Keyryx witness's findings file is read beside it. [Vouchryx](https://it-rat.com/services/vouchryx.html) reports a delegation issued, denied or revoked, and [CostCrew](https://it-rat.com/services/costcrew.html) reports spend spikes, budget thresholds and every move its crew makes on a finding. CostCrew's events have their own sentences here. Vouchryx's delegation events have none yet, so a mail about one says the box has no description for the event until one is written.

## What changed in November

| shipped in | what it does |
|---|---|
| v0.9.0 | A dependency_failed repeats on the dependency, so a provider storm is one mail per window instead of one per failed call. |
| v0.9.0 | The key of a dependency_failed mail is now dependency_failed:dependency/provider/call-failed. An acknowledgement made against the old per-run key does not hold the new one, so acknowledge the new key. |

## What changed in v0.8.0

| shipped in | what it does |
|---|---|
| v0.8.0 | Mail is sent only over TLS: STARTTLS by default, implicit TLS on port 465, and plain only to a loopback relay. A server that does not offer STARTTLS is refused, so set HERALDYX_SMTP_TLS for your server before you upgrade. |
| v0.8.0 | Every SMTP connection has a 10 second dial deadline and a 60 second session deadline. |
| v0.8.0 | Stream files the notifier creates are mode 0640, so only their owner and its group can read them. |
| v0.8.0 | The checkpoint gate is off by default; with it on, a stream is read only while a signed checkpoint covers it (see the boundaries). |
| v0.8.0 | Heraldyx reads a stream another service wrote only as the file's owner or in its group: a stream created at 0640 needs Heraldyx in that group. |

## What the notifier gained in v0.7.0

| shipped in | what it does |
|---|---|
| v0.7.0 | A daily pulse mail says the notifier is running and gives the counts it saw, so a quiet box can no longer look like a dead one. |
| v0.7.0 | Quiet hours hold alerts below critical every day, in a window the operator sets and in the time zone the operator names. |
| v0.7.0 | A maintenance window, opened by hand for up to 24 hours, can hold alerts from one source while that source is being upgraded. |
| v0.7.0 | An operator can acknowledge a known condition for four hours by default, seven days at most. Its repeats are counted instead of mailed, and one mail says how many alerts were held when it ends. |
| v0.7.0 | A critical is never held, whether by quiet hours, a window or an acknowledgement. |

Every release from 1 to 15 October 2026, with what each one shipped, is in [the stack's changes for October](https://it-rat.com/changes-2026-10.html#heraldyx).

## The boundaries, stated rather than discovered at three in the morning.

### It does not queue

A message that cannot be delivered is logged, written into the dispatch record as a refusal, and dropped. A retry queue inside the one process allowed out would be the opposite of the design, and the event itself is still in the log, which outlives this process. Quiet hours and maintenance windows are holds, not a queue: they hold alerts below critical and, when the hours or the window end, send one mail saying how many were held. A critical is never held.

### It does not talk to any plane

No API, no credential, no client. It holds nothing that could act on an agent. If a fact is not in the event log, heraldyx does not know it.

### It does not report anything about a whole organisation

The shared envelope requires an agent id, so a fact about an org has no subject to travel under, and no producer is allowed to invent one to make it fit. Those facts live in the console and in each plane's own API. A mail whose subject line named an agent that had not done the thing would be worse than silence.

### It does not carry history

A first run starts at the end of the log. A month of old incidents arriving at once is how an operator learns to filter this sender to trash.

### And what is not closed yet

- Vouchryx's delegation events have no sentences yet, so a mail about one says the box has no description for the event until one is written.

- The source check does not stop a process that creates a plane's file before that plane does, or a writer forging its own stream. The checkpoint gate, from v0.8.0, narrows that for streams a producer signs: with HERALDYX_CHECKPOINT_GATE=on, a stream is read only while a checkpoint signed by a pinned key covers it. It is off by default, it trusts a pinned key until an operator removes it, and it holds only if each producer alone can write its stream and checkpoints. No launcher has a producer writing signed checkpoints yet.

- The record says a mail server accepted a message, never that it was delivered, and the first record of a chain cannot be verified.

- The burst of 120 events is a scripted scenario for the rules, not a measurement of a real fleet.

## Back to the room.

The [Heraldyx room](https://it-rat.com/services/heraldyx.html) has the burst replay, the drawing of the four checks and the sample mail, and [the guides index](https://it-rat.com/guides.html) has the field itself.


---

<!-- https://it-rat.com/engram-guide.html -->

# Engram guide

> How Engram works, the live runs against real Claude, how to install it, what changed in v3.0.0 and v3.1.0, and what it does not do yet, in full.

The [Engram room](https://it-rat.com/services/engram.html) keeps the simulation, the drawing of one file on disk and the common questions. This guide keeps the rest of what the room used to say: what a memory holds and how each part works, the three live runs against real Claude, how it ships, what changed in v3.0.0 and v3.1.0, and what it does not do yet.

- [At a glance](https://it-rat.com/engram-guide.html#overview)

- [How it works](https://it-rat.com/engram-guide.html#how-it-works)

- [Recall is one part of a memory](https://it-rat.com/engram-guide.html#recall)

- [The live runs](https://it-rat.com/engram-guide.html#live-run)

- [Where it sits](https://it-rat.com/engram-guide.html#where-it-sits)

- [Running it](https://it-rat.com/engram-guide.html#run)

- [What changed](https://it-rat.com/engram-guide.html#changes)

- [What changed in November](https://it-rat.com/engram-guide.html#changes-november)

- [Limits](https://it-rat.com/engram-guide.html#limits)

## Engram at a glance.

- **The memory that remembers why:** an embeddable memory in one SQLite file.

- **Release:** latest, on PyPI as engdbram. **Core:** Python 3.11+.

- **Storage:** a single SQLite file plus sqlite-vec.

- **Recall:** hybrid BM25 and vector.

- **Integrations:** MCP, LangChain, LlamaIndex.

- **Licence:** Apache-2.0.

### What it is

Engram is an embeddable memory in one SQLite file. It stores raw episodes, distills them into facts with confidence scores, records when each fact was true, and answers why() for every belief it holds, with the episodes it came from. Two beliefs that disagree are recorded as a contradiction. No server, no Docker, and writing the first memory needs zero API keys.

## Not a log of text. Beliefs with receipts.

### One file on disk. Model calls only when you ask.

Your agent calls observe() and recall() against one .engram file: SQLite plus sqlite-vec, in-process, nothing between the agent and its memory. Inside: episodic and semantic memory, bitemporal facts, spreading activation and Ebbinghaus decay. The only calls that leave the machine are reflect() and compress(), through a pluggable LLM adapter, and even those can route through TokenFuse; the embedding model downloads once, about 64 MB, on first use.

### Single file, embeddable

One .engram file on SQLite plus sqlite-vec: no server, no Docker, no config file. pip install, two lines of Python, and the first memory is on disk. A write takes a median of 8 ms (200 writes on an Apple Silicon Mac, 2026-10-13) because no LLM sits in the write path.

### reflect() distills facts

A background reflection loop groups recent episodes and asks an LLM to extract subject-predicate-object facts, each with a confidence score. Every fact keeps a why() chain: which episodes produced it, which run extracted it, which model, at what confidence.

### Facts that know their dates

Every fact carries two timelines: when it was true in reality, and when the system learned it. When Ivan changes jobs the old fact is closed with an end date, never deleted.

**Two timelines, and the questions only two can answer.** A fact in Engram carries `valid_from` and `valid_to`, which say when it was true in reality, and `recorded_at` and `superseded_at`, which say when the system learned it and when it stopped believing it. Those are different clocks, and collapsing them into one is how a memory quietly starts lying.

With both, you can ask what the agent believed as of March and get March's answer rather than today's. That is the difference between an audit you can defend and a database that only ever shows the present. A support agent that promised a refund policy in March should be judged against the policy it knew in March.

It also makes correction safe. When Ivan moves from Acme to Globex, the old fact is closed with an end date and the new one opens; nothing is overwritten, so the reason the agent said what it said in March survives the correction.

### A person's own fact outranks a model's

A fact is the person's own when its provenance is `user` and it was not written quarantined. A reflection pass whose extraction is not the person's own no longer closes such a fact by recency, and neither does a refutation that is not. The newer fact is recorded beside it, `contradictions()` lists the pair, and the existing `contradiction_found` event, with the same two data keys, names both. `reflect()` does not count that conflict in `contradictions_resolved`, because nothing was resolved. `assert_fact()` never closed anything and still does not; it now emits the same event for such a conflict. Between two facts that are both the person's own, the newer one still wins.

A fact stamps its provenance when it is written, so the protection does not end when its source episodes are forgotten, compressed or pruned. `reflect()` stamps a fact with the least trusted provenance of all the episodes in its window, so a window that mixes `user` and `external` episodes yields facts that are not the person's own. Engram stores the provenance the caller declares and does not verify it. Over MCP a caller cannot claim `user`, and a fact written through MCP is `unknown`, so it can never be a person's fact.

### A fact can be refuted without being erased

`refute_fact()` closes a fact and keeps it: `valid_to` and `superseded_at` are set, `refuted_by` is recorded, and there is no replacement, so `timeline()` and `as_of` keep what was believed before. Every fact derived from it, at any depth and across agents, gets the refuted fact's id in `undermined_by` and stays active. A private fact of another agent is marked too and is not named in the result. `assert_fact(derived_from=[...])` records the derivation. Refuting twice changes nothing, and the person's own fact can be refuted only by the person. `forget_fact()` is unchanged: erasure stays the owner's right, and refutation is the path that keeps history.

The store moves one schema step, recorded in `PRAGMA user_version`, with three nullable columns on facts: `provenance`, `refuted_by` and `undermined_by`. The step is idempotent and rewrites no row, and export and import carry the columns.

### Three ways to recall

Cosine vectors for meaning, BM25 blended with vectors when exact terms matter, and spreading activation that walks the entity graph.

**Three retrieval modes, one call.** One API, three modes, because one retrieval strategy does not fit every question.

**cosine** is pure vector similarity: good when the query means the same thing as the memory but says it with different words.

**hybrid** blends SQLite's FTS5 BM25 with cosine, normalised, for when exact terms carry the meaning. Identifiers, error codes and product names are precisely the tokens an embedding smooths away.

**spreading** starts from cosine nearest neighbours as seeds, then walks the entity graph along Hebbian edges that co-access reinforces, with activation decaying per hop. Results rank on similarity, activation and importance together. This is the mode that surfaces Project X for a question about Ivan when the two texts share no words at all, because the graph, not the wording, connects them.

### GDPR forget, scoped

Erasure is real and targeted: one episode, one fact, or everything about a person. Since 2.2.1 an agent can forget only its own episodes; erasing a person reaches every agent in the file, on purpose.

**What erasure actually removes.** `forget()` erases a single episode. `forget_fact()` erases one semantic fact. `forget_entity()` cascades: the episodes about that person, the facts derived from them, and the graph edges that made them findable, and it reports how many of each it deleted.

That cascade is the part most stores get wrong. Deleting the raw text while leaving a derived fact and a graph edge behind means the person is still reachable by association, which is exactly what an erasure request was about.

Since 2.2.1 `forget()` is agent-scoped: in a shared store, one agent cannot reach into another agent's episodes by id. A delete that crosses that line is not a convenience, it is a way for one tenant to destroy another's evidence.

Two erasures cross it on purpose. Facts and entities are shared by every agent in the file, so `forget_fact()` removes a fact for all of them. And `forget_entity()` reaches every agent's episodes about that person, because a request to be forgotten is about the person, not about one agent's copy.

### MCP server, stdio only

engram-mcp speaks stdio: no network listener, no port to guard. Claude Desktop, Claude Code and Cursor get remember, recall, why and forget against the same store with zero integration code. reflect() is deliberately not exposed to clients.

## Recall is one part of a memory.

Engram keeps a vector index in-process. It also keeps when each fact was true, where it came from, and whether two beliefs disagree.

| Question an agent asks | What answers it |
|---|---|
| Find what I mean, not only what I typed | Hybrid recall: BM25 and cosine, blended |
| What was true in March, before we knew better | Bitemporal facts: valid time and recorded time |
| Why do you believe that | why(), a chain back to the source episodes |
| These two things disagree | Contradictions detected and recorded as events |
| Whose word counts when two disagree | A person's own fact is never closed by a lower provenance |
| That is wrong, but keep the history | refute_fact(): closed, not erased, with derived facts marked |
| Reach what the match is connected to | Spreading activation over Hebbian edges |
| Stay useful instead of growing | Importance decay, and reflection prunes the bottom |
| Forget a person | Targeted erase by episode, entity or fact |
| Run it anywhere | In-process, one file, no server and no key to write |

## Three runs against real Claude, and what they settled.

Before any of this was published, Engram's Anthropic adapter was run against a real Claude model on real infrastructure, three times, on three different box topologies. Until then the reflection pipeline had only ever seen fixtures and a deterministic stub, which is a comfortable thing to test against and proves very little.

| Run | Episodes in | Facts out | Contradictions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Three-node loopback cluster | 5 | 10 | 0 |
| Cross-machine, four separate hosts | 5 | 10, identical to the first run | 0 |
| Enriched multi-agent campaign | 8 | 17, confidence 0.80 to 0.95 | 0 |

What that settles: the reflection prompt and its parsing hold up against real model variance, not just the tidy stub output CI uses; confidence scoring is stable across three independent runs on different infrastructure; and `why()` traces a belief back to the exact observations it came from on real-model output, not only in unit tests. No contradiction was missed in any run.

The method mattered as much as the result. The boxes were disposable and deleted after each run, the code arrived as a git archive with no repository history and no secrets in it, the API key lived in a root-only file and was revoked afterwards, and the service bound to `127.0.0.1` only. Nothing from those runs is still standing.

## The plane that remembers.

Engram is the knowledge plane of the stack. Its own reflect() calls can point base_url at [TokenFuse](https://it-rat.com/services/tokenfuse.html), so even thinking has a budget. Every memory_written, reflection_run, contradiction_found and memory_forgotten goes out as an agent-event on the same NDJSON bus [Idryx](https://it-rat.com/services/idryx.html) correlates into the identity graph. The envelope they travel in is the [Agent Passport contract](https://it-rat.com/services/platform.html): one spec, every service, including this one.

Provenance is one of the questions a governed fleet has to answer; the others are in [AI agent governance](https://it-rat.com/ai-agent-governance.html).

## Engram ships as a package.

```
pip install engdbram
```

Install it from [the repository](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/engram#readme), where the command lives beside the version it belongs to.

The PyPI name is engdbram (the plain name was taken); the import stays `from engram import Engram`. Your first memory needs zero API keys: an LLM enters the picture only when you ask for reflect().

### How this one ships

No per-platform binaries here either: this one is a Python library you import, so the package index is the download. The install command lives in the repository, next to the version it resolves.

## What changed in v3.0.0.

Engram's own list for 1 to 15 October 2026 is in [the stack's changes](https://it-rat.com/changes-2026-10.html#engram).

### Where each memory came from

Released as v3.0.0 on 2026-10-18. The library records a source for every observation: user for what the person typed, tool for what a tool returned, and external for anything else. Recall returns the source with each result, and why() reports the least trusted source behind a fact. Over MCP the server sets the most a write may carry, which defaults to external, so a caller cannot claim user. A server started with an agent id serves that agent alone; one started without serves the whole file and says so on stderr. A fact is private to its writer unless it is shared.

## What changed in November

| shipped in | what it does |
|---|---|
| v3.1.0 | A person's own fact is never closed by a lower provenance: a model's extraction or refutation is recorded beside it, and contradictions() lists the pair. |
| v3.1.0 | refute_fact() closes a fact without erasing it, and marks every fact derived from it as undermined. |
| v3.1.0 | The documents no longer claim procedural memory: the store never modelled it, and remember(kind="procedural") is refused. |
| v3.1.0 | A fact stamps its provenance when it is written, so a person's fact stays the person's after its source episodes are forgotten or pruned. The store moves to schema generation 2 with three nullable columns on facts, and assert_fact takes provenance and derived_from. |

## What it does not do, and what is still open.

- The server cannot see what an agent read outside engram. A session turns untrusted when recall or why returns a memory that is not the user's own or is quarantined, when the caller labels its input or passes read_untrusted, or when the server is started with the untrusted flag.

- Procedural memory is not part of the store: `remember(kind="procedural")` is refused.

- Refutation emits no event, because the shared event contract has no type for it. The row it leaves in the store is the record. An older Engram that opens a migrated file ignores the new columns.

- reflect() is deliberately not exposed to MCP clients.

- Agent events (memory_written, reflection_run, contradiction_found, memory_forgotten) are opt-in and off by default.

- The only calls that leave the machine are reflect() and compress(), through a pluggable LLM adapter, plus the one-time download of the embedding model on first use.

- No per-platform binaries: this one is a Python library you import, so the package index is the download.

- Nothing from the three live runs is still standing: the boxes were disposable and deleted after each run.

## Back to the room.

The [Engram room](https://it-rat.com/services/engram.html) has the simulation, the drawing and the common questions, and [the guides index](https://it-rat.com/guides.html) has the field itself.

<!-- https://it-rat.com/platform-guide.html -->

# Platform guide

> How the Agent Passport contract works, how to run the stack on a laptop, one box or a cluster, and what it does not claim, in full.

The [Platform room](https://it-rat.com/services/platform.html) keeps the simulation, the drawing of the envelope and the common questions. This guide keeps the rest of what the room used to say: what the contract pins down, the full text for running the stack on a laptop, on one box or on a cluster, the downloads, and what the contract does not claim.

- [At a glance](https://it-rat.com/platform-guide.html#overview)

- [How it works](https://it-rat.com/platform-guide.html#how-it-works)

- [Running it](https://it-rat.com/platform-guide.html#run)

- [On your own infrastructure](https://it-rat.com/platform-guide.html#deploy)

- [The contract for your own agent](https://it-rat.com/platform-guide.html#try-it)

- [Where it sits](https://it-rat.com/platform-guide.html#where-it-sits)

- [What changed](https://it-rat.com/platform-guide.html#changes)

- [Limits](https://it-rat.com/platform-guide.html#limits)

## The contract at a glance.

- **The boring layer that makes a dozen services one system:** a three-repo platform under the services.

- **Passport schema:** v0.1 and v1.0, stable. **Event envelope:** v0.1 to v1.0, NDJSON.

- **Go binding:** agent-stack-go, latest.

- **Conformance:** agent-conform, for files and as a chain watcher.

- **As code:** taipan_budget, taipan_unit_budget, taipan_agent_passport, taipan_wardryx_policy.

- **Licence:** Apache-2.0.

### What it is

Under the services sits a three-repo platform. agent-passport is the spec: one agent:// identifier, one Passport document, one event envelope. agent-stack-go is the Go binding, with the agent-conform checker. terraform-provider-taipan turns budgets, passports and policies into PR-reviewed code. No shared runtime, no shared database; adopting it is a naming agreement plus a few optional fields.

## Boring on purpose. Load-bearing anyway.

### One envelope, end to end.

The room's simulation is labeled as one: a replay of the envelope's normal day. A passport is issued, the planes emit their own event types into one NDJSON stream, two schema versions ride side by side, and agent-conform validates the whole stream at the end. Exit 0.

### Everything meets at the envelope.

Fifteen registered sources write one shape: twelve onto one NDJSON bus, and heraldyx, scopyx and the keyryx witness into files of their own (dashed). Five required fields, six optional ones. Five consumers read it back: the agent-conform CLI validates against embedded copies of the canonical JSON Schemas and, on the box, re-checks every stream's hash chain and writes what it finds to a stream of its own, which is how it is also one of the fifteen sources; Idryx folds events into the identity graph, TokenFuse Cloud files them into evidence packs, Heraldyx mails the operator about the few worth interrupting them for, and Trailryx seals the stream into a hash-chained record. The keyryx witness also reads every stream; its findings go to a file of their own, off the bus, which Heraldyx mails and the Genaryx console shows as incidents through a read-only mount. On the right, the part your platform team owns: budgets, passports and policies as Terraform resources.

### The passport

One agent, one URI: agent://trust-domain/path, at most 255 bytes, aligned with SPIFFE without requiring it. The document behind the ID names an owner, a runtime and one of six attestation methods. The delegation chain is ordered root first, acyclic, and capped at 32 entries.

### The envelope

Five required fields: schema, ts, source, type, agent_id. Four versions stay live by design: v0.1 with a closed source enum, v0.2 with an open string, v0.3 adding a self-declared, claimed agent_id, and v1.0, which is v0.3's shape under the 1.0 compatibility promise. The passport document has two, v0.1 and v1.0. Event types live in a per-source registry, so tokenfuse can add a type without asking engram.

### The Go binding

agent-stack-go ships four packages: passport, event, chain and delegation (the RFC 8693 delegation token and offline verification of an agent's own access token). It ships passport.Parse, an append-only event.Writer and chain.Validate. passport and chain need only the standard library; event adds one dependency, gowebpki/jcs, for the RFC 8785 canonical JSON its hash chain is computed over. Since v2.0.0 the module path is github.com/TAIPANBOX/agent-stack-go/v2, and a stream file is created with mode 0640. It is the same validation Idryx runs on ingest: a passport that parses in your pipeline parses in the graph.

### agent-conform

A standalone conformance CLI with the canonical JSON Schemas embedded. Files are classified by their own schema field, and unrecognized content is a FAIL, never silently skipped. Exit 0 or exit 1; it has already caught a real 63-versus-64 hex character prev_hash defect. Since agent-stack-go v1.1.0 it also runs on the box as `watch-dir`: it re-checks every stream's hash chain and writes `chain_broken` (high), `chain_unchained` (low) or `chain_restarted` (medium, or high when no signed resume checkpoint explains it) to its own stream; with `-checkpoints` and `-checkpoint-keys` it also checks each stream's signed checkpoint. It exits 2 on a usage or I/O error. It ships as a signed, distroless image, `ghcr.io/taipanbox/agent-conform`, and runs by default every five minutes on the single box and every fifteen on a cluster.

### Governance as code

Four Terraform resources: taipan_budget, taipan_unit_budget, taipan_agent_passport, taipan_wardryx_policy. Run budgets, business-unit budgets, passports and policies get PRs, plans and diffs like everything else, and edits made out of band surface on the next plan. Where the API has no delete, the provider says so instead of pretending.

### Honest scope

The provider is published on the Terraform Registry as `TAIPANBOX/taipan`: a normal `required_providers` block and `terraform init` pull it, GPG-verified, no build-from-source needed. The passport is metadata, not a token, and the spec is not an authentication protocol. Small claims, kept.

### One contract, shared by every service.

Every event carries one agent_id and an explicit schema field. The canonical JSON Schemas ship with agent-conform, which checks a file against them. Anyone can implement the contract; it is Apache-2.0.

## Run the live stack locally.

Two ways in, and they are for different machines. On your own laptop the sandbox builds from source and binds loopback only. On a Linux box you own, one line pulls the published images and the whole governed stack is up in under two minutes.

### On a box you own, fastest

```
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TAIPANBOX/stack-single/main/install.sh | bash
```

Nothing is compiled: every plane is pulled from the public registry at a pinned version. Measured on 2026-09-13 on a fresh 2-vCPU cloud machine, from that line to a console answering on loopback: **109 seconds**, with every one of the installer's own checks green; on 2026-09-17, on a mini PC that already had Docker, **61 seconds** for the first run (exit 1: 22 checks ok, and one that fails by construction, since it probed loopback whatever the bind address was; fixed by stack-single #59) and 36 seconds for the second, with the same 22 checks ok. It needs root on Debian or Ubuntu, and docker and git; it comes back after a reboot (measured once, on 2026-09-17, on a box whose gateway sat on a tailnet address: the first reboot lost the gateway until the installer learned to order Docker after the tunnel, the second brought it back on its own); and it is reachable by agents running anywhere else, which the same day proved from two clouds at once.

### On your laptop, no Docker

```
git clone https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/stack-up
cd stack-up && ./up.sh
```

The sandbox, and it builds from source on purpose: nothing but your own compilers touches it. That is the cost as well as the point, so it wants Rust, Go, Node and Python already installed. Measured on 2026-09-01 from an empty build cache: **221 seconds** to a working dashboard. A cold run with both optional planes took **325 seconds** on 2026-09-13. Binds `127.0.0.1` only, stops on Ctrl-C, keeps nothing.

### What the first run actually does

Open the link it prints and you are looking at your own local money plane, live, with a short demo dataset already in it. Point an agent's OpenAI base URL at the gateway to feed it your own.

It builds and starts the stack's long-running services from source. Those are TokenFuse's gateway, cloud and dashboard, plus Wardryx, Idryx and Scopyx, and Keyryx (custody and witness): eight ports on loopback, as the stack-up README's port table lists them. Heraldyx is pinned to file mode there, writing what it would have mailed rather than mailing it. Trailryx is built and wired as a sealing routine rather than a port. Engram, Qryx, Verdryx and Mockryx are deliberately not servers: they are libraries and one-shot CLIs, installed into your home directory and started when you want them, each with its own try-it on its page. The delegation plane, the FinOps console and the typed-answers service stay behind a flag, `--with-delegation`, `--with-finops` and `--with-typed`, because one needs an issuer to trust, one is a different product and one is optional.

Press Ctrl-C and it stops clean, with no orphaned processes.

### What comes up

| gateway | :4100 · budgets |
|---|---|
| cloud + dashboard | :8080 · :3000 |
| wardryx | :8090 · policy |
| idryx | :8081 · identity |
| every bind | 127.0.0.1 only |

git, Rust, Node and Python; Go adds the policy and identity planes. macOS or Linux. A sandbox to try the stack, not a production deployment.

## The stack is a control plane. Your agents can be anywhere.

Nothing here has to sit next to the agents it governs. An agent points its model endpoint at the gateway and asks the policy plane before it acts, so it can run in EKS, in GKE, in a CI job or on a laptop while the stack runs once, on infrastructure you own. That is the whole deployment question: where the control plane lives, not where the work does.

### One box

The shape the stack is actually built for: the planes share a filesystem, which is how they talk. One script puts all of it on a box you own, and it comes up closed.

| install | one script |
|---|---|
| gateway | host loopback, published only on purpose |
| every other plane | no host port at all |
| the console | over WireGuard the box issues |
| images | the same as the cluster path |

**The commands, and the checks that have to fail to pass.**

```
git clone https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/stack-single
cd stack-single && ./install.sh
GATEWAY_BIND=0.0.0.0 ./install.sh
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://<your box>:4100
```

It comes up closed: the gateway lands on the host's loopback and everything else has no host port at all, so a box that just ran an install script is not serving an enforcement plane to the internet because nobody typed anything. One variable publishes the gateway when you mean to. Same images and same service names as the cluster deployment, because Docker resolves `http://wardryx:8090` exactly the way a Kubernetes Service did.

[The sandbox above](https://it-rat.com/platform-guide.html#run) is this shape already, with one deliberate difference: it binds loopback only, so nothing on it is reachable by an agent on another machine. That is correct for trying it and wrong for serving a fleet.

It also brings up a WireGuard server for the people who run the box, so the console is reached over a tunnel it issues rather than an SSH forward you keep alive by hand. That is the one port here published on purpose: WireGuard answers nothing at all without a valid key, unlike an HTTP plane.

It ends by verifying itself, and three of its checks have to FAIL to pass: the money plane and the policy plane must not answer on the host, and a gateway bound to one address must not answer on loopback. Three more test the credential rather than the port, because a plane with a malformed key spec starts cleanly, stays reachable, and authenticates nobody. One more reads back the rule Docker actually wrote for port 4100 instead of trusting the variable meant to set it, because a default that says loopback while the port says otherwise is worse than no default at all.

### Or a Kubernetes cluster

For teams whose answer to everything is a cluster. One script brings up k3s across your nodes with the CNI, storage and hardening the stack actually needs, then the workload applies from plain manifests.

| install | one script |
|---|---|
| proven on | Hetzner, AWS and GCP |
| what it buys | high availability |
| what it costs | a ReadWriteMany volume |
| traps | 159 documented, with whose fault each was |

**The commands, and the one thing a cluster costs you.**

```
git clone https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/stack-k8s
cd stack-k8s && ./deploy.sh --servers ... --hcloud-token ... --trust-domain <your domain>
```

Both paths are one command, and both ask what they need before the long part rather than failing on it afterwards. So the trade is not convenience. Kubernetes buys high availability and costs you the one thing a single box gets for free: the planes couple through a shared event log, so a cluster needs a ReadWriteMany volume for it.

That trade, and every other thing that bites, are documented in the repositories rather than discovered by you. The same manifests came up on six clusters across Hetzner, AWS and GCP, and exactly one line of Kubernetes configuration differs between the three: Calico has to encapsulate unconditionally on GCP, because a GCE VPC routes every packet by destination and a pod address matches no route. Every trap we hit is written down and already fixed in the files.

## The contract for an agent of your own.

```
# install: https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/agent-stack-go#install
agent-conform passport.json events.ndjson
```

This installs nothing of the stack: it is the contract itself, for an agent of your own. Exit 0 means every file and every NDJSON line conforms; exit 1 means at least one did not. That is the whole interface.

### agent-conform, every platform

Every one of those addresses always serves the newest release, so a link saved today still works after the next one. The asset names carry no version, which is what makes that true; the version lives inside the binary, where `agent-conform -version` reads it back.

## The layer every other page stands on.

Every other page on this site is a producer or a consumer of this contract. [TokenFuse](https://it-rat.com/services/tokenfuse.html) pushes its incident taxonomy through the envelope verbatim, zero renaming. [Wardryx](https://it-rat.com/services/wardryx.html) answers policy_deny in schema v0.2. [Engram](https://it-rat.com/services/engram.html) writes memory_written and reflection_run into the same stream, and [Idryx](https://it-rat.com/services/idryx.html) reads everything back into one identity graph, checking passports with the same passport.Parse this platform ships. Different rooms, one grammar.

What the contract is for, in practice: [AI agent governance](https://it-rat.com/ai-agent-governance.html) and the controls it lets independent tools share.

## What changed.

The platform's own list for 1 to 15 October 2026, the agent-stack-go releases, agent-passport and the Terraform provider on main, is in [the stack's changes](https://it-rat.com/changes-2026-10.html#platform).

## What the contract does not claim, and what the sandbox leaves out.

- The passport is metadata, not a token, and the spec is not an authentication protocol.

- Where the API has no delete, the provider says so instead of pretending.

- The laptop sandbox is a sandbox to try the stack, not a production deployment. It binds loopback only, so nothing on it is reachable by an agent on another machine.

- In the sandbox Heraldyx is pinned to file mode, writing what it would have mailed rather than mailing it.

- The delegation plane, the FinOps console and the typed-answers service stay behind a flag: `--with-delegation`, `--with-finops` and `--with-typed`.

- Engram, Qryx, Verdryx and Mockryx are deliberately not servers: they are libraries and one-shot CLIs.

- The one-box install coming back after a reboot was measured once, on 2026-09-17.

## Back to the room.

The [Platform room](https://it-rat.com/services/platform.html) has the simulation, the drawing and the common questions, and [the guides index](https://it-rat.com/guides.html) has the field itself.
